items.title: Gold Wavers Around $4,300 as Traders Await Fed Rate Decision
body: Gold held a decline as increasing disruptions to oil flows from the Middle East reinforced expectations the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates as soon as this week.

Bullion was trading around $4,290 an ounce, after falling more than 1% the previous session to a five-week low. The prospects of higher energy prices stoking inflation have piled pressure on the Fed to make its first rate increase in three years, with traders pricing in a 92% chance of it happening when the central bank meets in the coming days. Higher borrowing costs are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

Oil rose, after Saudi Arabia closed its East-West pipeline due to attacks last week. The halt puts at risk millions of barrels a day that were moving through it to circumvent the turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz, at a time when markets are clamoring for supply. The kingdom has yet to say how long the disruption will last and how quickly it can increase Hormuz shipments to offset the shutdown.

The 10-year Treasury yield briefly touched 5% for the first time in nearly three years on Monday on concerns over inflation and swelling government and corporate borrowing needs, which is another headwind for non-yielding bullion.

The precious metal is down more than 3% in September, after trading above $4,600 an ounce in late August, as traders repeatedly recalibrate the outlook for Fed policy. Despite the near-term headwinds, many investors are still betting that bullion will grind higher as it rediscovers its traditional value as a portfolio hedge.

Spot gold fell 0.3% to $4,288.18 an ounce at 7:48 a.m. in Singapore. Silver was down 0.2% at $63.11 an ounce, after declining 2% the day before. Platinum and palladium edged lower. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was stable after rising 0.4% the previous session.

items.title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump's Mail Ballot Curbs for Midterms
body: The US Supreme Court refused to clear the Postal Service to enforce new restrictions on mail-in ballots for the congressional midterm elections, rebuffing the Trump administration’s request to intervene after several states launched early voting.

The justices’ decision on Monday came after North Carolina and Alabama began mailing thousands of ballots to voters and many more states prepared to do the same in the coming days. The order followed last-minute legal wrangling and uncertainty about whether states would have to suddenly upend months of planning for the Nov. 3 midterms, when Republicans are defending their slim majority in Congress.

The Supreme Court denied the Justice Department’s request to lift a Boston federal judge’s order that barred the Postal Service from making its new mail-in ballot rules mandatory through the November contests.

In the brief, unsigned order, the court held that the Trump administration was unlikely to win the merits of its challenge to the lower court’s injunction and that officials failed to show that they had a stronger case for immediately reviving the rules ahead of the midterms. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented.
Read More: Fight Over Trump’s Mail Ballot Curbs Runs Into Midterm Deadlines

The legal fight over whether the agency can ultimately adopt the controversial rules for future election cycles may still continue. A federal judge in Washington entered a fresh injunction blocking the contested rules on Sept. 13, however, delivering another setback to the administration.

In a short concurring opinion on Monday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that “there is at least a fair prospect” that the Postal Service ultimately will prove that it has legal authority to adopt the contested rules. But he said it would be unlawfully “arbitrary and capricious” for the agency to rush to implement them for the midterms “because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”

Alito, joined by Thomas, wrote in the dissent that the challengers’ “Hail Mary pass is unlikely to be successfully completed here” because “the Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail.”

He wrote that he took “seriously” the concerns raised about the ability of states to upend their midterm election plans to comply with the new rules “but it is not enough to convince me” to side against the government. Alito pointed to the group of GOP-led states that joined the legal fight to support the administration and blamed the challengers for pursuing a strategy that he said caused more delays.

A coalition of Democratic state officials and voting rights groups sued to challenge the Postal Service’s plan, arguing that permitting “massive changes” so late in the election cycle would be “profoundly disruptive” and carried a high risk of errors that would disenfranchise voters.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement that the Supreme Court’s order “is a victory for our democracy and a powerful affirmation of the rule of law.”

Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project, said in a statement that “the president does not run our elections, the Postal Service does not get to decide whose ballot counts, and voters — not the White House — will decide November’s elections.”
Spokespeople for the Justice Department and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The contested rules would require states to meet revised envelope design standards and submit information on the voters set to receive ballots to a new centralized portal. Postal authorities would be empowered to return election mail to states if envelopes didn’t feature a barcode that matched the voter information on file.

The American Postal Workers Union, AFL-CIO, which represents nearly 200,000 postal employees nationwide, filed a brief urging the Supreme Court to leave the injunction in place, warning that there isn’t enough time to train clerks to implement the new rules. The union said that the “hurried launch of this unprecedented system, at odds with the normal workflow of the Postal Service, will inevitably grind the operation of the postal system to a halt.”

The Justice Department argued that the rules represented “modest” changes to how election mail is handled and that the administration had an interest in uniformly enforcing the rules nationwide. The Postal Service adopted the rules after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March directing various federal agencies to play a larger role in ensuring only eligible citizens can vote. Studies have repeatedly found that noncitizen voting is rare.

The Supreme Court’s latest order isn’t a final ruling on the merits of allegations that the Postal Service’s actions are an unlawful intrusion into state power to run elections under the US Constitution. By declining to let the agency enforce the rules right away, the court rejected the administration’s stance that its interests in uniformly carrying out its policy nationwide outweighed harms that many states and voting rights advocates said they would face.

North Carolina’s early deadline to start mailing ballots on Sept. 4 was widely seen as an unofficial but critical deadline for courts to resolve whether the Postal Service could compel states to follow new rules if they want the agency to deliver their ballots.

More than a dozen states are preparing to mail ballots by the middle of September. Shortly before the Justice Department took the fight to the Supreme Court, the Postal Service had told a lower-court judge that the portal wasn’t ready yet for states to use.

The Supreme Court’s order came after a federal appeals court late last week denied the administration’s request to halt the injunction from US District Judge Indira Talwani. The appellate judges wrote that Talwani “made detailed findings about the chaos and widespread disenfranchisement that would occur” between now and Nov. 3 if the contested rules took effect right away.
The case is US Postal Service v. California, 26A305, US Supreme Court.

items.title: Singapore's Air Worst Since 2019 as Haze Blankets Region
body: Singapore was shrouded in haze on Tuesday, with smoke from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia raising islandwide pollution to levels that pose a health risk.

All five regions of the city-state recorded unhealthy air-quality levels, the first time that’s happened since September 2019, according to the National Environment Agency. Singapore’s air currently ranks among the 10 most polluted cities in the world, according to IQAir data, with the capitals of Malaysia and Indonesia also among the top spots.

Indonesia often battles wildfires during its annual dry season, but hotspots this year have been higher than normal. There were more than 9,000 recorded in August, the most for the month in data going back to 2015, and more than 7,000 have been recorded so far in September, according to the Forestry Ministry’s fire-monitoring platform SiPongi.

The situation is being exacerbated by the strengthening El Niño weather pattern, which causes drier weather in much of the region. Little immediate relief is expected from the weather, with dry conditions expected to persist across much of the south of Southeast Asia in the near term, according to the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre.
“The hotspot and haze situation in the region is expected to remain escalated with a continued risk of transboundary smoke haze,” the centre said in its latest forecast.

Air quality in parts of Indonesia’s Kalimantan and Sumatra regions, where the fires are concentrated, was at dangerous or very unhealthy levels as of Tuesday, government data show. Malaysia has also suffered, with choking haze in late August prompting the government to move its leader’s annual National Day speech to an indoor venue. A state of emergency was declared for part of Sarawak state earlier this month.

A hotspot is defined as a location where satellites detect an elevated surface temperature, indicating a potential fire. Slash-and-burn methods used to clear farmland have previously been linked to the fires, and dry undergrowth can also ignite carbon-rich peatland, which can smolder for long periods and be difficult to extinguish.

Smoke plumes from fires in Kalimantan drifted toward Singapore because of a shift in winds, alongside smoke haze from Sumatra, the National Environment Agency said on Monday. The agency expects the haze to persist over the next 24 hours, with air quality ranging from high-moderate to mid-unhealthy conditions.

Indonesia’s forestry ministry said in a statement that this year’s surge in forest fires was due to a combination of El Niño-driven dry weather and human-caused ignition, adding that each incident must be investigated individually. The country has expanded aerial firefighting operations, including with helicopters provided by Japan, it said. Malaysia has also offered assistance to tackle the blazes.
Read More: El Niño May Force Major Drop in Indonesian Nickel Production

The fires in Indonesia add to a bad year for wildfires globally, with parts of Europe and North America also reeling from recent blazes. The current El Niño has a 75% chance of becoming “a historic event,” surpassing all records dating back to 1950, the US Climate Prediction Center said last week.

There may be a slight uptick in rainfall in parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan next week, which could temporarily ease fire risks, according to Takahisa Nishikawa, senior decision support meteorologist at Atmospheric G2. “This may provide some relief, although it does not yet look like a widespread or sustained wetting pattern, and forecast confidence is lower at that range,” he said.

The dry weather is also affecting the mining and agriculture industries in Indonesia. A nickel producer there said on Tuesday it was halting the ramp-up of one of its processing plants due to water shortages, while the country’s biggest nickel complex warned earlier this month that it might have to slash output for the same reason. Palm oil production is also expected to take a hit as plantations struggle to apply fertilizer.

items.title: Firmus data center IPO, Whyalla steelworks, Trump AI
body: OpenAI and Anthropic might be talking about slowing down, but Firmus Technologies is going full speed ahead.

The Australian data center company, which started life as a bitcoin miner, is looking to raise as much as US$5 billion in an initial public offering in Australia by the end of October, Bloomberg reported on Monday. If the long-teased event happens, it will be one of Australia’s largest ever IPOs.

Firmus is not alone with companies along the AI supply chain undertaking massive fundraising around the world in recent months. A number of US and Chinese AI companies are looking at potentially huge IPOs before the end of 2026.

The Firmus IPO plan comes as Australia has become more and more appealing for companies looking to build data centers. In August, Jane Street backed Firmus as “helping build the infrastructure needed to support that next generation of AI,” joining groups like Coatue Management in a fundraising round that valued the company at more than US$10.5 billion.

Still, the outlook for the AI industry is not without uncertainty. The leadership of two of America’s AI giants have called for a slower development of new models over safety concerns, after reports that there was a non-zero chance the new technology could wipe out humanity.
OpenAI has even deferred its own IPO beyond 2026, saying that it is focusing on safety for the moment.
All eyes will be on Firmus in the lead up to the listing (and beyond) to see whether this Australian piece of the AI boom remains on track. - Ben Westcott, Melbourne reporter

Australia’s Whyalla steelworks will shut its 60-year-old blast furnace and halt steelmaking, with the potential loss of as many as 600 jobs as administrators look for a new owner for the troubled operation. KordaMentha, the administrator of the beleaguered South Australian site, said Monday that a months-long effort to restore the aging plant had failed.

Liquefied natural gas prices — which have surged since the start of the US-Iran war — are unlikely to drop in the short term, according to Chevron’s Australia president. “I have a hard time seeing the prices come down” in the next six months or so, Balaji Krishnamurthy said in a Bloomberg TV interview on Monday.

Investors are snapping up New Zealand bonds, betting sluggish economic growth will keep the central bank cautious on interest-rate hikes and extend the debt’s outperformance over global peers. The bullish bets come after New Zealand bond yields jumped to multiyear highs on Friday as a surge in oil prices fueled wagers of an October rate hike.

One Nation is proposing to cut the number of temporary migrants by about 750,000 over three years, in a controversial policy aiming to capitalize on discontent over cost-of-living pressures and a housing squeeze. Under One Nation’s proposal, which was criticized by business figures and both sides of the political divide, net overseas migration would turn negative over the three years, according to Hanson.

New Zealand tourist arrivals hit a record high for July, with overseas visitor numbers for the month finally exceeding pre-pandemic levels, aided by a surge in Australians cashing in on a favorable exchange rate.

Australian miner GM3 is gauging investor sentiment for a possible bond issue to refinance a $600 million private credit loan, adding to a list of borrowers turning to public debt markets to try to lower funding costs. The company has met investors this month to pitch a potential bond deal, Bloomberg reported on Monday.

A selloff in chipmakers dragged down stocks as leaders of AI giants proposed slowing the technology’s development, with elevated oil prices also weighing on sentiment. The rout in powerhouses like Nvidia and Broadcom sent a semiconductor gauge down by 5.9%, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.8%. Bank of America led losses in financial shares on chief Brian Moynihan’s trading revenue warning. Meanwhile Brent crude topped $105, raising concern about inflation before the Federal Reserve decision.

AI developers including Anthropic and OpenAI are clashing with the Trump administration over their calls for an industrywide slowdown in artificial intelligence development. In a social media post Monday, US President Donald Trump pushed back against any idea of new AI guardrails and criticized Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call for restraint, while the Chinese government accused the AI companies of “fearmongering.”

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto removed Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa just a year after his appointment, replacing a policymaker whose unorthodox approach and push for more spending had unsettled investors. Prabowo appointed Deputy Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara as the new finance chief.

Rather than rogue AI agents supposedly killing us all, Beijing has a more immediate nightmare: That the technology could help humans tear society apart first, writes Bloomberg Opinion’s Catherine Thorbecke.
• No major events scheduled.

Tragically, it is a story that Australia know well. Hundreds of workers across the US have recently sued the manufacturers of artificial quartz slabs, often popular as kitchen countertops, accusing them of peddling a needlessly toxic product and misrepresenting its risks. California’s Department of Public Health, the agency tracking these cases the most systematically, has identified more than 600 silicosis diagnoses in-state that are linked to artificial (sometimes called “engineered”) stone. Australia banned their use in 2024 - now some officials in the US are pushing for the same.

items.title: UK to Gain From Replacing Oil Windfall Tax Early, Lobby Says
body: The UK could raise an additional £15 billion ($20 billion) in tax revenue from oil and gas production over the next decade if Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government brought forward its new fiscal regime to next year, according to an industry lobby group.

Replacing the UK’s windfall tax with a permanent price-triggered mechanism in 2027, rather than waiting until March 2030 as currently planned, would boost investment and production, supporting employment in the industry, Offshore Energies UK said on Tuesday.
That could bring in £2.4 billion more in taxes on the oil and gas industry through 2035, with a further £12.6 billion from additional payroll taxes, according to the group’s annual economic report.

Growing the UK’s tax revenue has become a key issue for the government amid rising borrowing costs, uncertainty over the new prime minister’s spending plans and concerns about inflation triggered by the Iran war. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey may face some difficult choices in his debut budget scheduled for the end of October.

“These additional revenues will provide the Exchequer with greater flexibility, offering sufficient funding to eliminate fuel poverty across the UK or support household adoption of low-carbon technologies,” Ben Ward, market intelligence manager at OEUK, told reporters on Monday.

The current windfall tax, called the Energy Profits Levy, was introduced in 2022 by the previous Conservative government after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sent energy prices soaring. It was extended and increased both by that administration and when the Labour Party came to power in 2024.

The industry has blamed the EPL and Labour’s ban on new exploration drilling for a downturn in North Sea oil and gas investment. Several companies have reassessed their UK activities and opted to sell, merge or scale back operations.
BP Plc, the last remaining global oil major to have its own standalone North Sea business, said last month it is working to exit the area.

The UK’s aging North Sea basin needs “a competitive, progressive and stable regime that promotes investment,” OEUK said. The longer it takes to implement the Oil and Gas Revenue Levy that will eventually succeed the EPL, “the less impact fiscal change will have.”

OEUK reiterated that faster changes in the tax regime and “a pragmatic approach to licensing” that prioritizes domestic production instead of imports could unlock 111 additional projects and £50 billion of private capital investment that would almost double UK’s oil and gas production over the next 25 years.

“Our operators have clearly shown a willingness to invest, with projects that could begin delivering new domestic oil and gas within months should we see an announcement” in the next budget, Ward said.

That would allow the UK to produce as much as 288 billion cubic meters of gas, or 64% more than currently projected, from 2025 to 2035, allowing the nation to cover half of its needs and significantly reduce the share of liquefied natural gas imports, which have been significantly affected by geopolitical uncertainty, according to the report.

items.title: Yuan Popularity Boost Likely Focus of Hong Kong's Five-Year Plan
body: Measures to promote wider offshore use of the yuan are likely to feature prominently in Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, along with new financial products including commodities futures, according to analysts.

Such expectations have gained traction after Chief Executive John Lee said earlier this month that the city intends to expand offshore yuan investment and risk management products, as well as broaden market access to the stock, bond and wealth management links to mainland China. Lee will unveil the economic development blueprint on Wednesday.

Hong Kong’s 2026-2030 masterplan, which is intended to align with China’s own five-year plan, comes as the Asian financial hub recovers from a post-pandemic economic slump and seeks new initiatives to transform its growth model. Cementing its status as the offshore yuan financing hub is essential to Beijing’s long-term vision of a powerful currency that is more compatible with its economic clout.

“Liquidity is not an issue anymore,” said Raymond Yeung, chief economist for Greater China at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. “We’ve got a lot of deposits in the banking sector and there’s got to be some development in terms of different types of products so that they can use the currency and allocate to some yield-generating assets denominated in yuan.”

Offshore yuan deposits in Hong Kong rose to a record 1.13 trillion yuan ($168 billion) at the end of May, before retreating slightly in the following two months, according to latest Hong Kong Monetary Authority data. The surge in cash supply has also been driving an unprecedented initial public offering boom in the city.

One area of breakthrough may be offshore yuan-denominated debt known as dim sum bonds, where “the next step that they really need to try to do” is to encourage issuance by more foreign governments and companies, Yeung said. “Yuan can also be an alternative to the US dollar and Hong Kong can play a role or explore whether this is feasible.”

Dim sum bond sales have reached 863 billion yuan so far this year, the most ever for the period, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The issuance bonanza has partly benefited from offshore yuan interest rates that are hovering around record lows.

Further expanding that bond market will be part of Hong Kong’s focus as it is important for the development of an offshore yuan yield curve, said Kelvin Lam, senior China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. “Without a benchmark, you won’t be able to see how yuan will be priced and normally it will be of much higher costs,” he said.

Elsewhere, Hong Kong is poised to develop a local commodity trading ecosystem, with the launch of more offshore yuan-denominated products to support the yuan’s global use, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Michelle Leung wrote in a note.
“Beyond the planned gold futures, offshore yuan-settled futures are expected to expand to silver and base metals traded on the London Metal Exchange,” Leung wrote.

Hong Kong began in July the trial operation of a new gold clearing system, backed by several major banks, in a key step toward its ambition to become a significant bullion-trading hub with price-setting power.

“Through building links between the LME and Qianhai Mercantile Exchange — both owned by HKEX — Hong Kong could help build a strategic bridge between global benchmark pricing and onshore commodity markets,” Leung added.

items.title: Samsung Faces Local Hedge Fund's Push to Cancel Preferred Shares
body: A South Korean hedge fund is urging Samsung Electronics Co. to buy back and cancel preferred shares, becoming one of the first shareholders to directly press for the step in hopes of boosting valuation.

In a letter to Samsung’s board and management this week, Life Asset Management called on the Korean tech giant to repurchase and cancel the shares until their price gap with common stock is erased, according to the fund’s statement. Life Asset, which didn’t disclose its Samsung stake, asked the board to review the plan during an October meeting and cancel the shares by December.

Life Asset’s call hints at more shareholder pressure coming Samsung’s way after the chipmaker recently laid out plans to return as much as 110 trillion won ($81.7 billion) to investors this year to share an AI windfall. While Samsung hasn’t fully disclosed details, company watchers have emphasized buying back preferred shares, given their steep discount to common stock.
Samsung’s preferred shares rose as much as 3.3% on Tuesday, the most in nearly a week, while the common stock gained 1%.
The Seoul-based hedge fund said as much as 73 trillion won of the shareholder return package, after special and regular dividends, should be allocated for the equity buyback.

Its preferred shares now trade at more than a 25% discount to common stock. Market watchers expect Samsung to allocate a significant portion of the buyback to preferred shares given the move will be more cost efficient.

Samsung is now in position to cancel 1.36 preferred shares for the same capital needed to cancel one common share, according to Life Asset. The fund oversees $4 billion in assets, according to its website.

Steering the buyback away from common shares would also help Samsung sidestep a rule that could force its affiliates to sell down its holdings. A Korean law bans financial affiliates from holding more than 10% of voting common stock.

items.title: Junk Debt From Asia Is Beating Bonds Almost Everywhere in 2026
body: Asian high-yield debt has emerged as a surprising global winner in bond markets as ever-cheaper money in China burnishes issuer finances.

The junk dollar bonds have returned 4.3% so far this year versus only 1.8% for US peers, and beat two dozen key global debt gauges in the period, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The Asian notes, of which Chinese borrowers account for the largest share, extended their outperformance over the last month as the gap between Chinese and US benchmark yields widened to the most on record.

The dominance of Asian junk bonds boils down to stronger fundamentals: near record-low borrowing costs in China and faster economic growth in the region that are translating into fewer defaults. Yield premiums on the securities tightened to a record low last week, even as headwinds mount with a rate hike by the Federal Reserve later this week looking more likely and the Middle East conflict pushing oil prices higher. Elsewhere, concerns about rekindled inflation have dragged a growing pool of global debt into the red.

“The vast majority of high-yield issuers in Asia are also able to access local currency funding that is comparable or cheaper than offshore US dollar funding,” said Mel Siew, head of Asia public credit at Muzinich & Co. “The current level of credit spreads does require investors to remain vigilant.”

A recent Moody’s Ratings report showed that at least for the portfolio of companies it assesses, there were 43 corporate issuer defaults in the US this year through July, 20 in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and only one in the Asia Pacific.

But the recent run-up in US bond yields and a Fed rate hike would increase pressure on Asian central banks outside China to lift rates to stem outflows, making it more expensive for firms to borrow. In some markets like Australia, where policy rates are higher than in the US, the recent collapse of Australian builder Bathla Group is a potential harbinger of wider stress.

Still, Chinese junk dollar bonds have made 0.2% so far this month, while Asian high-yield notes more broadly lost 0.4% in the period. That is still better than most other bond classes where losses have been bigger, though floating-rate leveraged loans are outperforming in September, Bloomberg-compiled data show.

“Investors may begin migrating up the credit curve, favoring higher-rated credits where yields remain attractive without requiring them to assume the same level of default risk,” said Melvin Chan, director of fixed income for Asia at UOB Asset Management.

Driving the outperformance is also a rebound in notes of stressed borrowers including Hong Kong developer New World Development Co. and a lower volume of issuance than in other regions. But there are signs of a rebound in issuance, albeit from a low base. Asia ex-Japan junk bond sales in the US currency from non-financial firms have climbed 20% to about $12 billion this year from the year-earlier period. That compares with more than $220 billion of high-yield offerings in the US.

“You could start seeing the high-yield market really picking up over the next year” in Asia for issuance, if fundamentals remain intact, said Rishi Jalan, Citigroup Inc.’s head of Asia-Pacific debt capital markets. “Tech and data centers could be a good area where you see high-yield volume.”

The lower Asian junk issuance is partly a reflection of the meltdown in China’s housing sector and the retreat of Chinese property developers that once dominated the market, selling more than $50 billion of high-yield notes at their peak in 2019. But today, even lower-rated Chinese companies can sell shorter-dated bonds at about 1.7%, a local-currency credit gauge shows, as the world’s second-biggest economy battles deflationary pressures.

Japanese issuers are also becoming an increasing part of the broader speculative-grade bond market. SoftBank Group Corp. is planning a $10 billion to $20 billion debt offering, people familiar with the matter said last month.
For some investors, Asian junk dollar notes have been overlooked and there is still room to find bargains.

“We continue to project high single-digit returns for this year and the coming years given ample opportunity,” said Dhiraj Bajaj, chief investment officer of Asia fixed income and equities at Lombard Odier Investment Managers. “Most Asia high-yield investors are perhaps too cautious and are sticking to long-established credits, which leads to a lot of value still available.”

items.title: DOJ Says Millions in Iran Oil Proceeds Laundered on Binance
body: The US Justice Department is seeking forfeiture of $61 million it says was generated from Iranian black-market oil sales and laundered through the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

In a civil forfeiture claim filed Monday, federal prosecutors in Manhattan alleged that Iran used cryptocurrency to launder more than $1.5 billion in illicit oil money. According to US prosecutors, two Chinese entities used trading accounts on Binance as part of a scheme to funnel the oil proceeds to Iran, its agents and proxies where it was used to finance military and terrorist activities.

The two entities Blessed Trust Limited and Hexa Whale Trading Limited presented themselves as a wealth management firm and commodities broker respectively, prosecutors said. They allegedly also used the US financial system to send and receive tens of millions of dollars as part of the scheme. Blessed Trust didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment and contact information for Hexa Whale couldn’t immediately be found.

“Today we are seizing and seeking to forfeit more than $61 million of the Government of Iran’s money, which otherwise would have promoted hostile military action and terrorist attacks against the U.S. and our allies,” Manhattan Deputy US Attorney Sean Buckley said in a statement.

Prosecutors didn’t accuse Binance of wrongdoing. The firm said it didn’t permit any transactions with people who were sanctioned. “We will continue to cooperate with law enforcement on this matter, and where sanctions or illicit-finance risk is identified, we will always investigate, restrict or freeze accounts where appropriate, offboard users, and report to relevant authorities,” Binance said in a statement.

The forfeiture claim is the latest legal maneuver by US prosecutors involving Iran in recent months as fighting between the countries continues. The US alleged Monday that accounts holding the illicit oil proceeds were used to transfer crypto to an Iranian crypto exchange and money transmitters that are fronts for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Iran’s UN Mission didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

In February, the New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported on an internal Binance investigation finding more than $1 billion had moved through the platform to Iranian entities with links to terrorist groups. Following the reports, Binance said in blog posts that it cooperated with law enforcement officials and that its compliance program was robust. Binance has said it off-boarded Hexa Whale and Blessed Trust before the reports earlier this year.

The cryptocurrency exchange’s controls were under intense legal scrutiny in 2023 when the Justice Department charged the company and its co-founder for flouting anti-money laundering rules. In that case, prosecutors said terrorist groups, people living in sanctioned countries and cyber criminals used the platform to move hundreds of millions of dollars.

Binance paid a $4.3 billion fine to resolve the probe and co-founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to violating banking laws. He spent four months in prison. President Donald Trump granted Zhao a pardon last year.

items.title: Trump Energy Boss Says Fuel Export Ban Wouldn't Cut Fuel Prices
body: One of President Donald Trump’s top energy chiefs said a US ban on fuel exports or crude wouldn’t bring down pump prices.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the president’s National Energy Dominance Council, made his comments Monday on the sidelines of a Group of 20 energy summit in Houston.

With retail diesel at a record high of more than $6 a gallon and gasoline above $4, speculation has abounded that the Trump administration might resort to export curbs to stifle political alarm bells just weeks ahead of key midterm elections.
Read More: What US Fuel-Export Controls Would Mean for Prices and Markets
Industry analysts and market watchers differ over whether such restrictions would provide long-term relief to consumers.

“We would consider an export ban if we thought that it might actually lower prices, but that’s not the case,” said Burgum, who along with Energy Secretary Chris Wright has been speaking out against the wisdom of imposing such limits.
Read More: Trump Pressures Squeezed Refiners to Ease Pump Prices
Burgum was responding to a question about whether the administration would impose any sort of export restrictions on diesel, gasoline or crude.

While Burgum reiterated his position that all options are on the table, he said an export ban would only be considered “if there was a direct correlation between stopping exports and lowering prices at home.”

items.title: US 10-Year Breaches 5% Yield Mark: Evening Briefing Americas
body: It was a bit of a bad-news Monday for the US economy as 10-year Treasury yields surpassed 5% for the first time since 2023, worsening the collision between rising inflation and swelling government and corporate borrowing.

The yield, a benchmark for US mortgage loans and bonds globally, rose almost 5 basis points to as high as 5.01% before paring most of those gains. Bond prices fell globally, with UK and German debt sliding as Brent crude — responding to threats to another critical Middle East waterway — approached $110 a barrel. The rise in energy prices shows little sign of easing amid the stalemated US-Israel war with Iran, continued obstruction of the Strait of Hormuz and now Houthi rebels moving toward the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

In the US, the rise in the 10-year yield threatens to slow economic growth and weigh on equities that have been trading at lofty valuations. This looming threat has prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to boost government bond buybacks, encourage Japan to curb Treasury sales and open the door to potentially cutting long-maturity debt issuance.

But none of Bessent’s unorthodox measures have had their intended effect. Less than two months before the US midterm elections, the 10-year yield is now roughly a full percentage point above its level before the start of the Iran war.

After a weekend in which artificial intelligence experts, and later CEOs of some of the biggest AI companies, warned of a not-infinitesimal chance that unrestrained development of the technology could be very bad, Donald Trump weighed in.

In social media posts sprinkled with occasional all-caps words for emphasis, the 80-year-old president blamed a “SICK conspiracy” for voter backlash on AI data centers and increased concern about AI models. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” In another post, Trump said the idea that AI would destroy humanity is a “HOAX.” Both Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and House Speaker Mike Johnson had thoughts on the matter as well.

Trump has claimed that climate change is a hoax, too. On Monday, his administration rescinded climate controls on coal and gas-fired power plants in one of its most aggressive moves so far to unwind US environmental regulations.

The greenhouse gases produced by the burning of fossil fuels are the prime cause of global warming — and the climate change that results. If America’s power sector were a country, it would rank as the world’s sixth-largest emitter, according to an analysis of 2022 emissions data by New York University School of Law’s Institute for Policy Integrity.

Long sought by power industry special interests, the Trump administration decision announced Monday will effectively end the federal effort to regulate the largest industrial sources of greenhouse gases in the US.

Bank of America Chief Executive Officer Brian Moynihan said trading revenue will be “relatively flat” compared with last year’s third quarter, an unexpected break from the surge that Wall Street saw in the first half.

Investors didn’t take the news well, with the bank’s stock plummeting as much as 6% Monday after Moynihan’s comments, the biggest intraday drop since April of last year. Its shares closed down 5.1%, the worst performer among members of the KBW Bank Index.

items.title: Stocks Fall in Run-Up to Fed as Yields Stay High: Markets Wrap
body: Crude oil extended its rally and Asian bonds tracked Treasuries lower as higher energy prices fueled inflation concerns and strengthened bets on a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike. Gold dropped.

Global benchmark Brent climbed 1.3% to almost $107 a barrel, extending the gains this month to over 18%. Oil pushed higher as traders weighed risks to Middle East supplies, with a critical Saudi Arabian pipeline still offline after attacks.

Rising oil prices weighed on Asian bonds with government debt in Australia and New Zealand opening lower. That tracked a drop in Treasuries in the New York session, when the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield briefly breached the 5% mark for the first time since 2023. The yield on the 10-year was at 4.99% in Asian trading Tuesday.

Gold fell for a second consecutive day to trade around $4,285 an ounce as higher rates typically diminish the appeal of the non-yielding metal. A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar steadied after posting its biggest jump in more than two months. Asian stocks edged lower.

A surge in oil revived inflation concerns ahead of Wednesday’s Federal Reserve decision, with traders pricing in a 95% chance of an interest-rate increase. Global stocks retreated Monday after leading AI developers proposed slowing advances in the field, hitting semiconductor companies that provide the infrastructure underpinning the boom.

“There are a lot of underlying factors that make for a sustained selloff in rates as the path of least resistance for now,” said Zach Griffiths, head of investment-grade and macro strategy at research firm CreditSights. Ten-year yields could rise toward 5.5%, he said.
The bond selloff reflected broader pressure on long-term borrowing costs across major developed markets, with a gauge of global government yields still at elevated levels.
Widening fiscal deficits, heavy debt issuance and financing for AI investment are prompting investors to demand greater compensation for holding longer-dated debt.
The recent rout in the bond market has increased the stakes for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh going into the central bank’s policy announcement on Wednesday.

Treasury yields serve as a benchmark for borrowing costs across the economy and as a discount rate for valuing future corporate profits. As yields rise, those earnings become less valuable in today’s terms, putting pressure on stock valuations.

That risk is growing as yields approach levels that some investors see as a threat to equities near record highs. Higher bond returns may also lure investors away from stocks, challenging a rally powered by strong AI profits and a resilient economy.

“If you saw bond yields move to the 5% or 5.25% level I think that’s where you will see some indigestion from the equity market,” said Grace Peters, global head of investment strategy at JPMorgan Chase Private Bank. “5% psychologically has an impact.”

In other corners of the market, MSCI’s Asia Pacific Index of equities slipped 0.1%. The move followed a retreat on Wall Street on Monday, where the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbled 5.9% — its biggest drop in more than two months — with Nvidia Corp. and Intel Corp. among the decliners.

A 3,800-word missive by Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei — which was endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk — said development of the most advanced systems must be slowed in order to prevent AI slipping beyond human control and inflicting catastrophic harm.

US President Donald Trump attacked Anthropic’s chief for urging a slowdown in AI development, intensifying his opposition to new guardrails. He blamed a “SICK conspiracy” for voter backlash against AI data centers and growing concerns over frontier models, adding that “the only one that is happy about it is China.”
Chinese officials on Monday dismissed US tech leaders’ calls to slow AI development on safety grounds as “fearmongering” and rejected claims that China’s advances pose a global security threat.

“There’s already quite a bit of nervousness in the market and if you’ve got some of the major players now saying: hang on, we need to slow down a little bit, that adds to uncertainty,” said Chris Armstrong, a strategist at Berenberg. He added that the shift could send AI stocks 10% to 15% lower.

items.title: Latest Oil Market News and Analysis for Sept. 15
body: Oil pushed higher as traders weighed risks to Middle East supplies, with a critical Saudi Arabian pipeline still offline after attacks.

Brent advanced above $107 a barrel after adding 1% on Monday, while West Texas Intermediate was near $103. The East-West pipeline — a workaround for Strait of Hormuz flows — was shut last week, with Saudi Aramco yet to say how long the disruption will last. Riyadh is trying to raise shipments through the waterway further to compensate.

The pipeline — which carries oil across the kingdom to the Red Sea coast — will be out of service for several weeks, the Associated Press reported on Monday, citing two regional officials. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that he expected it to be back up and running “very soon.”

On the diplomatic front, Tehran said that there would be no talks with Washington until its conditions were met, according to Mohsen Rezaee, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in a post on X. That followed comments from US President Donald Trump, who flagged potential progress on the war, saying the Islamic Republic “wants to make a deal, quickly and badly.”

“Crude is caught between physical realities that continue to point to lost supply and rhetoric pointing toward potential de-escalation,” said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC Private Wealth Group. “Ultimately, the market will put more weight on barrels and infrastructure than on rhetoric.”

Brent oil has rallied almost 76% this year, as the US-Iran war spread across the energy-rich Middle East, with shipping in the Hormuz waterway attacked and oil fields shut-in. The prolonged upheaval — together with the fallout from the Russia-Ukraine war — has boosted inflationary pressures, helping the US 10-year Treasury yield to top 5% for the first time since 2023.

Trump and Ukraine offered differing accounts on a potential halt to strikes on energy infrastructure. While the US leader said Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to stop such attacks — which have helped to boost diesel prices — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said no deal had been finalized.

Market metrics are signaling concern about tighter supplies. Brent’s prompt spread — the difference between its two nearest contracts — was $5.11 a barrel in backwardation, up from less than $2 about a month ago. That’s a bullish structure, in which the near-term price trades at a premium to later contracts.

In the Middle East, US forces are blockading Iran’s ports to raise the pressure on Tehran. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said a tanker attempting to pass through a restricted zone in the southern Strait of Hormuz exploded after striking mines. US Central Command said the claim was false.

Investors are also tracking events in Yemen. Iranian-backed Houthis on Monday fired missiles and drones at civilian targets in the Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition posted on X.

items.title: Mitch McConnell Returns to Senate for First Time Since June
body: Republican Senator Mitch McConnell returned to the US Senate on Monday for the first time since suffering from a fall at his home on June 14.
“My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier,” McConnell said in a statement.

The 84-year-old, who is the longest serving Senate leader of either party, said he is “still not quite back to 100%” but will do his best to be present for “tough votes.” McConnell told reporters at the Capitol that he would work to pass a farm bill, help NATO and make sure the US was able to counter Russia.
Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, but GOP defections have frequently dogged party leaders.

McConnell, who had been criticized for not being forthcoming about his condition, is not seeking reelection and is set to vacate his seat in January. Representative Andy Barr won the Republican primary and is the favorite to win in November against Democrat Charles Booker.
“I’m glad to see you,” he told reporters Monday evening. “It’s time to get back to work and finish the job.”

items.title: Newsom Says He Won't Run for President If Kamala Harris Does
body: California Governor Gavin Newsom said he would not run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris enters the race, ruling out a potential primary showdown between two of California’s most prominent Democrats.
“I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see,” Newsom said in an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper in a clip posted Monday. “But I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

Newsom, who is prevented by term limits from running again for governor, has openly acknowledged considering a presidential bid and has increasingly raised his national profile, including by traveling to swing states such as North Carolina to campaign ahead of the midterm elections.
Newsom suggested that a contest between him and Harris, whose political careers have run alongside each other for decades in California, would limit both their chances at winning.

“First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else,” Newsom said while fly fishing with Tapper in Montana. “They can enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good.”

Harris has run for president twice, unsuccessfully seeking the Democratic nomination in 2020 and becoming the party’s nominee in 2024, when as vice president she took over from Joe Biden in the middle of the general election campaign and subsequently lost to Donald Trump. Harris said in April that she is “thinking” about a 2028 run.

items.title: Carney Courts Blackstone, Apollo for C$1 Trillion Canada Investment Drive
body: Welcome back to Canada Daily, the newsletter on business, economics and politics from Vancouver to Montreal and beyond. If this was forwarded to you, sign up.
After a career at Goldman Sachs, steering two central banks and chairing Brookfield Asset Management, Prime Minister Mark Carney has built what may be one of the world’s most enviable Rolodexes.
This week, he’s putting it to good use.

Carney has pulled global heavyweights collectively overseeing more than $70 trillion in assets — including Blackstone, Singapore’s Temasek Holdings and Apollo Global Management — to Toronto for the first Canada Investment Summit, where he’ll pitch them on his ambition of drumming up C$1 trillion ($720 billion) in public and private investment over five years.

“Canada is one of the most connected economies in the world. We have trade deals covering 1.5 billion consumers,” Carney said in an interview with Bloomberg News. “We also have been making some big changes over the course of the last year-and-a-half. Now’s the time to look at Canada afresh.”

The urgency is unmistakable. The collapse in trade talks with the US triggered a fresh round of 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian exports, deepening a fight already dragging on growth, hiring and investor confidence. But the rupture has also given Carney political room to push through changes long thought untouchable: pro-business tax and regulatory reforms, privatizing public assets like airports, and spending billions in government dollars to get Canada’s natural resources to foreign markets faster.

Executives say the shift is overdue. Canada’s regulatory and compliance regime is “congested” and the country “has been basically a branch plant for the US,” Dominion Dynamics CEO Eliot Pence said. The crisis is forcing a rethink of the country’s old constraints. “Ironically, I’ve never been more optimistic about Canada’s future than I am now.”

Carney told Bloomberg that more reforms are coming. Ottawa has taken steps to speed up project approvals, and he plans to “double down” with measures that apply across the economy. He said the dramatic breakdown with Washington may have at least helped US counterparts understand Canada’s negotiating red lines — sovereignty, culture and the freedom to strike trade deals globally. A “mutually advantageous” deal is still possible, Carney said, and Canada is ready to return to the table to negotiate one.

For now, Carney is looking elsewhere. After the summit, he’ll fly to France to join European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in outlining a deeper Canada-EU partnership spanning trade, security, supply chains and raw materials. The outreach is already paying off: Kepler Communications CEO Mina Mitry said the push for closer ties helped his company become the first Canadian prime contractor for a European Space Agency mission.
Carney’s bet is simple: if Canada can rewrite the rules fast enough, global capital will follow.
Also in this newsletter: Inflation holds steady at 3%. Major banks pledge tens of billions in new lending for Canadian companies. And the government fast-tracks tax rulings for big investments.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

Carney also told Bloomberg that Canada wants to see the creation of a global “technology stability” body to help oversee artificial intelligence and ensure it is safe. “There’s a need for coordination,” Carney said in the interview. “Ultimately, a technology stability board, in our view, along the lines of the Financial Stability Board would make sense.” The leaders of major AI labs have said development of the most advanced systems must be slowed in order to prevent AI slipping beyond human control and inflicting catastrophic harm.

BCE plans to expand its data center campus in Saskatchewan to as much as 1.2 gigawatts of capacity, the company announced Monday. Canada’s biggest telecommunications firm by revenue and the provincial government signed a memorandum of understanding to develop up to 900 megawatts of capacity, on top of the 300 megawatts already under contract to CoreWeave and Cerebras Systems at its Regina AI hub.

Canada’s inflation rate was unchanged at 3% last month, matching expectations as gasoline prices rose at a slower annual pace. While the conflict in the Middle East continues to put upward pressure on energy costs, prices at the pump were 22.8% higher in August than a year earlier, Statistics Canada reported on Monday. That followed a 25.7% increase in July. The agency delayed the release after heavy website traffic caused technical problems.

Toronto-Dominion Bank is pledging to provide C$150 billion over five years in new lending, advice and financing activities to sectors it sees as crucial to Canada’s economic future, joining a wave of financial players making similar commitments. Over the past week, Bank of Montreal, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Royal Bank of Canada and Bank of Nova Scotia all announced plans to allocate more capital to homegrown companies.

Canada will prioritize requests for income tax clarity related to investments of at least C$1 billion, a move meant to help international firms seeking to deploy capital in the nation. Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne announced the change Monday in Toronto, confirming an earlier report by Bloomberg News. Fast-tracked rulings for projects with substantial outlays may allow firms to make decisions more quickly, removing a potential barrier to investment flows.

Concord Pacific Developments acquired a field of 50 wind turbines from Potentia Renewables for several hundred million Canadian dollars, deepening the Canadian developer’s long-term bet on renewables, CEO Terry Hui said, adding that he’s working on a move into data centers. The Golden South Wind Project is the largest active wind farm in western Canada’s prairie province of Saskatchewan, with capacity of 210 megawatts.

Oil rose, with fears of a tightening market after Saudi Arabia closed a major crude pipeline pitted against signs that the US may still be seeking a diplomatic resolution with Iran. Brent edged 1% higher to settle below $106 a barrel, after earlier rising as much as 5%, while West Texas Intermediate was around $101. The commodity initially rallied on the halt of the kingdom’s East-West pipeline, which has the capacity to carry about 7 million barrels a day to the Yanbu hub on the Red Sea that has been key to bypassing the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war choked off exports from the Persian Gulf.
The S&P/TSX Composite Index closed roughly flat, with tech stocks rising the most and mining falling the most.

Hollywood honchos are used to taking over Toronto’s high-end hotels and restaurants during the city’s annual film festival. But this year, entertainment executives are competing for private dining rooms and penthouse suites with the heads of the world’s leading financial firms. Money managers invited to the Canada Investment Summit arrived in a city already buzzing for the Toronto International Film Festival, driving scarcity at luxury hotels, tables at gourmet restaurants, and helicopter transfers to and from the airport. And the city’s watering holes are competing to offer extravagant indulgences, from an C$8,888 feast at a renowned dim sum spot to a C$2,000 tableside cocktail at The St. Regis Toronto.

items.title: Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney Courts World's Top Investors at Toronto Summit
body: Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney is gathering some of the world’s top investors Monday night and Tuesday as he seeks to attract more investment into the country while reducing its reliance on the US and diversifying its markets.

A list of attendees to the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto show the Chief Executive Officer of the world’s largest asset manager BlackRock, Inc., Larry Fink, along with Blackstone Inc.’s Jon Gray, Apollo Global Management, Inc.’s Marc Rowan and KKR & Co.’s Joseph Bae.

The United Arab Emirates, which has committed to invest as much as $50 billion in Canada, was represented by its biggest oil producer Abu Dhabi National Oil Co., Investment Corporation of Dubai and Mubadala Capital LLC. Africa’s richest man Aliko Dangote, OpenAI’s head for countries and former UK Chancellor George Osborne, and China International Capital Corp.’s Chairman Chen Liang were all scheduled to be at the table.

Carney is attempting to attract as much as C$1 trillion ($719 billion) in private and public investments over the next five years, positioning Canada as a safe bet to invest in an uncertain world, while acknowledging the country has some structural economic problems.
“We’ve been slow on moving on a series of areas with respect to regulatory approvals and other factors,” he said in an interview Monday with Bloomberg News.

The government put in measures last year to speed up project approvals. There’s more to come, he said. “We’re going to double down on that strategy, you’ll see in the coming weeks, with additional measures that spread that across the economy.”
The summit will showcase a pitchbook laying out 167 projects worth tens of billions of dollars spanning data centers, advanced manufacturing, liquefied natural gas, ports and dozens of mines.

Carney met during the day with BlackRock’s Fink, Blackstone’s Gray, Macquarie Group’s Shemara Wikramanayake, Temasek’s Dilhan Pillay, the Qatar Investment Authority’s Mohammed Saif-Al-Sowaidi and the Kuwait Investment Authority’s Sheikh Saoud Salem Abdulaziz Al-Sabah.

Those expected to attend also included executives of JP Morgan Chase & Co., Pacific Investment Management Co., Bain Capital, LP, the UK’s Barclays PLC and Border to Coast Pensions Partnership Ltd., France’s Ardian SAS, Germany’s Deutsche Bank AG, Norway’s Norges Bank Investment Management and Japan’s Mizuho Financial Group. One group that was not attending, even though they were expected to come: Saudi Arabia’s $1 trillion sovereign wealth vehicle Public Investment Fund.

About half of the attendee list of more than 220 names are from Canadian banks, pension funds, investment firms, large corporations and governments. The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Public Sector Pension Investment Board were involved in organizing the summit.

items.title: Chip Stocks Fall After AI Leaders Call for Development Slowdown
body: Good morning. Chip stocks fell after warning from AI leaders. The Bank of Japan may test markets with more rate hikes. And Japan’s Showa retro aesthetic is catching on with tourists. Listen to the day’s top stories.

Chipmakers dragged down US stocks as the fallout spread from a proposal by leaders of artificial intelligence giants to slow the technology’s development. Donald Trump attacked Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for raising the alarm, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called for a global body to oversee AI. Microsoft released rules limiting its development of models. Treasury 10-year yields briefly surpassed 5% for the first time since 2023.Kioxia is considering raising at least $10 billion in a listing of American depositary receipts, people familiar said. The Japanese memory-chip maker is seeking more liquidity after buying back billions of dollars of shares at home.ByteDance lined up more than two dozen lenders including Industrial and Commercial Bank of China and HSBC Holdings for a $29.6 billion loan as the TikTok parent builds up its AI ambitions, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Jakarta will take over salary payments for hundreds of thousands of public school teachers and health workers previously paid by local administrations, shifting a payroll burden away from regions hit by steep funding cuts. Part-time local-government contract workers will gradually be converted into full-time civil servants at a cost of about 31.1 trillion rupiah ($1.75 billion).India’s inflation accelerated in August, climbing 4.82% from a year earlier, driven by firmer food prices, while restaurant and transport costs also kept broader price pressures firm. The reading is moving closer to the top of the central bank’s 2%-6% target range, potentially narrowing the scope for policymakers to leave interest rates on hold for long.
The Bank of Japan is expected to raise interest rates Friday for the third time in less than 10 months. That’s the fastest pace since 1990, when its asset bubble was bursting.

Beijing’s biggest AI fear isn’t machines wiping out humanity — it’s humans using them to sow chaos, Catherine Thorbecke writes. China’s security chief warned that deepfakes, influence campaigns and cyberattacks may threaten social stability.

items.title: AI Slowdown Shouldn't Be as Hard as AI CEOs Say
body: I’m Beth Kowitt and this is Bloomberg Opinion Today, a head-spinning few days of Bloomberg Opinion’s opinions. Sign up here.

It’s been a head-spinning few days in AI land, as fears over the technology’s threat to humanity have entered the mainstream. The only thing that’s clear is that no one can agree on what to do about any of it.

AI bosses are calling for a slowdown in development — what Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called “pacing the frontier” in an essay over the weekend. This position has Amodei and his brethren at odds with President Donald Trump, who posted on social media today that the “only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He added that there’s a “SICK conspiracy” against AI, which is making China happy.

China, for its part, has rejected the idea of a slowdown and instead wants global coordination — meaning it’s not just the US making the rules, as Catherine Thorbecke explains. “If the US and China can’t cooperate on the dangers already in view, there’s little hope they’ll manage the ones AI’s own builders warn could be the end of us all,” she writes.

Parmy Olson views all the talk of a slowdown as just that — all talk. She points out that the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI could simply pause their research if they wanted to. While that might sound extreme, there’s precedent for researchers deciding that some work is too risky to carry out without more stringent guardrails, she points out: In 1974, leading biologists called for a voluntary moratorium on certain gene-splicing experiments, and some countries, such as the United Arab Emirates, have agreed to forego uranium enrichment to reduce proliferation risks.

While a stoppage might seem like its own kind of Armageddon to investors, Parmy says there’s still plenty of value that companies can unlock by implementing what they’ve already built over the last several years. “Anthropic could still be an extremely valuable company if it focused primarily on helping businesses and consumers integrate its existing models into their work and lives,” she writes, “taking on the more boring role of IT provider rather than a laboratory racing to superintelligence.” That might not seem as sexy, but it certainly is safer.
Bonus AI Speed Reading: Sam Altman can wait a little longer for OpenAI to go public — but can Masayoshi Son? — Shuli Ren

It’s back-to-school season, which means government officials are playing politics with the childcare policies that US families rely on to manage their lives. The 2026 version: a draft plan from the Trump administration that would give eligible married couples with a stay-at-home parent up to $9,000 a year per child to help make up for lost earnings.

Sounds great! Love it! I’m all for making parents’ lives easier. (Full disclosure: I am one.) But, of course, there’s a catch: The money would come from a $12 billion fund that provides childcare subsidies to eligible working parents in low-income households. Mary Ellen Klas calls the plan an ideological trap. “My guess is that the idea has surfaced two months before the midterm elections to revive the ‘Mommy Wars’ debates of the 1980s and 1990s, which wrongly pitted mothers who stay home against those who earn a paycheck,” she writes. Mary Ellen argues that the proposal also serves as a distraction from some of the Trump administration’s less successful and popular policies. What it doesn’t do is come close to solving the very real childcare crisis that so many families face.

Distracting from policy failures as the midterms approach is becoming a familiar pastime for the administration. Just last week the president promised voters $5,000 in exchange for Republican turnout at the polls. “That Trump was compelled to resort to this sort of dubious measure is revealing,” writes David M. Drucker. David says the GOP’s congressional majorities are at risk because Trump hasn’t led on the issues that matter most to voters — the economy, and especially the high cost of living. Instead, Trump is focused on his priorities, which include building the “victory” arch and the White House ballroom.

It’s indicative of Trump’s Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde nature, David says. When he’s running as an outsider, Trump is a generational political talent. When he’s in the Oval Office, “he transforms into an incompetent campaign doppelganger.”

When it comes to employment, the era of big government is over. But spending? Not so much. Justin Fox crunched the latest BLS numbers and found that the administration has successfully shrunk its workforce, with the federal share of overall nonfarm payroll employment hitting a record low of 1.3% in July. Meanwhile, the federal government is spending about as much as it did before the cuts. So what’s the goal of all these job reductions then? The big picture shows a shift of resources to immigration enforcement and away from everything else — even at agencies that were never real targets. “All in all this feels less like a thought-out effort to reshape the federal government than a somewhat inchoate attempt to assert executive power, punish perceived political enemies and just be seen as doing something,” Justin writes.

Central banks have long responded to supply shocks by simply ignoring them. The argument is that supply disruptions (a military conflict, avian flu, a frost, etc.) create one-time price jumps that eventually revert to the mean. But “the look-through doctrine” no longer applies, in large part because the shocks aren’t so isolated, Jonathan Levin writes. Today’s consumers have contended with Covid-19 supply chain chaos, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, AI, tariffs and the Iran military campaign. “The biggest risk today isn’t accidentally triggering an economic slowdown with over-eager monetary tightening; it’s in delaying action on the basis of an old doctrine that never contemplated the era of Donald Trump,” writes Jonathan. Policymakers seem to agree. Last week the European Central Bank increased rates, and swaps and futures markets now indicate a high likelihood that the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan will follow this week. The Reserve Bank of Australia, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England may be next.
Malls are so back.
It might be worth fighting that insurance denial.

items.title: Apollo's Michaels Uses $101 Million of Tariff Refund to Cut Debt
body: Apollo Global Management Inc.-owned retailer Michaels Cos. used a windfall from tariff refunds to help cut its leverage, according to people familiar with the matter.

The company said in preliminary second-quarter earnings that it received more than $170 million related to IEEPA tariff refunds, including interest, and bought back $101 million of debt, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Net leverage shrank to 4.8 times earnings from 6.3 times the prior year, they added.

The refund also boosted Michaels’ adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to $178 million, compared with about $104 million last year. Without it, that measure would have been roughly $94 million, some of the people said.

Similarly, gross profit was $522 million, or a 46.6% margin, when including the tariff refund, but without it, would have dipped from a year ago to 33.1%, the people familiar said. Comparable sales were up 4.5% year over year, while net sales rose 4.8% to $1.12 billion.

Michaels, which Apollo took over about five years ago, has emerged as an unlikely success story in the retail sector. It has stockpiled assets from bankrupt competitors like Party City and fabrics retailer Joann, while also benefitting from a revival in demand for arts and crafts.
Read more: Apollo Steers ‘Grandmother’s Store’ Michaels to Unlikely Success

Apollo is reaching the point at which it would usually look to exit an equity investment. In the case of Michaels, the most likely route would be an initial public offering, Bloomberg previously reported.
The company’s 11% second lien notes, the securities that were bought back, traded at 97 cents on the dollar on Monday, up about 1 cent from last week, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

items.title: S&P 500 Seen Dropping 10% on Fed Hikes, MRA Strategist Says
body: Potential Federal Reserve rate hikes starting this week could spur a correction in the S&P 500 as reduced corporate margins hurt profit outlooks and markets brace for a tightening cycle, according to Macro Risk Advisors LLC.

The S&P 500 has dropped nearly 1% so far in September, historically its weakest month, amid concerns over elevated energy costs and recent inflation data that has driven US 10-year Treasury yields above 5% for the first time since 2023. That view has prompted traders to almost fully price in a quarter point rate hike by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh on Wednesday, up from about 60% odds a week ago.
A rate hike on Wednesday is likely to lead to more pain, Dean Curnutt, chief executive officer and founder of Macro Risk Advisors, said.

“We expect an 8-10% pullback in S&P with a potential second leg in December,” he wrote in a Monday note to clients. Rate hikes will “compress margins in companies that cannot pass costs through” as well as deliver a volatility shock into a market that is not positioned for it, he said.

Curnutt said the setup is akin to what investors saw in 2018, when the S&P 500 peaked in September and then plunged 10% over the course of October and November. That year, Curnutt warned, “The Santa Claus rally did not come” and the market took another leg lower in December, eventually dropping almost 20% from its peak.

Given the history, “a defensive posture is the correct approach,” he said. Similar to 2018, he is expecting the market to take another leg lower in December in response to multiple Fed hikes “into a K-shaped, low-churn economy.”

items.title: Nvidia CEO Puts Trump on Phone While Downplaying AI Risks
body: Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang took a live phone call from Donald Trump during a panel discussion Monday, allowing the US president to dismiss artificial intelligence dangers as a “hoax.”

During the call, which Huang received on stage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, Trump criticized the push to slow the pace of AI development as politically motivated or a Chinese scheme. Huang agreed with the president, saying Trump had seen through the complexities of the issue.
The AI pushback is “just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen,” Trump said. “And that could be political people. It could also be China.”
Read More: Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing AI Model Development

Even while downplaying AI risks, Huang praised an Anthropic PBC researcher who resigned over the fears. The employee, Jacob Coxon, was courageous to voice his concerns, the CEO said. Whistleblowers should be taken seriously inside organizations, he added.
However, the panic has created a false choice between fast innovation and AI safety, Huang said.

The potential danger of AI to humanity has become a topic of intense discussion in recent days. After Coxon resigned, saying Anthropic and OpenAI were “gambling with our lives,” calls have grown to curb the pace of development. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay — later endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — proposing a slowdown.
Read More: Anthropic Worker Quits Over AI Firms ‘Gambling With Our Lives’
US tech stocks slumped on Monday over concern about a potential deceleration in spending. Shares of Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, fell 3.4%.

Nvidia, whose chips help run artificial intelligence models, has been the top beneficiary of a massive AI infrastructure build-out. Trump, meanwhile, has emerged as a fierce advocate for data center construction, even in the face of growing opposition.
Trump criticized US states for refusing to give permits for the building of new data centers. Such facilities make people and states wealthy, he said.
“It’s the oil of the next 20, 25 years,” he said. “It’s bigger than the internet.”
