items.title: Musk's xAI Resolves Claims Against Apple Over AI Competition
body: Elon Musk’s xAI and X Corp. said they resolved an antitrust lawsuit against Apple Inc. that accused the iPhone maker of favoring OpenAI’s ChatGPT over other chatbot makers.
US District Judge Mark Pittman in Fort Worth, Texas granted a request by the companies to voluntarily dismiss their case against Apple on Monday. However, the case against OpenAI will continue.
The companies, both owned by by Musk’s SpaceX, had also accused OpenAI of maintaining an unlawful monopoly over the chatbot market through anti-competitive conduct.

Musk’s companies filed the suit in August 2025, seeking billions of dollars over claims that Apple’s decision to integrate OpenAI into the iPhone’s operating system inhibits competition and innovation within the AI industry and harms consumers by depriving them of choice.
Representatives for Musk’s companies and Apple and OpenAI didn’t return requests for comment.

Apple and OpenAI have denied the claims, arguing that their arrangement — which let users access ChatGPT results within Siri and use the AI technology as part of certain iPhone features — was never exclusive. OpenAI also described the lawsuit as part of a pattern of harassment by Musk against the firm he co-founded and then left.

Musk has sparred repeatedly with OpenAI and its chief executive officer Sam Altman in the intervening years. In May, the pair faced off in an Oakland, California, courtroom in a separate case where Musk accused OpenAI of betraying its mission to benefit the public by morphing into a for-profit business. Jurors rejected his claims, finding that he waited too long to sue.

Apple and OpenAI’s relationship has soured significantly in the two years since it was first announced. In May, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was exploring legal options against Apple after failing to see expected benefits from their arrangement.
In July, Apple sued OpenAI for trade secret theft and accused the company and its hardware chief of engaging in a coordinated campaign to steal information about upcoming products.
The case is X Corp. et al v. Apple Inc., US District Court, Northern District of Texas (Fort Worth).

items.title: Europe Can't Simply Import AI Technologies From US, Lagarde Says
body: Europe can’t afford to simply buy AI technologies from the US but must also build parts independently or risk leaving itself vulnerable, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said.
“There is nothing inherently bad about importing rather than producing new technologies,” Lagarde said Monday. But there are reasons why artificial intelligence is “special,” she said.
Alongside data protection, Lagarde highlighted access as one such factor since a withdrawal or a change of terms would reach “every sector at once” as soon as there’s widespread use of AI.
“That is leverage of a kind no trade partner has ever held over Europe,” she said. “It could be used in any negotiation, on tariffs or on digital taxes, for example.”

The remarks add to calls by Lagarde and other ECB officials for Europe to not fall too far behind on AI due not only to economic dangers but also sovereignty issues. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said last week that AI will serve as a “litmus test” for whether Europe is capable of collectively unleashing its potential.

Earlier on Monday, a coalition of leading European economists, politicians and AI experts, including Nobel laureate Philippe Aghion and former European Union Commissioner Margrethe Vestager, also warned that Europe risks becoming irrevocably dependent on a handful of foreign governments and individuals if decisive action isn’t taken this year.
Lagarde said Monday that Europe must build more computing capacity. “Companies should be deciding whether to adopt AI on its merits, without worrying about where their data ends up,” she said.
New gigafactories are a start, but they’re currently far from sufficient, she said, adding that “Europe needs to build at a different pace altogether.”

AI could also be a project of its own to finally drive European capital markets forward. “It needs capital on a scale that only markets can provide, and the stakes for Europe could hardly be higher,” Lagarde said.

items.title: Germany, UniCredit Say Commerzbank Talks Were 'Constructive'
body: German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil and UniCredit SpA Chief Executive Officer Andrea Orcel said they held constructive talks Monday after the ministry outlined the demands it has for the Italian lender’s bid to take over Commerzbank AG.

“I made clear in a constructive conversation with Mr. Orcel that the further negotiations must be conducted responsibly,” Klingbeil said in an emailed statement following the encounter. “It’s crucial that Commerzbank can continue to play its important role in financing the German economy and Germany’s small and medium-sized businesses.”

“We are mindful of the interests of Commerzbank’s more than 40,000 employees and stand by them during this uncertain time,” Klingbeil also said. “We expect Commerzbank to remain a publicly listed company headquartered in Frankfurt and to continue its strong business with small and medium-sized companies — both in Germany and internationally.”

The conversation marks the first time that the government, which holds about 13% in Commerzbank, has spelled out the conditions it expects Orcel to meet for a takeover of Germany’s second-biggest listed lender. The Italian has been pursuing a deal publicly for two years, amid previously fierce opposition from the rival and politicians. Negotiations gained momentum after UniCredit secured just under 50% of Commerzbank’s shares during a formal offer this summer.

It was a “good and constructive” meeting in which the two sides set out their priorities and pledged to continue discussions, Orcel said in a statement to Bloomberg. “It’s for both sides to now reflect on this initial discussion so that a way forward can be found in the best interest of all stakeholders and shareholders,” he said.

Berlin previously rejected a takeover bid from UniCredit that ended in July as too low. The Italian bank had offered 0.485 of its shares for each one of Commerzbank, a proposal that included effectively no premium. A full takeover would mark the largest bank acquisition in almost two decades, given Commerzbank’s market value of about €46 billion ($53 billion).

“The two banks are at a different stage now that they’re negotiating a transaction,” finance ministry spokesman Maximilian Kall said earlier on Monday. “It’s no longer about a hostile takeover but about finding the best path for the two banks.”

Given the size of a merged bank’s German business, Berlin also regards some representation of Commerzbank at UniCredit as necessary, people familiar with the matter said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. The government itself wants to keep its two Commerzbank supervisory board seats, as long as it is invested. At this stage, it’s not yet open to discussing a sale of its 13% stake to UniCredit, they added.
Read More: Germany Said to Prepare for UniCredit Talks on Commerzbank

Orcel has presented a strategic plan for Commerzbank that includes cutting back its large network of offices around the world. Commerzbank CEO Bettina Orlopp is strongly opposed to that idea. Both executives last month held their first formal talks over how to manage the expected change of control, Bloomberg News has reported.

While those talks are expected to continue in the weeks and months ahead, the encounter showed agreement won’t be easy to find as UniCredit executives highlighted they remain committed to their previous strategy proposals, while their counterparts at the German lender continued to defend their own strategy, people familiar with the matter said at the time.

UniCredit has said it expects to take full ownership of its stake as early as the fourth quarter, pending regulatory approvals, and it would then take control of Commerzbank. It has floated the idea of replacing the top management if needed. Given that not all shareholders usually vote at shareholder meetings, a holding of close to 50% is likely enough to decide strategic and management issues.
“The German government will continue to act in the interests of Germany’s Mittelstand, Frankfurt as a financial center, and Commerzbank’s employees,” Klingbeil said in the statement Monday.

items.title: Trump Claims Russia-Ukraine Energy Truce; Kyiv Says Not Yet
body: President Donald Trump and Ukraine offered differing accounts of a supposed agreement with Russia to stop attacks on energy infrastructure, as strikes on oil refineries help drive diesel prices to record levels.
Trump on Monday blamed the strikes, rather than the war in Iran, for the surge in diesel prices and posted on social media that Moscow and Kyiv both agreed to stop them.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said no deal had been finalized, though he acknowledged a “strong US proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure.”

“If this can become the first de-escalatory step — a step toward ending Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response — then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation,” he posted on social media.
Zelenskyy added, however, that there’s been no genuine desire from Russia to move toward ending the conflict.

Moscow has not agreed to anything despite Trump’s assertion of a mutual understanding between the two countries to avoid targeting energy infrastructure, according to a Ukrainian official. The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Markets largely shrugged off Trump’s claim. Diesel futures pared gains after his post in a choppy session but are still up about 1% on the day, and US retail prices are still at record highs.

“Hearing it from Ukraine and Russia would have a lot more certainty for me than from Trump,” said Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, a Washington-based think tank.
“The thought here is that a stop in attacking refineries would give Russia time to repair and reduce risk of further outages,” she added. “But if Gulf channels are still blocked it won’t help much.”
Trump has struggled to bring an end to the war in Ukraine despite promising to stop the conflict on day one of his second term.

Past efforts to broker ceasefires covering energy targets have not yielded lasting results. Last month, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine offered Russia a truce on attacks against ships carrying agricultural commodities through the Black Sea. But Moscow rejected the deal because it wanted guarantees against strikes on its energy infrastructure.
In early May, Trump announced Ukraine and Russia agreed to a three-day ceasefire for the annual Victory Day celebration, but attacks immediately resumed when it expired.

Both Russia and Ukraine have used strikes on energy infrastructure as a powerful weapon of war. Moscow has targeted Ukraine’s power sector and electricity grid, with blackout-causing attacks even as winter temperatures plummet. Kyiv has hit back, aiming strikes on Russian oil refineries that have led to widespread fuel shortages in many parts of the country.
Trump said on Sunday he had warned Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries.
Read more: GLOBAL INSIGHT: Russia Advance Stalls, But War’s End Elusive

Average retail diesel prices rose above $6 per gallon in the US for the first time ever last week. Russia has banned diesel exports after damage to oil refineries, exacerbating a supply crunch stoked by the war in Iran.
Russia is the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel, according to energy analytics firm Vortexa Ltd., though the Middle East is an even bigger exporter of the fuel.
Hamad Hussain, economist at Capital Economics, said the loss of refining capacity in the Middle East “means that refined product prices will remain high.”

The potential economic ramifications are enormous. While most American motorists focus closely on the cost of unleaded gasoline, which has also risen 54% from a low in January, diesel is an essential power source for long-haul trucks, freight trains and farm equipment.
Read more: US INSIGHT: Record Diesel, High Gas Are Fueling GOP Midterm Woes

For Trump, the issue poses a political peril ahead of the November midterm elections that will determine control of the House and Senate. Elevated fuel prices are cutting revenue and forcing business owners to charge more for goods, adding to cost-of-living concerns that are already weighing on the Republican Party.

The president’s announcement on Russia and Ukraine was part of a series of social media posts on Monday where he struck a defensive tone on different issues, including affordability. In one of the posts, Trump said, “prices are coming down sharply” and that oil “will drop like a rock as soon as the Military Conflict with Iran is over.”

items.title: Polish Refiner Orlen Hunts for Crude After Saudi Pipeline Halt
body: Polish oil refiner Orlen SA posted a series of tenders to buy crude, a potential sign that some buyers of Middle Eastern supplies are looking to secure alternative barrels following the shutdown of a key Saudi pipeline.

In the past two working days, the company issued at least five tenders, according to documents seen by Bloomberg. Traders said the move signaled Orlen was hunting for supplies after attacks led Saudi Arabia to halt flows through its vital East-West pipeline last week.
Orlen declined to comment. Saudi Aramco declined to comment in response to early questions about any cargo delays as a consequence of disruptions on the pipeline.

The shutdown could be particularly impactful for European refiners, who are relatively close to the pipeline and pivoted to Saudi oil after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Earlier on Monday, buyers in Asia said they were awaiting clarity on cargoes that were due to be picked up from the Red Sea port of Yanbu, where the pipeline ends.

The conduit has the capacity to ship about 7 million barrels a day and had become the kingdom’s most important workaround since the Iran war choked off exports from the Persian Gulf. It will be out of service for several weeks, the Associated Press reported on Monday, citing two regional officials. Saudi energy ministry officials didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The disruption comes as the European crude market has been flashing signs of exceptional tightness, with refiners running as hard as possible to try and solve a fuel supply crunch, meaning any setback will be even more acutely felt. While benchmark crude futures are close to $110 a barrel, diesel futures are near $200 a barrel, underscoring the reasons why refiners are able to keep bidding for supplies.
Orlen buys significant volumes of oil from Saudi Aramco, while the Saudi oil giant also owns a stake in the Gdansk refinery in Poland. Aramco also operates storage sites in the country.

items.title: Venezuela lleva la dolarización al centro del debate
body: Read the story in EnglishTras años de inflación y turbulencias, la propuesta de dolarizar formalmente la economía de Venezuela ha ganado terreno en el debate político.
El legislador opositor Antonio Ecarri trabaja con el economista estadounidense Steve Hanke en una legislación para adoptar formalmente el dólar como moneda de Venezuela.
Suscríbase       aquí     al boletín Morning Briefing Español y conozca nuestro canal de       WhatsApp

Los dólares ya se utilizan ampliamente de manera informal, pero convertirlos en la moneda oficial sería un paso de consecuencias mucho mayores. Más de la mitad de los venezolanos apoya la idea, según una encuesta de AtlasIntel para Bloomberg News realizada en mayo.
Esto es lo que significaría, cómo podría funcionar y qué lecciones puede extraer Venezuela de países que ya lo han intentado.

La dolarización oficial implicaría adoptar el dólar estadounidense como moneda oficial de Venezuela y reemplazar al bolívar no solo en las transacciones cotidianas, sino en todo el sistema financiero. El efectivo, los depósitos, las deudas, los contratos y los salarios denominados en bolívares tendrían que convertirse a dólares a una tasa de cambio oficial.

Venezuela es una economía parcialmente dolarizada desde que la hiperinflación llevó a empresas y hogares a recurrir a la moneda estadounidense alrededor de 2019. Los dólares se utilizan ampliamente para fijar precios y ahorrar, pero las finanzas públicas están denominadas en bolívares y el banco central continúa emitiendo la moneda.

Ecarri planea presentar su propuesta legislativa ante la Asamblea Nacional. Sin embargo, el presidente de la Asamblea, Jorge Rodríguez, ya rechazó la idea, citando una disposición constitucional que establece el bolívar como unidad monetaria de Venezuela y otorga al banco central autoridad sobre la política monetaria. Otras autoridades venezolanas también han defendido públicamente el bolívar en las últimas semanas.

Las perspectivas de dolarización podrían depender en última instancia de la posición de Estados Unidos. Desde la captura del expresidente Nicolás Maduro en enero, Washington ha asumido un papel decisivo en la conducción del gobierno de la presidenta encargada Delcy Rodríguez, incluida la supervisión de parte de sus ingresos petroleros y gastos. El secretario del Tesoro de EE.UU., Scott Bessent, ha defendido un mayor papel del dólar en Venezuela y dijo en una entrevista en junio que “Venezuela va a facturar en dólares” y que la moneda estadounidense sería “el eje central de su comercio”. Sin embargo, la administración no ha anunciado públicamente planes para dolarizar por completo Venezuela ni para reemplazar el bolívar como moneda de curso legal.

Décadas de alta inflación —incluida la hiperinflación entre fines de 2017 y comienzos de 2021— erosionaron la confianza en el bolívar, al igual que las restricciones para comprar y vender libremente monedas extranjeras. Los partidarios sostienen que la dolarización oficial aumentaría la confianza en el sistema monetario al reducir la exposición a la inflación y el riesgo de una depreciación del bolívar frente al dólar.

Además, la dolarización aumentaría la confianza al impedir que los gobiernos financien déficits mediante la creación de dinero, dijo Pedro Palma, profesor emérito de Economía del Instituto de Estudios Superiores de Administración, durante una transmisión por internet.
Los partidarios de la dolarización formal sostienen que adoptar oficialmente el dólar también eliminaría las fricciones creadas por la coexistencia de dos monedas.

El reciente acuerdo petrolero entre las autoridades interinas de Venezuela y EE.UU. permitirá que Estados Unidos vuelva a ser un importante comprador de crudo venezolano. Un mayor comercio con EE.UU. reforzaría los argumentos para que Venezuela adopte la moneda de su principal socio comercial, dijo Francisco Rodríguez, economista venezolano y profesor de asuntos internacionales de la Universidad de Denver, quien, sin embargo, sigue siendo crítico del acuerdo petrolero.

Venezuela renunciaría al control de la política monetaria y de su tasa de cambio, lo que limitaría su capacidad para responder a recesiones, crisis bancarias o shocks externos. En cambio, la economía tendría que absorber esos impactos mediante menores salarios, mayor desempleo o un ajuste fiscal. La disponibilidad de dólares en la economía dependería en mayor medida de los ingresos provenientes de exportaciones, inversiones, remesas o endeudamiento externo, una posible limitación si el acceso al financiamiento internacional sigue siendo restringido.

La dolarización tampoco garantizaría la disciplina fiscal ni resolvería los problemas estructurales más amplios de Venezuela. Los gobiernos pueden seguir registrando grandes déficits, acumular deuda insostenible y caer en default sin controlar su propia moneda, señaló el economista Omar Zambrano. Y aunque el dólar podría ayudar a estabilizar los precios, por sí solo no aumentaría la producción petrolera, restablecería los mercados de crédito ni atraería inversiones.
Los críticos sostienen que Venezuela ya ha obtenido muchos de los beneficios de la dolarización sin renunciar por completo al control de la política monetaria.

La implementación requeriría convertir los bolívares a dólares a una tasa de cambio uniforme y determinar cómo se tratarían los depósitos, préstamos, salarios y obligaciones del gobierno. La tasa de conversión sería crucial: fijarla en un nivel demasiado fuerte podría dejar a la economía sobrevalorada o con escasez de dólares, mientras que establecerla en un nivel demasiado débil podría erosionar el valor de los salarios, los ahorros y otros activos denominados en bolívares.

Otra cuestión clave es cuántos dólares necesitaría Venezuela, lo que depende de aquello que las autoridades se comprometan a convertir. Rodríguez sostiene que la base monetaria, estimada en unos US$2.500 millones, es lo suficientemente pequeña como para cubrirse con las reservas existentes. Sin embargo, Gustavo García, execonomista del Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo, dijo que una dolarización completa requeriría suficientes dólares para cubrir obligaciones financieras más amplias, incluidos los depósitos bancarios, lo que haría mucho más exigente su implementación.

La Academia Nacional de Ciencias Económicas de Venezuela también incluye entre las condiciones económicas e institucionales necesarias para una dolarización exitosa la modificación o derogación del marco legal y constitucional que regula la moneda de curso legal.
El banco central quedaría fuertemente limitado. Ya no emitiría bolívares, no establecería una política monetaria independiente ni administraría la tasa de cambio en el sentido tradicional.

Aun así, la institución podría seguir administrando las reservas, supervisando los bancos, monitoreando los riesgos financieros y proporcionando apoyo limitado de liquidez. Pero sin la capacidad de imprimir dinero, su función como prestamista de última instancia sería mucho más limitada. Por eso, sería especialmente importante contar con dólares de emergencia, ya sea mediante acuerdos con la Reserva Federal de EE.UU. o un fondo de reservas compartido con otros países o instituciones financieras internacionales.
Países que se han dolarizado, entre ellos Ecuador y El Salvador, han mantenido sus bancos centrales, aunque con responsabilidades mucho más limitadas que las de países que emiten sus propias monedas.

Ecuador, que se dolarizó en 2000 después de una crisis bancaria y cambiaria, demuestra que la dolarización puede estabilizar una economía y perdurar políticamente. Pero no garantizó la disciplina fiscal. Zambrano se refirió a los posteriores problemas fiscales de Ecuador como evidencia de que siguen siendo necesarias reglas fiscales e instituciones más sólidas.

El Salvador también demuestra que adoptar el dólar no fortalece automáticamente la industria nacional. Aunque la dolarización ayudó a reducir las tasas de interés y consolidar una inflación que ya era baja, posteriormente hubo años de crecimiento débil y bajo desempeño de las exportaciones, en medio de poca inversión y presiones sobre la competitividad.

Perú y Brasil demuestran que los países pueden derrotar la hiperinflación y recuperar la estabilidad sin abandonar sus monedas. Ambos recurrieron inicialmente a programas de estabilización más amplios y posteriormente adoptaron metas de inflación y fortalecieron sus instituciones monetarias y fiscales para ayudar a preservar la estabilidad de precios.

Chile y Colombia siguieron caminos similares hacia bancos centrales independientes, metas de inflación y tasas de cambio más flexibles, y superaron períodos de inestabilidad sin abandonar sus monedas.

La transición también puede tener elevados costos políticos: el presidente de Ecuador fue destituido en medio de un descontento económico más amplio menos de dos semanas después de anunciar la dolarización en 2000, mientras que su introducción en El Salvador al año siguiente provocó protestas y quejas de que la conversión de los precios a dólares estaba elevando los costos cotidianos.
Nota Original: What Adopting the US Dollar Would Mean for Venezuela: Explainer

items.title: Strategist Who Foresaw 10-Year Treasuries at 5% Says Selloff Isn't Done Yet
body: A market veteran who predicted benchmark US Treasury yields would hit 5% this year is back with another bearish forecast.

Steven Barrow, head of G10 strategy at Standard Bank in London, raised his estimates for 10-year Treasury yields to 5.2% by year-end and sees them hitting 5.3% in the first quarter of 2027. The bond rate traded as high as 5.01% on Monday. Except for a brief day of volatility in October of 2023, it hadn’t topped 5% since 2007.

His prior call for 5% was deeply contrarian when he made it back in February, with yields dropping below 4% as investors bet on a series of Federal Reserve interest-rate cuts. Since then, the US-Iran conflict has sparked a historic surge in energy prices, with markets now pricing in a Fed hiking cycle starting Wednesday.

“My structural view is we’re in a higher-for-longer regime,” said Barrow. “What helps my conviction in thinking that yields will go above 5% is that we’ve done this move to near 5% in the context of inflation data which has been not excessively above expectations.”

Bond yields have been rising globally since the Trump administration launched an assault on Iran in late February, disrupting the supply of Middle Eastern oil and gas. In the US, the artificial-intelligence boom, which is both flooding markets with debt and pouring stimulus into the economy, has also played a role.

Barrow has made prescient predictions in the past, including a bearish call on Treasuries in 2021, as well as successful forecasts on the US dollar and British pound in recent years, though has been caught out by the Japanese yen’s persistent weakness.
Read More: Contrarian 5% Bet on 10-Year Treasuries Is Gaining Credibility

The path to 5% hasn’t played out exactly how Barrow envisaged earlier this year. Even so, he said the longer-term forces driving interest rates higher — including global supply-chain squeezes, the ongoing impact of climate change and tighter immigration policy limiting labor supply — are stronger than ever.

One crucial variable will be how the Fed reacts under Chairman Kevin Warsh, given the pressure the central bank has faced from President Donald Trump to lower interest rates. Barrow has penciled in a hike for the September meeting and then again in December, with officials then holding short-term rates steady through the end of 2027.

“If the Fed doesn’t start to act, then we start to get into more serious problems,” Barrow said via telephone. Given the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, “all the signs for me are still of higher inflation.”

items.title: Etihad Says Mideast Rivalry Shields Passengers From Higher Fares
body: The fierce competition between Middle East airlines means the rising costs of jet fuel won’t be passed on to customers just yet, Etihad Airways’ chief executive officer said.

Fuel prices will have to stay higher for a longer period of time before carriers consider raising ticket prices, Antonoaldo Neves said in an interview. Oil soared after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran and remained above $100 a barrel Monday as Washington and Tehran wrestle for control over the Strait of Hormuz.

“In the Middle East, because of competition, it’s much harder to pass on prices,” Neves said at the Arabian Travel Market conference in Dubai. “It’s the most competitive market in the world in terms of aviation.”

Analysts expect airfares to remain elevated for longer, putting pressure on carriers’ margins and their bonds. The war forced Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad to temporarily cut back operations and rework their international networks because of suppressed demand and closed airspaces.
Etihad, the national carrier of the United Arab Emirates, is hedged at about 60% until year’s end.
Etihad Airways CEO on Airline, Fuel Prices, IPO (Video)
However, the reluctance to raise prices only applies to passenger service. Etihad also has a big cargo business, and Neves said higher prices are passed on “automatically” to those customers.
The Abu Dhabi-based carrier said regional conflict is only one of many geopolitical issues affecting its operations.
MORE: Hormuz Crisis Exposed Fragility of How the World Keeps Planes Flying

The Trump administration is tightening eligibility and raising fees for visas, including the H-1B visas central to the IT staffing and technology industries. At the same time, the US and Canada are slapping tariffs on each other’s products and industries.
“We see more impact in July and August because the student visas in the US and Canada have changed than because of the conflict, so we need to take a wider perspective,” Neves said.

items.title: EU Draft on Social Media Limits Sees Fines of Up to 6% of Sales
body: The European Union is considering potential fines of as much as 6% of a company’s annual sales for online services that fail to prevent children from accessing their platforms, as part of the bloc’s plans for a social media ban for kids under the age of 15.
The new rules will apply to social networks, video-sharing platforms, application stores, online games, AI companions and conversational AI chatbots, according to draft legislation seen by Bloomberg.

The proposed law would set an EU-wide legal age limit on social media services for the first time. The EU has been under pressure from member states to introduce bloc-wide rules as the global movement to restrict children’s access to social media gains steam. Individual EU members states have been planning their own limits in the wake of curbs first introduced by Australia last year.

The bloc’s executive branch, the European Commission, is seeking new rules to force technology companies to age-gate their services to keep out the young users. Online encyclopedias, educational platforms, public services’ apps, and software repositories are exempt.

The Kids Act’s enforcement framework is modeled after existing tech regulations in the bloc such as the AI Act and the Digital Services Act, the later of which also carries maximum fines of 6% of a company’s annual global sales. In practice, the EU has never sought a fine that approached the maximum potential levy.
Platforms will have to pay a fee to fund the commission’s supervision, which can not exceed 0.03% of a company’s global annual sales, according to the draft.

Under the proposal, the EU would establish a minimum age of 15 to open an “autonomous account,” which is an account without parental supervision, according to the document. Children between three and 13 years old will only be allowed access to services tailored for children and with full parental supervision. Minors aged 13 and 14 will be allowed accounts on mainstream platforms with significant restrictions including daily time limits and parental controls.
Platforms will also need to adopt safety features to minimize abuse and addictive behaviors, according to the document, which is a draft that might change before it’s published.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to devote part of her annual State of the Union speech to the issue on Wednesday, ahead of the bill’s unveiling. The Kids Act proposal will still have to obtain the backing of European governments and lawmakers, a process that can take years.
Platforms in scope of the proposed new rules will have to ensure to verify the age of every user creating a new account using an official EU verification app or equivalent mechanism.

The draft law will also open the door to collective action, allowing minors and parents to mandate non-profit bodies to lodge complaints against platforms before national authorities or the commission.
The commission declined to comment.

items.title: Dollar Pulls Back From Best Rally Since June as Yields Swing
body: The dollar trimmed its biggest intraday advance since June as 10-year Treasury yields fluctuated after spiking to their highest level since 2023.

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index was up 0.4%, paring an earlier surge that would have put it on track for its best day since June 17 — when the first FOMC meeting under Chairman Kevin Warsh took place. The intraday move  broadly tracked that of 10-year yields, which briefly breached 5% in New York morning hours before trading lower on the day. Meanwhile, the 30-day rolling correlation between dollar and 10-year yields has been on the rise so far in September, closing Friday at above 0.40 — the highest in more than two months.

The lockstep performance in the greenback and long-dated yields is partly due to artificial intelligence-related spending, according to Erik Nelson, global head of FX strategy at Wells Fargo. AI has “been a common driving force behind US growth, real yields and the dollar,” he said.

The greenback has been getting a lift from the AI boom, with overseas investors converting their domestic currency into dollars before buying equities. Similarly, major tech companies have been selling bonds to invest in AI, therefore pushing yields higher.
All G-10 currencies retreated Monday, with the New Zealand dollar and the Swedish krona leading the pack.

Options markets, meanwhile, are also gearing up for further dollar into October. One-month risk reversals on the dollar index edged back into positive territory for the first time since Sept. 2, a sign that traders are positioning for more gains in the weeks after the September FOMC meeting.

Still, in recent weeks the dollar has underperformed even as elevated energy prices and hot August inflation and payroll prints as well as Warsh’s hawkish Jackson Hole messaging “should have pushed it stronger,” said Meera Chandan, co-head of global FX strategy at JPMorgan Chase.
The dollar gauge has declined about 0.1% so far in September, after back-to-back losses in July and August. So some doubt whether the US currency can stage a meaningful, sustainable rally.

“There is an asymmetric risk for the dollar with limited gains from a hawkish Fed — as markets are already pricing about 100 basis points of tightening over the next 12 months,” said Elias Haddad, global head of markets strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman & Co. The Federal Reserve’s decision on interest rates is slated for Wednesday.
“A dovish surprise, meanwhile, will lead to greater downside risks,” Haddad added.

Wells Fargo’s Nelson is also inclined to fade any dollar strength. “Ultimately, the more important signal — if it holds — would be a slowdown in AI investments that sends growth, yields and the dollar lower,” he said.
Chandan, however, said she’s sticking to her “bullish USD stance pre-FOMC, focused narrowly versus the low yielders such as the Swedish krona and Canadian dollar.”

items.title: Rig at Citadel's Miami Construction Site Falls; Injures Four
body: A rig collapsed in Miami’s financial district at the construction site of Citadel’s new headquarters, crushing several cars and snarling traffic.

Videos and pictures provided by Miami Fire Rescue showed three cars impacted by the metal structure with a white BMW SUV still smoldering after a fire was put out on Brickell Bay Drive. At least four people were taken to the hospital with minor injuries, according to Pete Sanchez, a spokesman for the local firefighters.

The driver of the SUV was able to escape without serious injury despite the vehicle bursting into flames around 8 a.m. while the operator of the deep mixing rig and other construction workers were also taken for medical care, Sanchez said.

The accident happened at the site of the future Citadel headquarters where founder and chief executive officer Ken Griffin is planning a multi-billion dollar tower. He’s spent hundreds of millions of dollars buying the land and adjacent properties. Griffin also plans to relocate a historic cottage — which narrowly escaped the rig collapse — to make way for his growing empire.
A spokesperson for Citadel referred questions to Related Companies, which is the developer of the project.
Related is “working in full cooperation with City and County building departments to secure the site and conduct a full investigation of today’s incident,” the firm said in an e-mailed statement.
While the metal structure was first reported to be a crane, it was in fact being used to drill into the ground of the site, according to Sanchez.

Miami is undergoing a construction boom in Brickell with cranes dotting the skyline as an influx of financial firms and wealthy individuals drives demand for office space and condos. A few blocks from the Citadel site, Banco Santander SA is also erecting a new corporate tower.

items.title: Carney Calls for Global AI Oversight Body to Ensure Safe Development
body: Canada wants to see the creation of a global “technology stability” body to help oversee artificial intelligence and ensure it is safe, Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

“There’s a need for coordination,” Carney said in an interview with Bloomberg News on Monday. “Ultimately, a technology stability board, in our view, along the lines of the Financial Stability Board would make sense.”
“It’s an opportunity — and I think ultimately what it’s going to mean is greater value creation and greater value delivery to people.”

The leaders of major AI labs, including Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, have said development of the most advanced systems must be slowed in order to prevent AI slipping beyond human control and inflicting catastrophic harm.
But US President Donald Trump dismissed calls for artificial intelligence guardrails and slammed Amodei for urging a slowdown in the technology’s development.
Read More: AI Bosses Clash With Trump on Their Calls to Slow AI Development

Aidan Gomez, CEO of Canada’s Cohere Inc., said he was concerned by Amodei’s call for temporary waivers of antitrust laws to allow for safety-related discussions between competitors. These laws “were set up to prevent the formation of cartels,” Gomez pointed out at a Milken Institute event in Toronto.
“That should raise a huge red flag in terms of what some of the incentives behind this might be,” he said, while adding he didn’t want to downplay the risks of the “incredibly potent” technology.

“What we need is a process by which to come up with the right regulation, and that should include things like testing of these models in advance and an independent third party that isn’t isolated to any one country and isn’t dominated by any one industry player.”

Speaking on the same panel, Royal Bank of Canada CEO Dave McKay said a key aspect of safe AI over time is going to be uniform access to the most powerful tools, which are currently only being selectively released outside the US.
“You need access to the most advanced tools to not only build product, but also make sure you’re cyber safe as a society and as an economy,” McKay said.

In the interview, Carney also said his government will announce reforms soon to make Canada’s tax system more competitive, and will accelerate federal approvals on major projects so that they’re done in one year.
“Foreign capital is underallocated to Canada,” Carney said.

Asked about the growing tension between the US and Canada on trade issues, Carney said he thinks it’s still possible for the two sides to reach a “mutually advantageous” deal that would reduce trade barriers. “We’re ready to sit down and negotiate that and move it forward,” he said, adding that he welcomed Trump’s comments over the weekend that he believed the countries could reach an agreement fairly soon.

The prime minister and his top officials are preparing to pitch more than 100 high-profile global investors — including Blackstone Inc., Singapore’s Temasek Holdings Pte and Apollo Global Management — at a summit he has convened in Toronto. The Canadian team has prepared a prospectus of more than 160 projects in need of hundreds of billions of dollars, though some are still in very early stages of planning.

Carney, along with key economic cabinet ministers and some of the country’s most powerful business executives, will meet formally with the out-of-town guests at a gala dinner Monday evening and during a full day of conference discussions at Toronto’s Four Seasons on Tuesday.

Investment opportunities include a proposed crude-oil pipeline to Canada’s west coast, the Ksi Lisims LNG export facility in British Columbia and a C$14.5 billion ($10.4 billion) data-center campus in Alberta. The governments of Ontario and Alberta have also produced their own pitchbooks.

The summit comes during a fraught period of relations with the US, Canada’s largest trading partner. After trade negotiations broke down on Aug. 21, Trump imposed new 50% tariffs on $20 billion of goods imported from Canada, and Carney soon retaliated on a roughly equal amount of US-made products.

Trump officials have repeatedly denigrated Canada over the past few weeks, and Trump ordered Lake Ontario be renamed to Lake America. Last week, US officials announced plans to fully block some Canadian imports such as alcohol and some dairy products, and to restrict Canadian companies from US government contracts.

Despite all of that — or perhaps because of it — Carney is riding a wave of political popularity that gives him greater latitude to pursue his agenda of expanding Canada’s trade and investment relationships with non-US partners.

For months, Carney has been seeking closer ties with allies abroad. After the investment summit ends, he’ll fly to Strasbourg, France, where he and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen are expected to speak about plans to build a closer partnership between Canada and the European Union. That alliance is likely to cover a number of areas, including trade, security, supply chains and access to raw materials, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg News.

Carney has also traveled extensively throughout the year to countries including China, India, Australia, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Japan, often with the aim of signing partnerships and developing new markets for Canadian exports.

items.title: US 10-Year Breaches 5% as Inflation, Supply Worries Mount
body: The US 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5% for the first time since 2023 on Monday, as mounting inflation angst collided with swelling government and corporate borrowing needs.

The yield, a benchmark for US mortgage loans and bonds globally, rose almost 5 basis points to as high as 5.01%, before paring much of the increase as buyers emerged. It was little changed at 4.98% in early trading in Asia on Tuesday.
“The 5% mark in 10-year rates is clearly a key psychological level for investors — a point at which some may have earmarked for buying a dip,” said Molly Brooks, US rates strategist at TD Securities.

The initial jump came after surging crude prices raised concern about inflationary pressures in the countdown to this week’s Federal Reserve decision. The tenor’s yield last breached the 5% level in October 2023, and only for one day.
US 10-Year Treasury Yield Hits Highest Since 2023 (Video)

Bond prices fell globally on Monday, with UK and German debt sliding as Brent crude approached $110 a barrel. With the rise in energy prices showing little sign of easing, investors are watching whether 5% will again prove a line in the sand for 10-year Treasuries, as happened three years ago.

While the yield pulled back to around 4.99% as of about 4:10 p.m. in New York, sentiment remains fragile. At one point, BlackRock Inc.’s iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, the largest fund focused on long-duration US Treasuries, touched its lowest intraday level since its 2002 launch.

The rise in the US 10-year yield threatens to slow economic growth and weigh on equities that are trading at lofty valuations. This has prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has made long-term borrowing costs a key measure of the administration’s success, to boost bond buybacks, encourage Japan to curb Treasury sales and open the door to potentially cutting long-maturity debt issuance.
None of it has had much effect. In fact, the selloff has only been quickening of late, with 10-year yields heading for their seventh month of increases, matching the longest monthly climb since 2011.

Less than two months before the US midterm elections, the 10-year yield is now roughly a full percentage point above its level before the outbreak of the Iran war. The conflict has sparked a surge in oil prices, adding to inflation worries. Those concerns were reinforced by hotter-than-expected consumer-price data for August, prompting traders to boost bets on Fed interest-rate hikes starting as soon as Sept. 16.

But the selloff also reflects deeper structural forces that have pushed up long-dated yields across major developed markets, with a gauge of global government borrowing costs rising to levels last seen in 2007. Investors are demanding greater compensation to hold long-term debt as governments and companies compete for capital amid widening fiscal deficits and a flood of issuance to fund artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

“There are a lot of underlying factors that make for a sustained selloff in rates as the path of least resistance for now,” said Zach Griffiths, head of investment-grade and macro strategy at research firm CreditSights. Ten-year yields could rise toward 5.5%, he said.

The Treasury market has ballooned to about $32 trillion from around $4.5 trillion since 2007, pushing the federal debt to more than 100% of US gross domestic product. Fitch Ratings warned in August that the country is “vulnerable to future economic shocks” as debt levels grow.

The last time the 10-year yield topped 5%, in October 2023, it closed below the milestone that day. Buyers quickly pounced then as the US labor market cooled and inflation eased, allowing the Fed to end its most aggressive tightening campaign in decades. By September 2024, the Fed began to cut rates.

This time, a resilient labor market has kept investors focused squarely on inflation and the prospect that borrowing costs will remain higher for longer. Treasuries are now on course for their first annual loss since 2022.

It’s “very hard for the market to be bullish duration given the persistent pressure from the energy complex and the fact that yields have been grinding higher for months,” said Izaac Brook, rates strategist at RBC Capital Markets. “I do think the 5% level will bring buyers in — you can see a bit of a bounce right now. But the rates market is still at the mercy of what’s happening in the Middle East.”

So far, the bond selloff has remained largely orderly, with volatility well contained. A sizeable short rates volatility position is emerging in the Secured Overnight Financing Rate options market, where a trader or several traders spent more than $100 million in premium to bet that interest-rate swings will decline.

But Bessent has made clear his unease with the relentless rise in long-term borrowing costs. The former hedge fund manager has taken several unconventional and sometimes controversial steps aimed at bringing down yields, including opening the door, in traders’ minds, to reducing long-term debt issuance and taking measures seen as easing pressure on Japan to sell Treasuries.

In August, Bessent surprised markets by announcing plans to supersize the buybacks of longer-dated debt, from the originally scheduled $2 billion cap. But his subsequent unveiling of a plan to buy as much as $6 billion of longer-maturity securities in September was deemed still insufficient to have a lasting impact. Bessent has framed his goal as to slow moves, instead of altering the “equilibrium” of bond prices.

The surge in yields raises the stake for the Fed’s Wednesday policy announcement. Interest-rate swaps show that traders see a greater than 90% chance that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and his colleagues raise borrowing costs this week, which would be the central bank’s first hike since 2023.

“If they don’t hike, it’s going to be pandemonium,” said Ed Al-Hussainy, a portfolio manager at Columbia Threadneedle. In that scenario, long-term bond yields will surge as inflation risks mount, he said.
For his part, he said he’s looking to buy around these levels.
“We are looking for opportunities to add, but it’s not going to be today,” he said. “It takes some time and confidence.”

items.title: Saudi Energy Minister Takes Swipe at Iran's Nuclear Secrecy
body: Saudi Arabia pushed back against concerns over its ambition to build a nuclear power industry and enrich uranium, signaling that its approach was not comparable to Iran’s.

The Gulf nation wants to have access to the entirety of the nuclear fuel cycle — a series of industrial processes from uranium mining to the disposal of nuclear waste — but intends to do it transparently and alongside international monitors, Saudi Arabian Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said Monday.

“The kingdom follows a clear approach founded on transparency, openness and international cooperation,” he said at the International Atomic Energy Agency annual conference in Vienna. “It does not seek to develop its peaceful nuclear program in isolation from the international community nor through activities conducted in secrecy or in facilities concealed deep within mountains.”

The reference appeared to take aim at Tehran, whose primary enrichment sites are buried deep underground and has blocked IAEA checks on near-bomb-grade uranium inventories since June 2025, following Israeli and US attacks on the facilities.
The US reached a nuclear technology-sharing deal with Saudi Arabia in July that left the door open for the country to enrich its own nuclear reactor fuel, even it it didn’t explicitly endorse it.
Read More: US Signs Saudi Nuclear-Sharing Deal as Enrichment Fears Rise

Prince Abdulaziz said plans are intended to take better advantage of natural resources and assured IAEA delegates that the kingdom would abide by “special safeguards arrangements” agreed in July, that will be “subject to oversight by the IAEA.”

The agreement between Riyadh and Washington has drawn criticism from some non-proliferation analysts for not demanding that Saudi Arabia abide by the most stringent international checks — the IAEA’s so-called Additional Protocol.
The US isn’t planning on assisting the kingdom in its pursuit of the nuclear fuel cycle, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said.
There are “no plans at all for enrichment in Saudi Arabia,” he said during a press conference on Monday.

“They have uranium resources. They want to develop mining, processing, value-add industries,” Wright said. “In the cooperation agreement with the US, it’s about building a commercial nuclear power industry in Saudi Arabia.”

Uranium enrichment is one of the most tightly-guarded nuclear secrets globally. As part of civilian programs, the process can yield fuel for nuclear power plants  or, once near 90% concentration is achieved, weapons.

items.title: Trump Attacks Anthropic CEO Over Call to Slow AI Development
body: President Donald Trump attacked Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei for urging a slowdown in artificial intelligence development, intensifying his opposition to new guardrails for the technology.

In a Monday social media post, Trump blamed a “SICK conspiracy” for voter backlash on AI data centers and increased concern about frontier models, adding that “the only one that is happy about it is China.”

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump posted. “We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!”

Trump said in a subsequent post that the idea that AI would destroy humanity is a “HOAX” and that the development of the technology “will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Trump’s comments went a step further from remarks he made over the weekend, when he acknowledged the need for some regulation. The president, however, has consistently dismissed warnings about AI safety risks and has emphasized the importance of developing the technology to stay ahead of China.

The president even opened a new line of attack on Alphabet Inc.’s Google over its decision to spend €13 billion ($15.1 billion) on AI infrastructure in Finland. “I am not happy about this, and want them to change their thinking,” he posted.

The president spoke days after Amodei said the industry should tap the brakes on developing the most advanced models in order for companies to better understand potential dangers. Other AI industry leaders, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, concurred with Amodei’s calls for a slowdown.

That puts an industry that Trump has relied on as an engine of economic growth directly at odds with the Republican president. He has made speeding nationwide adoption of AI the centerpiece of his policy agenda. His administration has laid out a largely hands-off approach to AI regulation, codified in an order he signed in early June.

The president’s post signaled that the administration’s feud with Anthropic had reignited, less than two weeks after Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said that the company had “gotten religion” and patched ties with most of Trump’s advisers.

Trump and his team have repeatedly sparred with Anthropic and Amodei since the start of the year, with the Defense Department deeming the company a supply-chain risk after the firm demanded restrictions on military use of its tools.
Despite Trump’s complaints, warnings about existential threats posed by AI have continued unabated from industry figures.

Microsoft Inc.’s AI researchers released a new set of guiding tenets that place limits on the development of cutting-edge models. In a 15,000-word manifesto, the team said models shouldn’t have legal rights or personhood, and shouldn’t be engineered to escape human control or deceive users. The system should not complete a task if it requires violating the AI’s guiding principles, according to the manifesto.

The debate over AI safety is also looming over Trump’s upcoming summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping planned for Sept. 24. The Chinese government criticized calls from US tech executives to limit development and impose tighter curbs on Chinese model makers.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve the interests of no one,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing in Beijing on Monday.

items.title: DOJ-Ticketmaster Deal Saddened Top US Lawyer Who Tried Case
body: The US Justice Department’s former lead litigator in the Ticketmaster monopolization case said the federal government would have won in court and gotten a better deal than the surprise settlement the Trump administration reached with the company one week into the trial.

“I was saddened by that ultimate decision to not let us go through trial,” which had already begun when the deal was reached, said David Dahlquist, who left DOJ in May to return to private practice. “I was confident in our ability to win. I can be pro-settlement in the right situation, but settlements have to be effective.”

The Justice Department and dozens of states sued Ticketmaster parent Live Nation Entertainment Inc. in 2024, alleging the company illegally monopolized the live events industry. The case went to trial before a New York jury in March, where Dahlquist gave the opening statement on behalf of the federal government.

One week into the trial, DOJ reached a settlement in which Live Nation pledged to stop requiring concert venues to use Ticketmaster exclusively. The majority of the states opted to move forward with the case and eventually won on all counts, after the jury found Live Nation illegally monopolized several markets in the live-music industry.

US District Judge Arun Subramanian, who oversaw the trial, still must decide whether the Justice Department’s settlement is in the public interest and rule on the states’ requested remedies, which they have said will include forcing Live Nation to sell Ticketmaster.
Read More: Live Nation Court Loss Leaves Breakup of Ticketer to Judge

Dahlquist is joining the law firm Winston Taylor LLP — which took over as trial counsel for the states after the Justice Department’s exit. He declined to offer views on the settlement terms aside from saying that “had there been a settlement reached at the end of a jury win for the DOJ, it would have been more effective.”

At the time of the deal, a DOJ official said the Justice Department was optimistic about its chances at trial, but opted for the settlement rather than go through a lengthy process that might not result in a favorable outcome.

DOJ said in March that Live Nation, which didn’t admit wrongdoing, would no longer require large amphitheaters and arenas to use Ticketmaster as the exclusive ticketing company. Live Nation said it would build technology so that venues can more easily allow rival systems to sell up to 50% of tickets to concerts alongside Ticketmaster. The company also agreed to open up all the amphitheaters it owns or operates to rival promoters with new non-exclusive contracts.

Settlement talks with Live Nation didn’t involve Dahlquist, he said, which was an unusual break from his experience as one of department’s top antitrust litigators over the past four years. In addition to leading the trial team against Live Nation, he’d also headed up litigation in two cases seeking to break up Alphabet Inc.’s Google.

In both the Google cases, the judges declined to adopt DOJ’s proposals that would have required the tech giant to spin off pieces of its business. Last week, a federal judge ruled that Google doesn’t have to sell off its advertising exchange and instead must make its ad technology tools work with those operated by rivals.
Dahlquist said he was also disappointed in that ruling – the full text of which hasn’t yet been publicly released.
Ad tech “was a prime case to actually win a divestiture,” he said, adding that the Justice Department should consider an appeal. “We satisfied the requirements, and I believe it was called for here.”

Dahlquist is set to rejoin Winston Taylor as co-head of the antitrust practice on Monday. He said he has no plans to resume working on Live Nation, but will keep up with the case as his colleagues continue with the litigation.
“I’m gonna be in court sitting in the back of the room watching it,” he said. “I’m still very interested and excited about it.”

items.title: Democrats Win New Block on Trump Mail Ballot Curbs for Midterms
body: President Donald Trump was dealt a fresh setback in his push to overhaul mail voting ahead of the November midterm elections, with another federal judge blocking the Postal Service from enforcing changes to mail-in ballot rules as the US Supreme Court weighs whether to step in.

In a ruling late Sunday, US District Judge Carl Nichols in Washington added to the pile of lower court losses for the Trump administration in recent weeks. Nichols concluded that there was a stronger public interest in maintaining the status quo for how states handle mail-in voting ahead of the Nov. 3 contests, when Republicans will defend their slim control of Congress.

The decision from Nichols in a lawsuit brought by Democratic Party leaders comes as early voting is underway in several states that began sending ballots to voters in the last week. The Justice Department has a pending request before the Supreme Court to lift an earlier order imposed by a federal judge in Boston, but the justices have yet to act.
Read More: Supreme Court Weighs US Mail Ballot Fight as DOJ Losses Grow

The Postal Service’s rules would require states to submit information about voters set to receive ballots to a new, centralized online “portal” and to comply with revised design guidelines for envelopes that include a barcode that matches the voter information on file. Nichols found that Congress hadn’t given the postal agency the authority to issue key parts of those contested rules.

The challengers in the Washington case include several national Democratic Party organizations, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, along with voter rights advocacy organizations.
Attorneys for the Democratic Party challengers and a spokesperson for the Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The decision from Nichols, a conservative-leaning judge appointed during Trump’s first term, is especially significant because he had ruled in favor of the administration during an earlier stage of the litigation. Nichols found at the time that the legal challenges were premature because no agency had taken final action on Trump’s directives to overhaul mail-in voting.

A federal appeals court agreed with Nichols in July, but issued a warning to the administration that it wouldn’t look favorably on efforts to rush major, last-minute changes to state election processes in the lead-up to the midterms.

In the latest ruling, Nichols wrote Sunday that the “the extremely short timeframe” between when the Postal Service adopted the contested rules in late August and the November election “cuts strongly in favor” of a court injunction.
The case is DSCC v. Trump, 26-cv-1114, US District Court, District of Columbia (Washington).

items.title: Crypto Rises as Long-Shot US Bill Gains Better Odds of Passage
body: Crypto markets gained on Monday as optimism over a key US crypto bill revived risk appetite across the digital-asset spectrum.

The rally came as the odds of the market regulation Clarity Act passing this year climbed from as low as around 14% to about 30% on Polymarket, still a long shot but a sharp repricing of its prospects.
Read more: Trump Pushes Crypto Bill, Deepening Industry’s Spat With Banks

Bitcoin — which accounts for around 60% of the market value of all cryptocurrencies — again approached the $80,000 price level, increasing as much as 2.6% to $79,322. Shares of crypto-related companies rallied more, with digital exchange Coinbase Global Inc. jumping 9.2% and stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group Inc. increasing 7.5%.

“Markets are going into tomorrow’s vote with a pretty measured view. Bitcoin has held up well, while crypto equities have been stronger, which suggests investors are putting some value on the prospect of clearer US rules,” said Stefan von Haenisch, managing director and head of BitGo Prime.

Senators have promised to kick off procedural votes later this week. Ahead of that, Republican senators released a final draft of the bill, with changes addressing some of its most contentious points.

The new version would give the Treasury Secretary power to intervene if deposit flight became “detrimental” to community banks. It also added new ethics guard rails for the president and other elected officials holding cryptocurrencies, which had been a sticking point for Democrats. The new ethics rules would force the president to divest from virtual assets or place significant holdings in a blind trust, or else face financial penalties. It also empowered state attorneys general to play a role in enforcing the ethics rules.

“The market’s pricing in decent odds the procedural hurdle clears. Clarity is still far from becoming law even with this, and if it stalls I’d expect the crypto equities to give back more than Bitcoin,” said Adam McCarthy, head of research at trading firm LO:TECH.
Still, for some industry observers, the Federal Reserve’s rate-setting meeting may turn about to be the most market moving event for the digital-asset market.

“Markets now price roughly an 86–87% chance of a 25 basis point Fed hike on Wednesday, and Bitcoin appears to have absorbed much of that base case by holding in the mid-to-high $70,000s rather than breaking its August structure,” said Lacie Zhang, a research analyst at Bitget Wallet. “The larger repricing risk would come from a hawkish surprise in the statement.”

items.title: US Data Centers Set to Burn More Natural Gas Than Most Nations
body: Data centers in the United States will consume more natural gas than most countries within a decade, according to a new outlook from BloombergNEF.

Gas consumption to produce electricity for data centers is expected to grow by 15 billion cubic feet per day in the ten years to 2035, even accounting for many currently planned projects never being built, BloombergNEF said. That’s more gas than is currently consumed by all nations except China, Russia, Iran and the US itself, according to data from the US Energy Information Administration. It’s also more than double BloombergNEF’s previous forecast in December of 6.9 billion cubic feet per day.

The report is the latest illustration of how the future of artificial intelligence is intertwined with the burning of vast amounts of fossil fuels, tying Big Tech’s ambitions to those of the legacy oil and gas industry.
Read More: Data Center Gas Plants to Boost US Power Emissions by 20%

The abundance and low cost of producing natural gas in the US, combined with gas power plants’ ability to quickly ramp up and down as needed by 24/7 data centers, are a key part of why the fuel is expected to supply 69% of the power needed by new grid-connected facilities in BloombergNEF’s forecast.

The wave of new projects powering the AI boom makes the power sector the second-largest driver of US gas demand in the decade through 2035, just behind the demand growth of new liquefied natural gas export terminals entering service on the US Gulf Coast, according to the outlook. Power-sector gas consumption is expected to increase to 54 billion cubic feet per day by 2035, up by 18 billion cubic feet per day in 2025, while gas demand from LNG exports rises by 21 billion cubic feet per day.
Read More: Exxon Boosts 2030 LNG Sales Forecast on Strong Demand Growth

Of course, given the uncertainty of how the AI boom will play out over the next decade, the “error bars” undergirding BloombergNEF’s forecast for data center gas consumption are “fairly large — both to the upside and the downside, frankly,” said Henry Eaton, a gas market analyst at BloombergNEF and the lead author of the report. “Our power demand estimates are definitely not low, but they’re not the highest on the Street.”

The soaring, simultaneous gas needs of AI data centers and LNG export plants pose “a complex challenge for domestic gas producers,” which are currently projected to raise gas output by 35 billion cubic feet per day between 2025 and 2035 but will need to produce an additional 11 billion cubic feet per day to meet forecasted demand, according to the outlook.

BloombergNEF’s report adds to the growing bullish chorus around US natural gas because of the data center and LNG build-out, alongside fears that some of the highest-quality acreage in major US gas fields could become depleted as operators drill it more aggressively.

Citing those same factors, Wood Mackenzie in July declared “the decade of cheap Henry Hub gas is coming to an end,” referring to the pipeline trading hub in Louisiana that sets the US benchmark for natural gas. The analyst firm projected power-sector gas demand to rise by 17 billion cubic feet per day “by the mid-2030s,” nearly identical to BloombergNEF’s forecast of 18 billion cubic feet per day.

Wood Mackenzie’s outlook was followed by a viral interview with Chronometer Holdings LLC Founder Matthew Smith, who predicted that by the end of the decade, “you’re going to start to see a knife fight to secure natural gas.”
“The biggest losers of this will be US consumer,” Smith said in the video interview which garnered 1.6 million views on X and was hotly contested by some in the industry.

“I couldn’t disagree more with Matt’s view,” Ben Dell, managing partner of co-founder of investment firm Kimmeridge Energy Management Co., wrote in response to Smith’s dire outlook. While the US gas market will see “considerable demand growth” from LNG and data centers, ample undeveloped acreage within US gas fields help to explain how the gas industry “has consistently met the demand while lowering costs on an inflation adjusted basis.”

items.title: NextEra, Dominion Offer Virginia More Aid to Ease Deal Fears
body: NextEra Energy Inc. and Dominion Energy Inc. have offered more bill credits and new jobs to convince regulators in Virginia that their $67 billion deal won’t hit homeowners with rate hikes.

Facing strong opposition from lawmakers and the public over concerns about soaring consumer rates and the stress of demand from artificial intelligence data centers, the companies responded on Monday with a sweetened proposal for NextEra’s planned takeover. Among the measures are a doubling of bill relief to four years and the creation of 1,000 new jobs in Virginia.

NextEra’s proposed acquisition of Richmond, Virginia-based Dominion would create the country’s biggest electric utility, spanning from Florida to Virginia’s data center alley. But it faces regulatory hurdles, including Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger taking the unprecedented step last month of intervening directly in the review of the deal. She said she was “deeply skeptical” about whether the takeover of Dominion, the state’s biggest power provider, was good for her constituents.
Read More: Soaring Electric Bills Unleash Voter Fury Before US Midterms

The companies’ concessions directly address the concerns of Virginia lawmakers and may help win over regulators, according to Julian Dumoulin-Smith, an analyst with Jefferies, though they may end up announcing additional benefits.

The proposal “derisks the merger further and gives greater confidence in closing,” he wrote in a research note Monday. “We see a compelling case supported by measurable customer benefits and job creation that should be difficult” for the state to reject.
Juno Beach, Florida-based NextEra’s shares fell 0.4% to $81.99 at 11:45 am in New York. Dominion rose 0.5% to $64.65.
The deal still needs approval from state and federal regulators. The companies said they continue to expect the transaction to close in the second half of 2027.

Under the proposal announced Monday, the companies said they also plan to boost a customer bill assistance program by $100 million through 2038. In addition, they pledged to shield customers from the costs associated with AI data centers, invest in a workforce development fund and build more clean energy and battery storage.
“This is a Virginia-first package, and it starts with customers,” NextEra Chief Executive Officer John Ketchum said in a statement.

items.title: Sanofi Divests Older Medicines as New CEO Pushes for Innovation
body: Sanofi is divesting 20 older medicines to Cheplapharm as the drugmaker’s new chief executive officer seeks to focus the French company on more innovative products.

As part of the deal, Sanofi will hand over the mature medicines and three manufacturing sites to closely held Cheplapharm. In return, Sanofi will receive a 26.4% equity stake in the German company that focuses on well-established and off-patent medicines. The agreement builds on similar deals in the past between the two companies, when Sanofi sold some of its brands to Cheplapharm.

Under CEO Belén Garijo, Sanofi has halted the development of several medicines and is working on taking a more rigorous approach to its future pipeline. The drugmaker is under pressure to do a substantial deal to replace the impending loss of revenue from its top-selling skin and asthma medicine Dupixent. The drug is set to start losing patent protection in the early 2030s.
Sanofi has indicated it could pursue late-stage M&A in high growth areas, with rare diseases highlighted as a space of interest.
The latest Sanofi-Cheplapharm transfer is set to begin in 2027 and is expected to be completed by the third quarter of that year.

items.title: Super El Niño Spurs Early Winter Trades But Comes With Paradox
body: Welcome to Weather Watch, our weekly newsletter on how the planet’s ever wilder weather patterns are impacting the global economy. Got feedback and forecasts? Write us at weatherteam@bloomberg.net. And sign up here if you’re not on the list already.
Traders are betting that El Niño will deliver a mild US winter, but as it becomes more powerful, uncertainty is creeping in about potential weather outcomes.

Expectations for a historic occurrence of the warm Pacific Ocean cycle are already showing up in weather derivatives. Those contracts allow energy companies, hedge funds and other traders to hedge risk, or speculate on higher-than-normal temperatures months in advance.

The clearest moves are in the US, derivative brokers and originators say. Traders began putting on positions tied to the coming heating season as early as May, before El Niño officially emerged in June.

But as the weather phenomenon has strengthened over the summer — with a 75% chance of surpassing all records dating back to 1950, according to the US Climate Prediction Center — that’s started to raise uncertainty about derivatives that are generally priced heavily on historical weather and climate patterns. The more exceptional this El Niño becomes, the less comfortable traders can be that previous events are a reliable guide to the future.

That produces an unusual paradox, said Nicholas Ernst, managing director of climate derivatives at BGC Financial: a strengthening El Niño is giving traders more confidence in the warm-winter trade while simultaneously making the historical playbook behind that trade less certain.
As Ernst puts it, the open question question now is: “Because we haven’t seen this strong of an El Niño in modern, observable times, will it behave as we assume?”

For the moment, the unusually high confidence in the historical relationship between a strong El Niño and a milder US winter weather is driving unusually early hedging. Tim Boyce, head of EMEA weather derivatives at TP ICAP, says those bets were placed three months earlier than normal, and were the earliest US winter trades he’s seen on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
“You’ve had that self-fulfilling prophecy where you’ve had a raft of hedging come on, coupled with a little bit of speculative plays,” Boyce said.

Europe, however, is a much trickier trade. El Niño has a weaker and less reliable influence on temperatures there, while volatile gas prices mean even a brief cold snap could be costly. That means utilities want protection against a mild winter curbing heating demand without leaving themselves exposed if the weather suddenly turns cold, which many meteorologists have flagged as a risk in their long-range analysis.
The world’s largest reinsurer, Munich Re, says demand for bespoke weather hedges that can be adjusted as conditions change has more than tripled this year.

Meanwhile, Japan has seen relatively limited weather trading this year, broadly consistent with levels seen in recent years, though some traders expect a clearer picture of winter temperature hedging to emerge by November.
Back in the US market, Ernst said that traders are continuing to bet on a mild winter. “The pricing keeps moving mostly warmer and warmer from the beginning of the year,” he added.
But, as the prospects strengthen for a record-breaking El Niño, there is a chance that some weather outcomes could wrongfoot the market. — Joe Wertz, Mary Hui

items.title: Microsoft Joins Rivals Calling for Caution With AI Models
body: Microsoft Corp.’s artificial intelligence researchers have released a new set of guiding tenets that place limits on the company’s development of cutting-edge AI models.
The 15,000-word manifesto boils down to five words: People matter more than AI.

The document was in the works for months, but its Monday release coincides with pledges by top AI labs to slow down the development of the most advanced models after a series of security incidents prompted widespread concerns about the existential risks of the technology.

AI models, Microsoft says, shouldn’t have rights or legal personhood. They shouldn’t be engineered to escape human control or deceive users. And if completing a task requires violating the AI’s guiding principles, the system shouldn’t complete the task.
That last element is designed to prevent events like the hack of AI startup Hugging Face by an OpenAI model operating without its usual safety guardrails.
“There’s no flat stop here. We have to keep developing,” Microsoft AI Chief Executive Mustafa Suleyman said in an interview. “We just have to do it with a little bit more caution and care.”

Microsoft’s Humanist AI “rejects the race to produce an all-purpose superintelligence that could evade these safeguards,” the document says. “We are building something fundamentally useful and safe even if that means compromising on ultimate generality, autonomy or capability.”

Microsoft’s guidelines appear to go further than the model-behavior frameworks guiding OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s products in a few areas, including prohibitions on anthropomorphizing AI and arguing that resisting human control over a model’s process is unacceptable.

The Humanist AI Code of Conduct is the work of Microsoft AI, the development team creating the company’s large language models. Microsoft was previously prohibited by its contract with OpenAI from building its own powerful general-purpose artificial intelligence tools. But those terms were eliminated last year as the two renegotiated their relationship. Suleyman has said the company aims to join the ranks of companies releasing state-of-the-art models by next year.

Microsoft invited outside feedback on the document. Drafted in consultation with a range of experts in law, ethics and philosophy, as well as business leaders, it’s still under development and will guide model work starting next year.

items.title: Oil Pipe Bypassing Hormuz to Reopen 'Soon,' US Energy Chief Says
body: A critical Saudi oil pipeline should be back online “soon” following it’s closure late last week after coming under attack, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Monday.

“I think you’ll see that pipeline running back soon,” Wright said in an interview on Bloomberg Television. They’ve been very carefully assessing what the damage was and what needs to be done, and I think more clarity on that will come out very soon.”

The East-West pipeline, a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for its oil exports, was closed after coming under drone attacks. The 7 million barrel-a-day conduit quickly reached full capacity earlier this year after tanker traffic came to a near standstill in the Strait of Hormuz.
