items.title: About Half of Health Insurance Denials Get Reversed, Analysis Finds
body: Few patients appeal when insurers decline to pay for their care. Many don’t even know they can. But new data show that when they do, they frequently win — in some plans, nine out of 10 times.

That dynamic means many Americans can’t get the care their doctors have prescribed without first wading through a bureaucratic process known as prior authorization. Insurers use the practice to decide whether they’ll cover a procedure or drug, and to help avert what they deem unnecessary care. But the high rate at which some companies overturn their own decisions raises questions about why they’re denying so many doctors’ orders in the first place.

Five large publicly traded insurers denied more than 10% of standard prior authorization requests in 2025 for most Medicare, Medicaid and Affordable Care Act plans, according to a Bloomberg News analysis of recently released data. Patients won about half the time on appeals, according to information made available. The five companies together insure more than 160 million people across all their businesses, including commercial health plans not reflected in the new data.

Insurers disclosed this data on their prior authorizations earlier this year to comply with a new federal rule. Even with some blind spots, it paints the fullest picture yet of an inconsistent practice that some have called to abolish.

The impact is broadly felt. A third of insured adults called prior authorizations a major burden in a poll this year by health researcher KFF. The practice drew renewed attention in the backlash to insurers that followed the 2024 shooting death of UnitedHealth Group Inc. insurance chief Brian Thompson.

Under pressure from the public and the government, health insurers aim to standardize and automate this gatekeeping process.  They defend it as a crucial check against overtreatment that’s estimated to cost as much as $100 billion a year. AHIP,  which represents insurers in Washington, said companies are reducing prior authorization requirements and they respond to most requests in less than a day, faster than federal requirements.
Still, denials can be calamitous for patients.

Amy Smith’s health insurance covered chemotherapy for her rare and hard-to-treat bile duct cancer. Experts at UT MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston thought she might be a candidate for a liver transplant. “It’s the only chance of a cure,” said Smith, 57, a longtime teacher from Kentucky.

Smith’s insurance paid for extensive testing to check if she’d be eligible. She needed to be stable for at least six months, without the tumor spreading beyond the liver. But when doctors finally gave the green light, the insurance company said it wouldn’t cover the transplant itself. “My hopes were up so much, I never in 100 years imagined it would get denied,” Smith said. “I was at their mercy.”

Blue Cross Blue Shield of Texas denied approval multiple times. “We’re done,” her husband Donnie recalled thinking. “There’s nothing else to do.” Smith ultimately got the transplant approved with the help of Claimable, a company that uses AI to help write appeal letters. She got her new liver in May and has been recovering since. BCBS of Texas didn’t address questions about  Smith’s case but said it’s committed to expanding access and aims to help members get appropriate care quickly.

Even some insiders concede the industry has been too slow to act. The reforms underway are “a little late,” said Sachin Jain, CEO of Scan Group and Health Plan, a nonprofit Medicare insurer based in California.

The industry is finally admitting “there’s been a lot of harm that’s been introduced through all the friction that we’re now addressing,” he said. “On the other end of the friction is a person who has a potential cancer diagnosis.”

Archelle Georgiou, a former insurance executive, believes much of that administrative burden could be removed — to the benefit of patients and without hurting companies’ bottom lines. She was chief medical officer at UnitedHealthcare in the 1990s, when the insurer abolished prior authorization, only to bring it back a decade later.

She aimed to turn the newly revealed data into a metric that’s easier to interpret that she calls a “Friction Index.” Her gauge gives extra weight to coverage denials that are overturned when patients appeal. “That is the most egregious because the plan overturned its own original decision,” she said, which needlessly delayed care.

Georgiou, now a strategic adviser to healthcare companies, argues that many insurers could dramatically scale back the most burdensome prior authorizations without giving up valid guardrails against inappropriate care. The metrics are “a starting point, not a verdict,” she said, adding that she’s hopeful they light the way for those changes.

Paring back the number of services that require prior authorizations could mean an insurer’s denial rate — the percentage of requests they deny — goes up “because it’s so much more targeted,” she said. The Friction Index aims to give a clearer picture of the overall burden, not just the percentage of denials.
Regulators aimed to improve transparency with the publicly available data. But it’s often buried on insurers’ websites.

“What we have today kind of misses the mark,” said Michelle Long, senior policy manager at KFF. The data don’t reflect prescription drug denials. The employer health plans that cover most working-age Americans don’t have to report denial rates.
Two large insurers — Elevance Health Inc. and CVS Health Corp.’s Aetna unit — didn’t publish raw numbers of approval requests and denials for some markets, and declined to share them with Bloomberg.
Even so, any data helps shed light on what has long been considered a black box.

Bloomberg News analyzed average denial rates, not weighted by membership, at the level insurers were  required to report them, which varies by line of business. Across the five insurers reviewed, the denial rates varied widely.

Centene denied the highest share of standard prior authorizations in Medicare plans by unweighted average, according to Bloomberg’s review of the data from insurer websites and AuthDenied, a private website that’s aggregating the reports. The company also had the highest rate of reversals.
Medicare plans see the bulk of appeals and reversals compared to other markets.

A spokesperson for UnitedHealthcare, the company’s insurance unit,  said that comparing denial rates between companies isn’t useful, because insurers cover different types of patients and require prior authorization for different procedures. The company says it’s reducing the volume of needed authorizations by 30% with many requirements lifting in October.

A representative for CVS Health said the company has standardized 88% of prior authorizations and requires approvals for fewer services than its competitors. A Humana spokesperson said the company has removed a third of prior authorization codes for outpatient services and offers decisions in one business day for “complete” electronic requests. It’s also launching a program to waive the requirements for doctors that adhere to guidelines. UnitedHealth already has such a program.
A representative for Elevance didn’t respond to requests for comment on the data. Centene declined to comment.

AHIP, the insurer trade group, said it’s working to increase the share of requests done electronically and standardizing data doctors need to submit, to simplify and automate the process. The group said plans have eliminated prior authorizations on 11% of medical services, resulting in 6.5 million fewer requests. Companies committed to honoring previous authorizations for three months when patients switch insurance plans.  AHIP said it’s flawed to assume that services with high approval rates shouldn’t be subject to prior authorization. Denials can reflect when doctors fail to submit the right documentation.

Some healthcare providers say they’ve seen progress. At Duly Health and Care, a large Illinois practice, digital links to insurance companies have cut the time it takes to get a decision, according to Chief Revenue Officer Kerri Balbone. The medical group has fewer staff working on the requests as a result.

Balbone said that in her practice, about 60% of the cases overturned on appeal had been denied because of some administrative error, like missing records or confusion about what was required. The remaining cases involved clinical discussions.

Ben Vallier, CEO of The Iowa Clinic, a physician-owned group with more than 250 providers, said he’s not seeing much improvement. The group still employs about 30 people to work on prior authorizations, the same as last year, he said.
“We kind of laugh when we hear they're going to voluntarily do this or that,” he said. “There’s no voluntary process by which an insurance company is going to give up the ability to make more money.”

The Trump administration this year proposed a rule to streamline prior authorization requests for prescription drugs, requiring insurers to handle the process electronically. It would also make them disclose denial rates for prescriptions. Trump health officials have praised insurance companies for pledging to lower barriers to care. Some say voluntary action isn’t enough. The American Economic Liberties Project, an influential group critical of corporate power, has called for banning the practice in its current form. Multiple Democrats in Congress have also called for overhauling or abolishing the practice in Medicare.

Some question whether the system, which was devised to help keep healthcare costs down, ultimately saves money. When the denial and appeals process delay necessary treatment, patients’ conditions can worsen in ways that make them more expensive to treat, said  Miranda Yaver, a health policy assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh who wrote a book on coverage denials.
“If a patient winds up in the ER or the hospital because they can’t get their important medication, then are we really having the cost savings that we’re promised?” she said.

items.title: Intel-Backed Construction AI Firm Buildots Raises $130 Million
body: Buildots, a startup that uses artificial intelligence to help speed up construction of expensive mega-projects like data centers, chip factories and hospitals, has raised $130 million in new financing.

The investment was led by billionaire Eyal Ofer’s OG Venture Partners, with participation from Lightspeed Venture Partners, Intel Capital, and others, the US-Israeli startup said in a statement on Monday. The company has raised $297 million since its founding in 2018.
With the new investment round, the startup’s valuation is approaching $1 billion, Chief Executive Officer Roy Danon said in an interview.

Buildots’ platform compares actual construction progress against design plans and schedules, identifying bottlenecks and predicting delays, according to the company. Its customers include chipmaker Intel Corp. and data center builder Digital Realty, along with large US construction firms STO Building Group and JE Dunn Construction Co.

The technology aims to avert the costly delays that Danon said developers routinely underestimate. It can show whether “electrical work is moving slowly, it’s also blocking the mechanical work and it’s blocking the commissioning and we can start showing you that knock-on effect that it has on every other activity on the job site,” said Danon. “You need the whole trail of data to get to those conclusions.”

These delays are a particularly acute problem for data center developers, according to Danon, due to the fast-moving advancements of artificial intelligence. Tech giants are spending billions of dollars to build out data centers, many of which have seen major delays and cancellations.

“From the moment you start working on a data center, those GPUs, those CPUs will not be relevant in a few years,” said Danon, referring to AI chips’ short economic life. “You need to redo the whole thing. So the shorter you can make construction, then the more active lifetime those projects have.”

The company, which is headquartered in Tel Aviv and Chicago, employs more than 400 people. It plans to use the investment to roll out new products that cover additional parts of the construction cycle.

items.title: Fetterman Draws Shadow Primary From Democrats Eager to Replace Him
body: I’m Jonathan Tamari, senior Washington reporter for Bloomberg Government, and each weekday I’ll be coming to you with inside-the-room reporting and insights that reveal what’s really happening in Washington—and how it impacts you. Email me with feedback and comments here. If this newsletter was forwarded to you sign up here.
Today: Democrats’ post-Fetterman plans, resistance to an AI slowdown, and Mark Carney’s next challenge.
When it comes to John Fetterman, a consensus is emerging among Pennsylvania insiders: he won’t be a Democratic senator after 2028.

I’ve asked five of them about it in recent weeks and each predicted he won’t run again when his term ends in two years (with a big caveat: Fetterman is unpredictable and has few political friends close enough to know his thinking).

The reasons: Fetterman has never appeared to enjoy the job. He’s hardly raising money (less than $400k in each of the last four quarters). He’s torched his standing with Democratic voters (though delighted Republicans) by repeatedly attacking his own party. And he’s shown no sign of the effort required to win again in a state as competitive as Pennsylvania.
His video appearance at Donald Trump’s GOP midterm convention last week punctuated the striking turn by a pol I’ve covered since 2016.

There could be more drama this week as senators return to Washington for the first time since the convention and following a Wall Street Journal story portraying a dismissive approach to his basic work as a senator. (An X account purporting to be run former aides is promising damaging new revelations.)

Most immediately, there’s the question of whether Fetterman leaves the Democratic party and potentially tilts the Senate’s balance of power, though he has repeatedly downplayed that idea, including last week.
But whatever he chooses, Democrats are already laying the groundwork to run against him in 2028, or replace him if he retires or switches sides.
Among them:

Representative Chris Deluzio has been the most open and aggressive, with a travel schedule taking him well outside his district in suburban Pittsburgh. (I wrote about his moves last year, including a high-profile clash with Trump.)
A spokeswoman, however, told me Deluzio is squarely focused on this year’s elections.
Former Representative Conor Lamb ran against Fetterman in the 2022 Senate primary and got trounced. But many Democrats (AOC among them) now have regrets over not giving him a closer look.

Lamb has also traveled around the state and posted that the conduct reported by the Journal — including Fetterman declining meetings with hospital officials and paralyzed veterans — is “an insult” to Pennsylvanians.
Representative Brendan Boyle hasn’t been out and about as much as the others, but has been sharply critical of Fetterman and has a $5.6 million campaign fund, more than double the senator’s.

Boyle, though, is in line to become House Budget chair if Democrats win the majority and down the road could potentially head the powerful Ways and Means panel, raising questions about whether he’d later ditch those options for an uncertain Senate bid.
Fetterman’s office didn’t respond to my request for comment, but last week he called the Journal story “lies, half-truths, innuendos, smears and anonymous,” per a statement to CNN.
His political options beyond this term don’t look great.

While some Republicans have courted him amid his many Fox News hits, it could be an awkward fit, given his liberal views on abortion, LGBTQ issues, and other social concerns. Fetterman has said he’d be a “terrible” Republican.
He could go independent and still caucus with Democrats, but that’s a short-term solution. Running for reelection without either party’s support would be extremely difficult.
And his poll numbers suggest he has little chance in a Democratic primary should he seek reelection.
Whatever he chooses, fellow Democrats are preparing to take things into their own hands.
Financial markets reacted negatively to the calls for an AI slowdown, showing additional pressure that tech leaders face to keep pushing.
Trump downplayed the growing alarm after OpenAI’s Sam Altman and xAI’s Elon Musk endorsed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to slow down.
China, meanwhile, criticized the warnings about AI and cautioned that a Chinese advantage could threaten American national security.
The returning Senate plans to hold floor votes to advance crypto and college sports legislation, but its pre-November agenda holds off on the biggest pocketbook issues for voters.

Republicans released the final text of the Senate crypto bill, adding new ethics guardrails for Trump and others holding cryptocurrencies, which had been a sticking point for Democrats. The bill still faces opposition from banks.
Oil prices rose as Saudi Arabia closed a major crude pipeline following attacks, disrupting an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. Brent rose to above $108 a barrel before paring gains.
A meeting between Iran and several Gulf Arab nations over a temporary shipping lane through the strait was postponed, partly due to Saudi Arabia’s frustration.

Kevin Warsh’s latitude from Trump will be tested this week as the Fed faces mounting pressure to hike interest rates to tame elevated inflation. The president reiterated Sunday the US should have the world’s lowest rates.

The Kennedy Center could close as soon as Tuesday as its Trump-appointed board says it faces bankruptcy unless it adds the president’s name so it can secure his fundraising support, The Washington Post reports.
Trump, while at a golf tournament at his family course in western Ireland, said he would remove US tariffs on Irish whiskey. He also reignited debate over reunification of Ireland.
Mark Carney made a politically popular move in walking away from trade talks with Trump. Now he has to contend with the economic challenges.
Trump’s immigration crackdown is slowing the Sun Belt’s population growth, undercutting a major factor in its economic growth.
Venezuelan officials will attend a G20 energy summit in Houston this week, underscoring the rapid rapprochement between Washington and Caracas.
Brandon Johnson will seek a second term as Chicago mayor, likely facing an uphill battle against well-funded rivals ahead of next year’s race.
The Trump administration’s attempt to revive prosecutions against Letitia James and James Comey will go before a federal appeals court this month.
Trump’s push to turn US ports into incubators for nuclear-powered merchant ships is running into cautious companies.
Tribal governments are lobbying over prediction markets in the landmark crypto bill, saying the platforms are an “existential” threat to their economies.

Of the 14 House Republicans running for reelection in races rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report, nine of them will get votes on a sponsored bill — or two — in the chamber’s last working week before Nov. 3.

BGOV’s legislative analysts have the details on all the bills that are scheduled to see action starting this afternoon, including ones sponsored by vulnerable Rep. Gabe Evans (Colo.) on data center costs and fentanyl-related production. Embattled Rep. Max Miller (Ohio) sponsored a bill that would give tax relief to scam victims.

Some of the measures will address a presidential fitness council, officially naming a post office, and ensuring there are enough lifeguards at federal beaches; while certainly part of lawmakers’ bailiwick, those issues don’t resonate deeply with voters’ anxieties.
Fifty days until the November elections.
The House and Senate return from recess.
Canada holds a major investment summit through Tuesday.
SEC Chairman Paul Atkins and Senator Cynthia Lummis are among the speakers at the “Solana Summit: Washington x Wall Street.”

items.title: Bessent Touts American AI Superiority, But Has Beefs With Its Champs
body: I’m Chris Anstey, a senior economics editor in Boston. Today we’re looking at the US Treasury chief’s issues with AI champions. Send us feedback and tips to ecodaily@bloomberg.net. And if you aren’t yet signed up to receive this newsletter, you can do so here.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent regularly touts the global dominance of American developers of artificial intelligence. One refrain in that context that he rolls out regularly is that the US last year had 55% to 60% of global computing power, and that “we’re going to have 80%” by 2028.

That’s not to say he doesn’t have issues with the so-called hyperscalers building out the data centers on which AI runs or the software companies pushing the technology’s frontier. And a new one might have just emerged over the weekend.

Leaders of the world’s biggest AI platforms — all American — said it’s time to slow the development pace of their most advanced models, citing escalating risks of the technology. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, issued a lengthy blog post Saturday urging a slowdown, and his call was quickly endorsed by OpenAI chief Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who runs xAI.

But just four days prior, Bessent was arguing for going full steam ahead. “We can’t pause,” he said in a Breitbart News event Tuesday. “You can’t, because the Chinese won’t pause. Even the North Koreans, they won’t pause.”

The Treasury secretary’s key point is that, if the US falls behind its chief geopolitical rival, China will have an advantage with dangerous implications. “If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter.” In remarks on Sept. 2, he said, “I am in charge of managing the relationship with China, and we are ahead on AI,” but “the Chinese are right behind us,” by about six months. If Beijing wins, he said, “they will be able to hack into everything.”
The Treasury didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.

President Trump, in remarks over the weekend, emphasized the importance of staying ahead of China. He also said, “We can put guardrails. We can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up.”
China showed no signs of favoring a halt in development either, with a foreign ministry spokesman on Monday warning against “fearmongering.”

National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Sunday that AI safety a “solvable problem.” House Speaker Mike Johnson indicated the potential for summoning AI industry leaders to “one big meeting,” and said any federal legislation shouldn’t be rushed.

Bessent has had other beefs with the AI companies, repeatedly blasting them for failing to explain to the broader American public what the benefits to them will be. (For his part, Open AI’s Altman agreed, saying on Bloomberg Television the industry “has done a terrible job of this, on the whole.”

The Treasury chief has also suggested the hyperscalers have erred in borrowing large amounts of debt — to some degree in competition with the federal government — at longer ends of the maturity curve. He indicated in August that the 5-year maturity would be a better place for them.
Central banks from much of the Group of Seven face a pivotal week as mounting inflation risks heap pressure on them to raise interest rates.
Three decisions, starting with the Fed on Wednesday and followed on successive days by peers in the UK and Japan, may recast the global monetary policy landscape for the rest of 2026 and beyond.
Elsewhere, Chinese industrial data, inflation numbers from the UK and Canada to India and Japan, and a probable rate cut in Brazil will be among the highlights.
See here for the rest of the week’s economic events.

Framing his return to the policymaking stage after a decade and a half, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh on Aug. 31 observed that he’d departed at a time when the narrative was about a “global savings glut” and stagnant growth prospects, whereas today, “if I were to try to characterize this moment, it would be one of a global investment surge.”

Extending from that same observation, Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, says this is a key reason interest rates are rising. “When capital is abundant and projects are scarce, projects compete for capital, and they compete by accepting a lower return. When projects are abundant and capital is scarce, capital competes for projects, and it competes by demanding a higher return. The return that clears the market is a higher yield.”

It’s also logical that longer-dated rates are rising more than the short-end ones, he wrote in a note Saturday. “Data centers, power generation, transmission and government deficits are all long-duration claims on savings,” he says. They’ll be around for what’s likely to be decades to come. “The competition for capital concentrates at the long end of the curve, which is why long rates have moved more than short rates.”

items.title: Germany to Lobby EU on China Policy, May Seek More Tariffs
body: Germany is preparing a far-reaching package of economic-security measures to shield strategic industries from China that may include new tariffs on hybrid electric vehicles.

German ministries are mapping vulnerabilities to China and assessing countermeasures, with potential proposals including new tariffs, mandatory joint ventures, strengthened inbound and outbound investment screening and a bolstered export controls regime, according to people familiar with the plans. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government is targeting cabinet approval on Oct. 14 before seeking broader European Union support.
Read More: Europe Is Trying to Gauge How Much Pain It Can Take From China

The work is an indication of the hardening shift in Germany’s China policy, which has traditionally been cautious given Berlin’s export-driven economy and deep commercial ties with Beijing. The EU’s trade deficit with China now exceeds €1 billion ($1.2 billion) a day and Germany’s industrial downturn has produced tens of thousands of announced job cuts, with Volkswagen AG planning to increase global cuts to 100,000.

The new plans are a concrete indication of the tougher German stance that seeks to create a more reciprocal relationship after Merz said earlier this year that “we underestimated China’s power and economic strength,” adding that Europe is facing “a major strategic turning point.”

Berlin is working with Paris to build support among other EU members at a summit in Brussels in October and ahead of talks with Beijing later that month, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. The two capitals are working to finalize a joint position paper, which will be shared with the EU as a basis for bloc-wide measures.
A spokesperson from the economy ministry declined to comment. The measures have yet to be brought together in a single draft, and cabinet agreement isn’t assured.

Germany’s position has toughened as Chinese companies move rapidly up the value chain, challenging European manufacturers in industries including autos and machinery. German exports to China fell 9.7% to €81.3 billion in 2025, while imports rose 8.8% to €170.6 billion, according to Germany’s Federal Statistical Office.

European sales of Chinese plug-in hybrid models have gathered pace in recent years, with a record third of such vehicles registered in July made by brands like Chery Automobile Co.’s Jaecoo, according to figures from Dataforce. Chinese carmakers have been winning over consumers with more affordable hybrids at a time when household finances remain under pressure and gasoline prices have surged due to the Middle East conflict.

Merz has accused China of keeping the yuan artificially weak, saying it’s undervalued by 25% to 30%. Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has publicly floated extending EU tariffs to China-made plug-in hybrids, as well as requiring some Chinese companies to establish operations in Europe to form joint ventures under European majority control. He has also backed “Buy European” preferences.

The package under review spans trade defense, procurement, corporate supply chains, critical raw materials, investment screening and technology controls, according to the people. Options include stronger local-content incentives and procurement preferences, more forceful use of instruments such as the EU’s International Procurement Instrument, and stricter requirements for companies to diversify suppliers and their sourcing of critical minerals.

Officials are also considering tighter export controls, including on advanced artificial-intelligence technologies and semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, said the people. The push reflects concerns that China has used some products for military purposes even though they aren’t covered by existing dual-use restrictions, one of the people said.
Read More: Germany Aims for Tougher China Trade Package in Coming Weeks

Another strand would broaden inbound foreign-investment screening, according to the people. German law currently allows the government to intervene when an acquisition is likely to impair “public order” or “security.” The proposals would add considerations such as “economic resilience” and “strategic dependencies” or “asymmetries.” A new investment-screening law is already being prepared.

Outbound investment screening would be more contentious. Some officials want a regime that could review or restrict German investments in China in sensitive fields, they said. Such a step would go beyond the EU’s non-binding review framework, which has focused on semiconductors, artificial intelligence and quantum technologies, and would likely face resistance from free-market conservatives in Merz’s Christian Democratic Union.

Industrial state-support programs could also be redirected toward vulnerabilities along value chains, including financing alternative sources and processing capacity for critical raw materials, according to the people. One example cited is tungsten, which is used in cemented carbides by machinery manufacturers and where officials see heavy exposure to Chinese supply.

Germany has already moved to reduce its reliance on Chinese suppliers in telecommunications. Operators must stop using all critical components made by Huawei Technologies and ZTE in their 5G core networks by the end of 2026. They must also replace the critical functions of the companies’ 5G network-management systems in access and transport networks with technology from other suppliers by the end of 2029. Officials are considering extending that approach to other critical areas of digital infrastructure, the people said.

Many of the proposals are also expected to feed into a broader national economic-security strategy due later this year, according to the people. That would go beyond the economic-protection strategy adopted in March, which focuses chiefly on defending companies and research institutions from physical, digital and hybrid threats such as espionage, sabotage and cyberattacks.

items.title: Brazil Inc. Can Boom - If the Government Cleans Up Its Act
body: A tight formation of panettone streams past me on a conveyor belt. There must be what, 300 pieces? 400?  They move too fast to count, perfectly aligned, marching toward a giant resting area before heading into the packing line.

I’m in Bonsucesso, on the outskirts of São Paulo, South America’s industrial heartland, visiting Bauducco, the world’s largest producer of panettone. Its factory near the Guarulhos international airport is running at full throttle, turning out about 9,000 of the iconic Italian sweet bread every hour, contributing to the 100 million pieces the company makes annually in five Brazilian facilities. Panettone remains its signature product, but Bauducco also makes everything from biscuits and wafers to sliced bread and toasts.

The privately held, family-owned company, which recently opened a major manufacturing and distribution plant in Florida to serve the US market, has ambitious expansion plans. And Brazil’s consequential presidential vote next month won’t get in the way.

“For us, regardless of who wins the elections, we will continue with our growth plan,” Massimo Bauducco, scion of the Italian immigrant family that founded the company in 1952, told me. “We believe in Brazil’s potential and will continue investing.”

Bauducco isn't alone. During a recent weeklong trip to Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia and São Paulo, I heard a similar sentiment from businesspeople across industries: Brazilian executives may fret and rail about the government’s spendthrift ways and interventionist impulses, but they have little time to waste on political dramas. Despite the House of Cards unfolding daily in Brasilia, Latin America’s largest economy keeps expanding, buoyed by its vast domestic market, dominance in key commodities and corporate talent.

Consider the remarkable success stories that Brazilian capitalism has produced over the past few decades even amid political upheavals. Companies such as jet maker Embraer SA, industrial machinery producer WEG SA and pulp giant Suzano SA have evolved into global champions. Brazil’s banks are among the world’s most innovative and corporations have embraced stronger governance, compliance and digital systems, helping build one of the emerging world’s deepest and most sophisticated capital markets.

Of course, Brazil Inc. is hardly insulated from Brasilia’s shenanigans. Political indiscipline places real limits on the ambitions of companies of every size. While multinationals such as Vale SA and Itaú Unibanco Holding SA have the financial muscle to keep investing and growing through turbulence, the country’s other 25 million firms need Brasilia to create a more business-friendly environment. Imagine Brazil’s corporate creativity and size with fewer state diktats, a less punitive tax and labor system, lower interest rates and greater regulatory certainty.

That is the real opportunity awaiting Brazil’s next president. Whoever wins the election will inherit an economy constrained by fiscal irresponsibility, excessive regulation and a Byzantine tax code. The prize is reviving Brazil’s animal spirits through a virtuous fiscal adjustment that unlocks investment, reduces state intervention and allows the private sector to do what it does best: raise productivity.

Before you say I am daydreaming, consider these numbers: My Bloomberg Economics colleague Adriana Dupita estimates that Brazil’s potential growth — the rate of expansion an economy can sustain at full capacity and employment — will average 2.3% a year between 2026 and 2035, more than double the 1.1% of the previous decade. Her forecast already assumes cautious fiscal improvement and some structural reforms that should drive a recovery in investment capacity and stronger productivity. That’s an encouraging starting point. But what if a shock of confidence improves expectations more dramatically? A bolder reform agenda could shift business sentiment and growth far beyond what the baseline suggests.

Interest rates are a good case in point. Whatever one thinks of the central bank’s tightening cycle, a 14% nominal policy rate — almost 10% in real terms — is unsustainable for any productive activity in the medium run. It’s no coincidence Brazil is experiencing a wave of corporate restructuring filings, including several high-profile cases. The dynamic is perverse: The government overspends, debt dynamics deteriorate, inflation heats up, the central bank responds with exceptionally tight monetary policy, and … companies starved for capital or burdened by debt go under.

The next president, working with congress, has a chance to break that cycle through aggressive but credible spending cuts, the kind of “expansionary austerity” championed by the late economist Alberto Alesina. Javier Milei, in next-door Argentina, has shown how quickly a new political cycle can reshape expectations when backed by conviction and parliamentary support. Adopting such radical change should translate into single-digit interest rates faster than many envision in Brazil.

Equally important would be measures to arrest the avalanche of labor litigation, which cost Brazilian companies a record of almost $10 billion just last year. Despite the 2017 labor reform, the activism of some courts, including the powerful STF, has boosted the number of cases processed in Brazil’s labor judiciary. During my recent trip, executives also shared astonishing stories of how companies must navigate the country’s bureaucracy and permanent tax modifications, retaining a battalion of accountants and lawyers on payroll simply to interpret the law.

Over the years, Brazil’s corporate and productive clusters have grown increasingly detached from Brasilia’s political frenzy. It’s as if they are becoming two different countries, speaking different languages, a divide you can sense simply by taking the 90-minute flight connecting the capital to São Paulo. It’s time for Brasilia to start giving a bit of love back to companies and entrepreneurs again. They are the ones who can turn Brazil into the front-rank economy it deserves to be.

items.title: Pakistan Keeps Rates Steady as Price Pressures Build
body: Pakistan kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged for a third straight meeting as policymakers balance the need to support growth against mounting inflation risks from the Middle East conflict.
The State Bank of Pakistan held the target rate at 11.5%, according to a statement Monday. The move was predicted by most of the analysts surveyed by Bloomberg.

The decision comes as Pakistan seeks to sustain an economic recovery after coming close to a sovereign default in 2023, with the conflict threatening to drive up import costs and strain its external finances.

Credit-rating upgrades and a record $3 billion junk-bond sale have underscored the improvement in investor confidence. But the country remains vulnerable to energy shocks after soaring oil prices earlier this year threatened to erode its foreign-exchange reserves.

Those risks are already feeding into inflation. Consumer prices accelerated to a faster-than-expected 11.15% in August, driven by higher food and energy costs and complicating the central bank’s efforts to bolster growth.
Any further escalation of the US-Iran war could intensify those pressures, with a significant share of Pakistan’s energy supplies passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Pakistan’s stronger financial position has also translated into improved sovereign ratings. Moody’s Ratings upgraded the country last month, citing a stronger external position, better fiscal metrics and lower domestic financing costs, following a similar move by S&P Global Ratings in July.

The SBP expects inflation to remain in the 5%-7% range in fiscal 2027, while GDP growth is projected at 3.5%-4.5%. The current-account balance is seen between 0% and 1% of GDP. The issuance of Eurobonds in September, along with significant FX purchases by SBP, helped boost FX reserves to $21.4 billion.

items.title: Zelenskyy Moves to Dismiss Ukraine Chief Prosecutor in Graft Row
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy took a step to dismiss Ukraine’s embattled chief prosecutor, siding with anti-corruption agencies in a showdown over a probe into an alleged call center scheme.

The president signed a decree Monday to remove Ruslan Kravchenko, paving the way for lawmakers to approve the decision in a vote on Tuesday. The top prosecutor had submitted his resignation last week after a senior official in his office was detained and accused of taking part in a protection racket.

But the move to dismiss Kravchenko may signal the growing clout of the anti-graft agencies, which have enjoyed broad public support. Zelenskyy’s attempts to curtail their activities last year sparked street protests and pressure from Ukraine’s main allies and donors.

While Kravchenko has denied any involvement in the alleged corruption scheme, he unexpectedly hit back Monday at the two anti-graft agencies, NABU and SAPO, saying their heads falsified documents. He also accused Zelenskyy of mounting political pressure against him before posting on Telegram that he’d left the country for a “business trip abroad.”
Read More: Zelenskyy Aims to Contain Anger Over Defense Minister Ouster
Ukraine’s ability to weed out corruption has come into focus after Kyiv told Western allies its funding shortfall this year will be bigger than initially planned and asked for more financing.

Zelenskyy has been trying to defuse domestic discontent and assert his authority as Ukraine gears up for another winter of Russian strikes with dwindling supplies of critical Patriot air defense missiles.
The head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, Semen Kryvonos, dismissed Kravchenko’s claims against him as “nonsense.”

“It is an unprecedented attack, but we anticipated such reactions,” Kryvonos told reporters in Kyiv on Monday. “Further investigative actions will take place within the framework of the published proceedings.”

items.title: Apple's iPhone Duo Tackles the Challenge of Taking Foldables Mainstream
body: Welcome to Tech In Depth, our daily newsletter about the business of tech from Bloomberg’s journalists around the world. Today, Ed Ludlow considers whether Apple’s folding phone, Duo, will shake up the market.
AI fears: Top executives at three leading artificial intelligence companies say it’s time to slow down development of the technology. They cite a surge in risks from their most-advanced models.
Chipmaker bonuses: Micron will give its Taiwanese employees a $31,600 cash bonus and additional stock rewards. Profits at the US-based memory-chip maker have soared.
Watches that listen: The new Apple Watch models have AI always-listening features. Legal experts say that might be a problem.
Death of a pioneer: William Draper III, the co-founder of the first venture firm on the West Coast, has died. In a career that began in 1959, he backed companies including Activision and Skype.

Firehawk Aerospace is in talks for a funding round valuing the defense technology company at $1.25 billion. The startup is seeking to raise $100 million to $200 million. Rochefort Asset Management is leading the round, and 1789 Capital, which counts the president’s son Donald Trump Jr. as a partner, is expected to participate, according to people familiar with the matter.
Of the roughly 1 billion smartphones that will ship this year, only a tiny fraction will fold.
Foldable phones have spent years as a niche product: expensive, sometimes flimsy and dogged by compromises like the crease. Growth has been slow. Then Apple finally made one.

The $1,999 iPhone Duo probably won’t transform the overall smartphone market overnight. But Apple’s arrival could transform foldables — pushing the form factor toward the mainstream and forcing rivals to respond.
Readers of my colleague Mark Gurman knew much of what was coming. He reported the Duo name, roughly $2,000 starting price, dimensions, screens and many of its features ahead of the event.

I got significant hands-on time with the Duo at Apple Park last Wednesday, and what struck me was how well it all comes together. Opening it doesn’t simply give you a bigger iPhone screen; the software changes with it, making the device feel closer to an iPad. My colleague Chris Welch went deeper in his hands-on review and came away saying it was the most excited he’s been about a new Apple handset since the iPhone X in 2017. His early verdict: Apple has “raised the bar” in a category where it’s playing catch-up.

And while Bloomberg had reported the roughly $2,000 price, it was well below what some forecasters had modeled — as high as $2,300 to $2,500 for the entry-level variant. For many, this was the catalyst to call it a game changer for foldables.

Before the unveiling, industry research firm IDC expected just 22.9 million foldables to ship this year, versus more than 1 billion smartphones overall. Without Apple, IDC said foldable shipments would have declined at a double-digit rate. With Apple, it expects the category to grow almost 13%.

That forecast may already be too conservative. After seeing the Duo and its $1,999 price, IDC’s Nabila Popal told us on Bloomberg Television that “we might just have to pull the foldable forecasts up a bit.”

Bloomberg Intelligence has raised its forecast, now expecting about 14 million Duo units to be sold in the first 12 months, potentially generating roughly $28 billion. BI called it one of Apple’s better-designed products in several years.

Bank of America had already seen signs of potentially significant volume: supply-chain checks earlier this year pointed to a wide range of 10 million to 20 million foldable iPhones. After the launch, Wamsi Mohan reiterated his “buy” rating on Apple and said the lower-than-expected price should help drive higher unit sales. When he joined me on Bloomberg Tech, Mohan also argued that Duo could expand the market rather than simply take share: Its larger screen and software make it a productivity device, potentially replacing an iPad Mini for some users rather than becoming another product to carry.

That gets at what Apple is really trying to do. During the launch, new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus mocked existing foldables as essentially two phones glued together. Duo’s pitch is different: An iPhone when you need a phone, and something closer to an iPad when you open it.
Apple arrived years late to foldables. The question isn’t simply how much of today’s tiny market it can capture. It’s whether Apple can finally give millions more consumers new reasons to want one.
The day’s most read story in tech and entertainment:

Anthropic says its AI model Claude has been misused in attempts to develop a wide range of military applications. Those in countries including China and Iran have tried to deploy Claude for building autonomous drones, develop software for missiles and investigate potential biological weapons, according to a report from the AI firm’s threat intelligence team.

items.title: Trump's Push to Cut Federal Jobs Lacks a Goal and a Vision
body: Wondering why so many things seem to have been going wrong this year, from contaminated lettuce to measles outbreaks to air-traffic-control-related flight cancellations? The reduction in federal government capacity caused by the Trump administration’s job cutbacks may be a factor.

The administration has made shrinking the federal workforce a top priority, and it has done so at a remarkable pace. But many of the job cuts don’t appear to have a coherent goal, and the overall result so far is a federal government that spends about as much money as it did before but by all appearances does a worse job of it.

The timeliest data available, from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, show a seasonally adjusted decline in civilian federal employment, excluding the US Postal Service, of 332,900, or 13.6%, since President Donald Trump moved back into the White House in January 2025. That’s a huge drop, surpassed over the nine decades for which these numbers are available only by the sharp federal employment drawdown after World War II and the slower decline after the end of the Cold War (as long as you don’t count the ins and outs of temporary US Census workers).

The US population and workforce have grown over this period, of course, leaving federal employment’s share of overall nonfarm payroll employment at a record low of 1.303% in July. Measured by employment at least, the age of big government is long past. Measured by spending it is not, but employee pay and benefits amounted to 10% of federal spending in the 2025 fiscal year, according to a Peter G. Peterson Foundation analysis of federal data, with civilian executive-branch employees — the focus of the Trump administration’s job reductions — accounting for just 5.5%. If the goal were to reduce spending, the richest targets are elsewhere, and in fact federal spending has risen since Trump returned to office, although noninterest spending has at least been roughly flat.

So what exactly has the Trump administration been up to with all these job reductions? The federal Office of Personnel Management (OPM) keeps tabs on monthly federal employment down to the subagency level, and the statistics paint a revealing if not exactly crystal-clear picture of the administration’s priorities. Agencies long in the crosshairs of conservative activists have shed lots of jobs, and the two immigration-enforcement agencies have unsurprisingly added many of them. But what is perhaps most striking is how widespread the job losses have been, with many agencies that I don’t think anybody in the administration really had in their sights struggling to get by with much-reduced workforces.

The table below ranks the nondefense agencies — plus the Army Corps of Engineers, which focuses mainly on defending us from water — with the biggest job losses since Trump took office. I left out defense agencies because their June and July numbers are incomplete and also because many defense job shifts were due to reorganizations and renamings that would take several columns to unravel. (The civilian defense employee total was down 89,668, or 11.6%, as of May.)

That the US Agency for International Development lost 95% of its employees is not news — it was the main early focus of temporary government employee Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency — but remains shocking. A smallish federal agency that had long enjoyed bipartisan support and funded some quite-effective global public health programs was effectively shut down with no input from Congress. Why? Musk spread unhinged conspiracy theories about the agency’s supposed sinister activities, which the president partially echoed, and the White House released a short list of questionable if mostly quite small expenditures. But my sense is that, because it didn’t have a significant domestic constituency, USAID was mainly just an easy target for an assertion of power meant to cow Congress and other agencies. With credible estimates now putting the loss of life from the health-program cutbacks in the millions, its destruction leaves a bloody stain on this administration and on Musk that will never go away.

By contrast, the huge employment reductions at the Internal Revenue Service were largely a rollback of increases in enforcement and customer-service staffing during the Biden administration. This rollback is almost certainly reducing tax revenue and increasing the deficit, but it was endorsed by Congress and popular with many Republican voters. Other agencies seen as suspect by some conservatives, such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (home of most federal climate research) and Bureau of Land Management (famously the target of armed protests by right-wing Oregon ranchers), have also experienced sharp staffing reductions. The same goes for the Department of Education, which the administration has vowed to close but doesn’t show up in the above table because the department wasn’t very big to begin with and is also divided in the OPM data into a number of subagencies (total department job losses so far add up to 1,832, or 44.6%).
The list of big winners is a lot shorter.

The biggest employment gain here is the result of a reorganization that consolidated financial management, human resources, communications and other functions previously performed separately by Interior Department agencies such as the National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Reclamation in the office of Secretary Doug Burgum. Overall Interior Department employment fell by 10,214, or 14.6%, from July 2024 to July 2026 — which is a better comparison than January to July because several of its agencies hire lots of summer employees. The employment increases at the two immigration-enforcement agencies were not just the result of shuffling people around and are on a scale not seen anywhere else in the federal government. The next biggest non-reorganization gainer was the Secret Service, with an increase of just 413 jobs, or 5.1%.

The overarching picture is of a shift of government resources to immigration enforcement and away from everything else. Even agencies not targeted for cuts by the administration suffered big job losses as employees signed up for the buyouts offered by DOGE and other early retirement programs. Did the president really mean to abruptly reduce staffing at the Transportation Security Administration and Federal Aviation Administration (which employs air-traffic controllers)? Probably not, but that was the result of his policies.

During Trump’s first term, federal employment rose. The fact that his second has come to be defined by job cuts owes much to the efforts of biotech-entrepreneur-turned-politician Vivek Ramaswamy, who during his campaign for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination pledged to reduce federal employment by 75%, then continued to push for huge job cuts after President-elect Trump appointed him and Musk as co-heads of DOGE (a job Ramaswamy left before Trump took office). This staff reduction was supposed to go hand-in-hand with big reductions in government regulation, but it was never clear how the two were linked — most federal government employees don’t spend their days writing or enforcing regulations, they provide services like medical care or disaster aid or firefighting or help with getting Social Security. White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought has argued that focusing on “the spending that is the easiest to cut practically” can build public support for the government-benefit reductions needed to get the federal deficit under control. But apart from some Medicaid and food-stamp cutbacks in the 2025 budget act, there hasn’t been much action on that front, and overall that legislation was deemed by the Congressional Budget Office to have increased the deficit by $3.4 trillion through 2034.

The push to reduce federal employment instead seems to have taken on a life of its own, proceeding at many agencies without any apparent vision for what it’s supposed to accomplish. Pushing out career employees and replacing them with Trump loyalists is clearly one goal, but at the place where that’s been most explicit, the Justice Department, it’s been quite a struggle to find qualified lawyers willing to work there. And while older workers have left in large numbers to take advantage of buyout and early retirement offers, the number of young federal employees has fallen even faster, with workers in their late 40s the only group experiencing gains. (These age-group numbers do include the defense agencies with their incomplete June and July data, so I’ve measured the change as of May.)

There haven’t been big differences in job-loss rates by educational attainment — the share of federal workers with college degrees is, at 53.5% as of May, about the same as what it was before Trump took office. There may be big differences by race but, this being the Trump administration, the OPM no longer provides data on that. It no longer breaks federal employment down by sex either, but the BLS still does in its payroll employment statistics. These show a marked change since Trump returned to office in the percent of federal employees who are women, although at 47.2% in August the share was still higher than at any time before 2024.

All in all this feels less like a thought-out effort to reshape the federal government than a somewhat inchoate attempt to assert executive power, punish perceived political enemies and just be seen as doing something. If federal agencies keep struggling to perform popular or essential tasks, the effort may increasingly be seen as doing something counterproductive.

items.title: US declining labor force and immigration
body: Geopolitical power comes from many different sources, from innovation to military brawn to resource riches. Throughout its 250-year history the US has had one consistent economic superpower though: a relentlessly growing population and an unmatched capacity to attract people.

Like many things, that’s a facet of the US that is changing dramatically. As my colleague Catarina Saraiva and I write for Bloomberg Businessweek magazine in a story out today, you can see it happening in cities like Houston. The consequences, though, are much bigger than the story of a single place.

Like many other Sun Belt cities, the Texas metropolis has over the past half century built an economy centered in large part on population growth. The Houston metro area has added 3 million people (almost 40% of its current population of almost 8 million) this century alone. Much of that growth has come in the form of international migrants who make up a third of the local labor force. But as President Donald Trump pushes through the biggest change in US immigration policy in 60 years, the flow into Houston is slowing dramatically.

The most recent comprehensive Census numbers available show the population of Harris County, the biggest county in the Houston metropolitan area, increased by just under 1% in the year ending July 1, 2025, the slowest growth since the pandemic.

Source of GrowthThe number of immigrants arriving in Harris County from outside the US had already fallen by more than 40% in that year to July 2025. And since then there’s plenty of evidence things have only slowed further amid Trump’s crackdowns. Which is why Houston is confronting the very real possibility of what would be the first decline in its population since a 1980s oil bust. In the words of Pia Orrenius, a labor economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, Houston is a “poster child” for what happens to US cities when you cut off immigration.

“Their population growth has entirely been due to international immigration,” she says. “What we’re worried about now going forward is, given a world of net-zero immigration, that source of growth, especially for Harris County, is going to be gone.”

More recent numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics show that in the first half of this year, Houston experienced its biggest contraction of potential workers this century, outside the pandemic. Houston’s story is evidence of a major shift in America’s economic story. Of the 14 Southern and Western states including Texas in the Sun Belt, 12 saw their populations grow by less than 1% and 13 recorded growth below historical trends in 2025, according to our analysis of Census data. Labor force data for the first half of this year suggest other Sun Belt metropolitan areas, such as Phoenix and Nashville are seeing the same trend as Houston. Trump’s immigration push, combined with a birth rate at a historic low and an aging population, means the US as a whole faces the possibility of the first population decline in its recorded history much sooner than demographers anticipated. All of which presages worker shortages, lower tax revenue, struggles to fund government programs like Social Security and slower economic growth. All that also raises questions about the future of American power. If America’s secret sauce for a long time has been its capacity to attract not just a vast pool of labor but the best and brightest from all over the world to its universities or to establish businesses, then what happens next? And what might that mean for the rest of the world? US pundits have for years already been pointing to China’s already shrinking population as evidence that its powers have peaked and of daunting domestic problems.

That too has global implications. One solution to China’s contribution to imbalances in the global economy that is often mentioned is boosting its domestic consumption. But if the pool of Chinese consumers is shrinking that becomes harder. Which explains partly why Chinese companies are so eager to grow overseas and the genesis beyond government policy of what is often called China Shock 2.0.

China ShockThat in itself has repercussions beyond China. A new analysis from Bloomberg Economics shows that the market share lost to Chinese manufacturers in recent years cost the 27-nation bloc 0.7% of its gross domestic product — or almost $150 billion — in 2025. A year earlier, the estimated impact was 0.5%.

Part of the economic allure of China for decades has been the promise of a new pool of global consumers. But Chinese consumption pales in comparison to the US’s. So what happens when the population decline happens in the world’s largest economy (the US) as well as its second-biggest (China) as plenty of other large economies confront the same? Once upon a time the American answer to the looming demographic problem was its superpower to import talent. These days, though, we are starting to learn what happens when you shut that historical allure down in cities like Houston. They are being forced to confront the need for a very different economic model. Eventually it will be the US doing so. Which matters for American power. And the world.

items.title: BYD's New EV Charges Ultra-Fast But God's Eye Self-Driving Software Needs Work
body: Welcome back to Bloomberg’s Auto Monitor, a weekly roundup of stories on the automotive industry from reporters around the world. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.

We took BYD’s new electric sedan for a spin through Shanghai to test its fast-charging technology. Our big story shows how the battery performed, and why you should be ready to jump in when letting the car’s software handle the driving.
We also have stories on Volkswagen’s restructuring plans, Ford getting rebuked over its business ties to China, and a quirky new electric Audi. All this and more, below.
I spent much of Thursday driving BYD’s new Seal 08 performance sedan around Shanghai to find out whether the company’s latest electric-car technology lives up to the hype.
When it comes to charging, the answer was an emphatic yes.

At one of BYD’s proprietary flash-charging stations, the car’s display showed that its blade battery had added 471 kilometers (293 miles) of range in just five minutes. Theoretically, that’s enough to drive from Los Angeles to Las Vegas. The entire stop lasted just over nine minutes, during which the battery juiced up from 16% to 97%.

The technology is key to the Chinese manufacturer continuing its expansion abroad and taking customers from the likes of Toyota and Volkswagen. Tesla’s latest Supercharger stations in China take 15 minutes to add as much as 250 kilometers of range.

There are some caveats to keep in mind. BYD’s flash-charging stations are limited mostly to China, so don’t expect access to that speed overseas soon. The manufacturer is rolling them out in markets including in Europe, but it’s a tedious undertaking because tighter regulation there tends to slow projects down.

Then there’s the range. My experience that day suggests that the 239,900 yuan ($35,767) model probably won’t often manage its advertised 785 kilometers in a real-world environment. I spent more than eight hours navigating small alleys, jammed city roads and multi-lane highways and got an estimated range of between 550 and 580 kilometers.

The difference is not unusual for a high-performance EV like the dual-motor, all-wheel drive version I got. A more entry-level variant with fewer sporty features may get a better range. The charging experience still was impressive, and it’s a big plus for EVs when juicing up the battery won’t take much longer than filling up the tank. The problem is getting your hands on a car that actually has this new technology.

Customers currently have to wait weeks or even months to receive their Seal 08 after ordering started in July. That’s because around half of BYD’s production capacity is still being updated to make the second-generation blade batteries that debuted in March, said Chris Liu, a senior analyst at Shanghai-based consultancy Omdia.

It’s a consequence of BYD’s vertical integration system based on making key components inhouse, a strategy that has helped the company keep costs down. But when an entire battery generation needs changing, the congestion “sits inside its own system rather than being diversified across suppliers,” Liu said. BYD expects to work down the bottleneck through the end of this year. I’d flag that the company provided me with a Seal 08 as the car hasn’t hit rental fleets yet.

Aside from the battery, a key selling point of EVs is software. Like most BYD models, the Seal 08 I drove had the so-called God’s Eye driver-assistance system installed. After a promising start, it soon became clear that the software still needs work.

God’s Eye performed well on major highways and clearly marked urban roads, making smooth lane changes and handling surrounding traffic including scooters and pedestrians confidently. It parked itself swiftly on the side of the road and in underground garages.

Yet in more complex situations, it had its shortcomings. The system unexpectedly disengaged on poorly marked roads and sometimes followed another lane’s speed limit. In one occasion, it attempted a left turn in a right-turn lane, and it stalled in a busy intersection until a traffic officer ordered me to take over.
Read More: Why It’s So Hard to Make a Reliable Self-Driving Car

Most concerning was an on-ramp merge, when the car cut aggressively onto the highway before apologizing and asking me to take the wheel. A robot mea culpa is a nice touch, but I’d rather have the system handle the situation better in the first place, or hand things over to me more quickly.

None of these incidents mean the system is entirely flawed. Most advanced driver-assistance products still have their limitations, as demonstrated by regulator scrutiny in the US over Tesla’s FSD system. Neither was my drive a proper, controlled test using standard benchmarks.
But what became clear was that God’s Eye still needs improvement. It often looked very capable until it suddenly wasn’t.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

China’s retail car sales slumped 24% in August as a persistent real estate crisis crimps big-ticket spending. Automakers are racing to escape a fierce domestic price war by pushing exports, which jumped 78% to 888,000 vehicles. BYD last week set an ambitious target to sell more than 2.5 million vehicles overseas in 2027. It delivered a little over 1 million to foreign markets last year.

Volkswagen is considering selling Italian motorcycle maker Ducati as it reviews its sprawling asset portfolio. The maker of high-performance bikes may be worth €1.25 billion ($1.5 billion) based on peers’ valuations. The automaker separately sealed a preliminary agreement with Israel’s Aurelius Capital that would repurpose VW’s Osnabrück, Germany factory to make military equipment with Israel’s Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.

President Donald Trump said he may allow a Chinese automaker to manufacture in the US if it did so with American workers, while pledging to maintain the effective US ban on Chinese imports. If China were to “open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be okay with it — Japan does it — but they hire our people,” Trump said.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blasted Ford over its business ties with China in a strongly worded letter. The maker of the F-150 pickup truck is licensing battery technology from CATL for a plant in Michigan, and earlier this year struck a joint venture with automaker Geely in Spain.

Duffy’s letter ignores that Ford’s Chinese competitors are now setting the pace in the global auto industry in critical fields like vehicle design and manufacturing, user experience and electrification, writes Bloomberg Opinion’s Liam Denning.

Audi is reviving its quirky A2 model as an EV tailored to European buyers, priced from €38,200 in Germany with a range of 646 kilometers on a single charge. The comeback bid reflects a broader strategic shift by brand head Gernot Döllner, who has put Europe at the center of Audi’s recovery after the brand lost market share in China and lacks US production to offset tariffs.

items.title: AI Bosses Clash With Wall Street and Trump Over Safety
body: Good morning.  AI chiefs are hitting the brakes, and Wall Street isn’t happy. Kevin Warsh may be about to test the limits of Fed independence. And Mark Carney rolls out the red carpet for some of the world’s deepest pockets. Listen to the day’s top stories.
— Hellmuth Tromm

AI’s safety debate is coming to a head, pitting increasingly cautious industry leaders against Wall Street and Donald Trump’s administration. The biggest players want to slow development, while the president is downplaying the risks. China is also pushing back against AI “fearmongering.” The warnings are rattling markets, with tech stocks leading a global selloff.

Adding to the unease, oil pushed higher after Saudi Arabia shut a major crude pipeline following multiple attacks, disrupting a key route for bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. Diplomatic efforts also stumbled, with talks on a temporary shipping lane through the strait postponed. Oman called for alternative LNG routes through the Gulf. The US, meanwhile, kept up pressure on Tehran, blocking a top Iranian nuclear official from addressing the IAEA.

Then there’s the Fed. Kevin Warsh is on a collision course with Trump, with markets overwhelmingly betting on a rate hike this week. Trump has threatened to escalate his trade wars if policy isn’t eased and continued to argue that US borrowing costs should be the world’s lowest. With the 10-year Treasury yield flirting with 5%, some investors say the Fed is already “behind the curve.”

Trump’s immigration crackdown is reshaping more than the border. Houston’s population-driven growth model is stalling, and the slowdown extends across the Sun Belt. As deportation orders surge to a record, the US may even be heading for its first-ever population decline.

Trump’s climate rollback is set to deepen, with the EPA poised to scrap Biden-era carbon limits on fossil fuel power plants. It already dismantled similar rules for vehicles and a landmark finding on greenhouse-gas risks. The Supreme Court struck down Obama’s Clean Power Plan in 2022, while Biden’s replacement required coal plants to capture most carbon emissions by 2039 or close — the mandate now being repealed.

Mark Carney’s brainchild, the first-ever Canada Investment Summit, kicks off today, drawing money managers overseeing more than $70 trillion. The charm offensive comes as Canada grapples with fallout from his politically popular decision to walk away from trade talks with Trump.
Magic Johnson called Mark Walter a mentor. Now, the Lakers legend’s business ties to the Dodgers owner are drawing scrutiny from investigators.
Big Take Podcast

Kevin Warsh has talked himself into a rate trap: underlying inflation is improving, but not enough to clear the bar he set for avoiding a hike, leaving the Fed little choice but to raise rates this week, John Authers writes.

items.title: Sazerac Buys UK Brand Au Vodka to Bolster Overseas Portfolio
body: Sazerac Co. completed its acquisition of UK-based spirits maker Au Vodka, as the US distiller behind Buzzballz expands its overseas portfolio.

Terms of the acquisition, already announced as a binding agreement with Au Vodka, were not disclosed in Sazerac’s statement Monday. The deal is worth more than £300 million ($404 million), a person familiar with the matter said.

Closely held Sazerac, which makes Southern Comfort whiskey and Buffalo Trace bourbon, is expanding at a time of weak demand across the alcohol industry, with companies struggling to offload underperforming brands.

Its $15 billion unsolicited takeover offer for Jack Daniel’s owner Brown-Forman Corp. was rejected this year. The Brown family had favored a potential deal with Pernod Ricard SA, Bloomberg previously reported, but negotiations with the French distiller broke down.

Au Vodka was founded in Swansea, Wales, in 2015 by Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn. It’s known for its flagship gold-colored bottles of vodka and ready-to-drink flavors, such as Miami Mango and Bubblegum.

items.title: Kioxia Is Said to Consider Raising $10 Billion in US Listing
body: Kioxia Holdings Corp. is considering raising at least $10 billion by listing American depositary receipts, people familiar with the matter said, potentially joining other artificial intelligence-related companies seeking to tap strong investor demand.

Kioxia has been speaking with lenders including Bank of America Corp., Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. on an offering that may take place next year, the people said, asking not to be identified because the matter is private. The Tokyo-based memory-storage maker is seeking to gain more liquidity in the US with the listing after it repurchased billions of dollars’ worth of shares in Japan, the people said.

Selling ADRs may also allow Kioxia to join a semiconductor-focused stock index, they said. Considerations are preliminary and details such as the size of the share sale and the bank lineup may change, the people said.
Representatives for Kioxia, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan declined to comment, while Bank of America didn’t respond to a request seeking comment.

Semiconductor companies and other AI-related firms globally are seeking to capitalize on interest in the sector. South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix Inc. raised $26.5 billion in its US listing in July, breaking the record for the biggest first-time share sale by a foreign company.
Kioxia, a key supplier of NAND storage, has already said it plans to offer ADRs in the spring of 2027, but it didn’t provide any further information.

Kioxia is weighing the share sale at a time when stock markets are being roiled by a potential slowdown in artificial intelligence development. Nasdaq 100 futures sank 1.8% and an exchange-traded fund tracking key chip stocks dropped 4.7% in early trading after AI leaders in the US discussed ways to introduce safeguards and assess the safety and impact of the most advanced models.

Kioxia gave a muted earnings outlook in July after results missed expectations. It also announced a 3-for-1 stock split and a buyback of up to ¥800 billion ($5.2 billion) to broaden its shareholder base and reduce volatility.
Kioxia’s Tokyo-listed shares have surged almost 400% this year, giving the company a market value of about $180 billion.

items.title: Immunology Drugmaker Electra Seeks to Raise $347 Million in IPO
body: Electra Therapeutics Inc., a clinical-stage developer of immunology drugs, is seeking to raise as much as $347 million in a US initial public offering.

The San Francisco-based company, which is backed by OrbiMed, is offering 21.67 million shares for $14 to $16 each, according to its filing Monday with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. At the top of the price range, the company would have a market value of roughly $978 million, based on the outstanding shares in the filing.

Electra’s lead drug candidate is designed to treat secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, a severe immune system overreaction. The company is conducting a global mid-stage trial of the drug in newly diagnosed patients, according to its filing. The therapy has received a Breakthrough Therapy designation from the US Food and Drug Administration as well as a Priority Medicine designation from the European Medicines Agency.

The IPO will hit the US market at an exuberant time for drug developers. Listings of biotech and pharmaceutical companies have raised $6.8 billion this year, versus $1.3 billion in the corresponding period in 2025, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

The company’s investors include entities affiliated with OrbiMed, Westlake BioPartners and Redmile Group. Electra raised about $182.7 million from a Series C funding round in October, led by a unit of French drugmaker Sanofi SA, OrbiMed and Redmile and carried $97.7 million of cash and equivalents at of June 30 this year, according to the filing.
The firm had a net loss of $58.6 million for the six months ended June 30, compared to a net loss of $25.4 million for the same period a year prior, the filing shows.

Electra’s offering is being led by Jefferies Financial Group Inc., Toronto-Dominion Bank, Evercore Inc. and Cantor Fitzgerald. The company expects its shares to trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ETRA.
