items.title: Trump's "Little War" With Iran Just Got Bigger Because of the Houthis
body: It is an unintended feature of President Donald Trump’s Plan B for defeating Iran — economic strangulation — that the more successful the policy becomes, the more risk the men who run the Islamic Republic are willing to accept to fight it. Judged on that metric, the American blockade and sanctions are working, but they’re also raising the stakes beyond what the US is willing to pay.

This begs the question of how long and disruptive the showdown with Iran is going to be, now that the US president has said he expects it to continue through the November midterms. At that point, Trump believes it will stop quickly, because the Iranians will no longer have the elections as leverage, implying that they’d then be ready to make a deal. That’s optimistic.

According to a Sept. 9 report in the Wall Street Journal, some of Trump’s most senior advisers (the same ones who advised against going to war in February) told him the conflict may outlast his presidency. They’re probably right and I hope they went a step further, warning him that it’s also likely to expand. His “little war” aimed at regime change in Iran is fast becoming a struggle to determine the future of the wider Middle East and the US role in it.

In truth, everybody is guessing at many of the factors that will decide this issue. We don’t know, for example, how many missiles or launchers the Iranians still have, nor what capacity they have to build new ones or how many they might be able to get elsewhere. We can’t be certain what will happen in energy markets, what political pressure will be brought to bear on Trump or what domestic unrest might unfold in Iran.

Nevertheless, it’s clear that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is capable of escalating the conflict in ways it previously avoided, knowing the Americans’ capacity to wreak the civilization-destroying devastation Trump has threatened. That’s something even the IRGC would try to avoid provoking for as long as it can — but the moment may have arrived.

One such provocation would be the destruction of a US warship, a humiliation for Trump that could leave hundreds of American service people dead or wounded and guarantee harsh retaliation. Iran has finally taken that risk, firing ballistic missiles at several US military vessels since Sept. 4. Even with none hit, the US responded by striking five Iranian oil tankers.

Another gun that long sat over the conflict’s Chekhovian fireplace was the potential for Tehran to get its Houthi allies in Yemen to block the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This waterway controls traffic in and out of the Red Sea, which is where Saudi Arabia has been diverting about 5 million barrels of crude a day — oil that would normally exit the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz. Disrupting this alternate route would amplify the effects of Iran’s blockage in Hormuz and could have a significant impact on the global trade costs and inflation.

The Houthis — reportedly aided by IRGC guidance and Iranian promises of money and arms — have now taken that gun off the wall. Last week, they fired multiple missiles into Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people, while the group’s land forces captured the port city of Mokha and, reportedly, several nearby islands. This could prove a huge win, both for the Houthis and Tehran, providing the potential to place Houthi missile launchers and fast boats less than 50 miles from the narrows that create Bab el-Mandeb.

These territorial gains, if consolidated, could prove enough to give the Houthis the kind of permanent control over the strait that the Iranians are now demanding over Hormuz. Together, they would put two broadly Shia, Islamist and anti-Western forces in control of major flows of oil, liquified natural gas and fertilizers from the gulf.

According to Axios, Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader Mohammed Bin Salman called Trump twice last week, asking him to order US air strikes on Houthi positions. The answer was no — Trump is understandably reluctant to open a second front in the war. But it’s too late for that. Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb would join the two fronts into one, and the capture of Mokha has put that within reach. At the weekend, drones fired from Iraq — likely by an Iran-backed militia — struck the East-West pipeline that transports Saudi oil to the Red Sea, forcing its closure and prompting a further spike in crude prices.

Trump may not recognize what a turning point this could be. Saudi Arabia will have a choice: Either fight the Houthis — which would require the involvement of the US or some other military power — or cut a deal with them. The latter would likely also require detente with Iran and mean significant changes to the balance of power in the gulf and on the Arabian Peninsula.

Iran’s nuclear program remains an important part of this wider struggle, even if it has been sidelined by the more immediate issues around Hormuz. And here, too, is potential for escalation. A Sept. 9 analysis of satellite imagery from the Center for Security and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, found there has been “a clear surge” in construction this year around Pickaxe Mountain, the nuclear facility the Iranians have been building near their uranium enrichment plant at Natanz, with more activity around the site than at any time in the past. (On the same day, the UN’s nuclear watchdog voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for non-compliance with its treaty obligations, the first time it has done so in 20 years).

None of the above suggests a short war or willingness on Iran’s part to compromise. To the contrary, IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi last week restated Iran’s maximalist demands for peace and said it would expand its zone of attack on “unauthorized” shipping through Hormuz.

These developments were unimaginable before the US and Israel went to war against Iran in search of regime change. But, as Gregory Johnsen, a non-resident fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute, said in a web briefing last week, Iran’s example in Hormuz has given the Houthis a new direction in their efforts to secure revenue and leverage. The Iranian regime, too, has new direction, sensing an opportunity to advance its preeminent strategic goal, which is to force an end US dominance and military presence in the Middle East.

Trump is right to want to avoid another forever war — this time in Yemen — but having started one in Iran, he may not yet grasp just how significant his refusal to help Saudi Arabia could prove.More from Bloomberg Opinion:

items.title: Inflation: Warsh Talked the Fed Into a Rates Trap
body: To get John Authers’ newsletter delivered directly to your inbox, sign up here.
To cut a long story short, the fed funds rate will rise this week. Following Friday’s inflation data for August, there can be no sensible doubt about this.

After surprisingly strong August employment data, and new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s strong words at Jackson Hole last month that inflation was still too high, the prices data have settled the issue. They’ve also completed a startling transformation in Fed perceptions since the eve of that speech:

This is true because Warsh has loaded the scales toward a hike, needing to see clear improvement in inflation to avoid one. That hasn’t happened, and with the bond market now in a turbulent mood, not hiking could leave him looking silly. Credibility is easily lost, and he needs to go through with a hike to maintain it, particularly in current conditions.

Warsh has set out a stall against giving forward guidance. But ironically, August’s numbers might justify keeping rates where they are, if only he’d been less explicit at Jackson Hole. This is our usual breakdown of inflation into its four main components. Core inflation is up, but only very slightly, core goods inflation (where we would expect to see tariffs show up) is tiny, and the overall rate of inflation is barely changed. So no worsening, but a clear improvement it is not:

The energy crisis, with the diesel price now at an all-time record, has much to do with this. Various measures of underlying inflation suggest that August saw the ongoing improvement that might have justified leaving rates on hold. Trimmed mean CPI, compiled by the Cleveland Fed, which excludes outliers in both directions, is its lowest since early 2021, while sticky prices (which are costly to move and rarely decrease) as measured by the Atlanta Fed, also slowed. The same is true of the median. The Fed’s “supercore” measure of services excluding housing did rise slightly, back to the upper bound of 3%. But steady, if painfully slow, disinflation continues:
There’s also one important price series that can explain August’s disappointing result. Wireless telephony charges are in long-term decline. Last month, they inflated the most since 2021:
According to Omair Sharif of Inflation Insights LLC, this on its own added 10 basis points to core inflation. It’s chiefly responsible for the rise in the supercore:

A further illustration that these numbers aren’t that bad is to see how many CPI components exceeded the 3% upper bound target. The exercise, carried out by Robin Brooks of the Brookings Institute below, shows that the proportion with strongly above-target inflation dropped sharply last month. It’s a bit above lows from the turn of the year, but shows, again, that August was a month of progress on inflation:

If the Fed’s response now appears clear, it’s because of the overriding importance of the bond market, which is threatening a riot. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s gambit to deploy increased bond buybacks to keep longer-term yields in check appeared last week to have failed. The 10-year yield leapt after the long-heralded details of the buyback were announced on Wednesday — and weren’t as great as some had expected — and again on Thursday when it emerged that the Treasury hadn’t bought all the bonds that it could have under its new mandate. Long yields matter, and the overriding purpose of the Fed must now be to avoid pushing them higher, for the sake of the housing market above all. The chart below shows the relationship between shares of homebuilders, a direct expression of housing market perceptions, and the 30-year mortgage benchmark bond yield:

The good news for housing, and for Bessent, is that in the immediate aftermath of Friday’s data, the 10-year Treasury yield fell while stocks had a good day. Inflation is bad for bonds; but it was seen as initially encouraging that the data more or less ensured that the central bank would be hiking. Any hikes now improve the chances of averting inflation in the longer term, and nibble away at the “debasement trade” — the bet that feckless government policies will erode the value of the dollar.

The positive reception didn’t last, however, and the 10-year yield ended the week at a three-year high, and a whisker away from returning to territory it last saw in 2007. As detailed last week, what happens when and if it goes through that watershed could be crucial:
Komal Sri-Kumar of the SriKonomics newsletter argued that bond markets had called Bessent’s bluff:
He argues for the Fed to consider a “jumbo” hike of 50 basis points as a mere 25 basis points might look more of “an acknowledgement of the problem rather than a determination to solve it.”

He’s not alone. Steven Blitz of TS Lombard argues: “Given Warsh’s disdain for the Bernanke slow-walk pace of hiking, why not surprise the market with a 50bps jump – leaving aside, for the moment, the resulting fracture of his relationship with Trump.”

The reason for not doing so is counterintuitive. To rein in inflation caused by strong federal spending, Blitz argues, the need is for lower equity prices. That makes capital harder to come by, slows the buildout of artificial intelligence, and removes inflationary heat. The way to do that, even if Bessent will not say so, is to allow the 10-year yield to rise enough to choke off the stock market. That’s more likely if the Fed doesn’t hike aggressively this week.
These are perilous times. Even though August’s inflation data weren’t in fact that bad.

The Treasury yield commands attention, but the global shift in yields could have its greatest impact in other jurisdictions where investors worry that government debt is out of control. The most worrying example is France.

French politics has been logjammed for two years, since snap elections left the legislature roughly equally divided between three political blocs. That gridlock won’t end before next spring’s presidential election, which might well at last give Marine Le Pen’s far-right Rassemblement National a turn in power.

The issue is whether the fiscal concerns boil over into a market crisis before or after the election. The spread of French 10-year OATS over equivalent German bunds is close to 1%, higher than during other political upheavals of the last 10 years. In absolute terms, the cost of financing French government debt is its highest since the crisis of 2008:
This has the hallmarks of an ungodly mess in the making. If Bessent doesn’t tame the Treasury market, the worst effects may well be felt in France.

The flood of artificial intelligence debt is pressuring spreads, with AI-related spending helping push total US convertible bond issuance to a record $131 billion in 2026. So far this year, tech convertible bonds, which give investors the option to swap their debt for equity, have returned 53%, but the strain is growing visible in other corners of the debt market. Spreads for non-investment-grade bonds have begun to widen:

Six months ago, high-yield spreads peaked before compressing to about 270 basis points. Goldman Sachs’ Miriam Wheeler told Bloomberg: “Most yields are trading below their new issue price, and that is a combination of heavy supply and the rates having some impact.”

By some estimates, US high-grade bond supply should approach $2 trillion this year. Barclays says this would top the 2020 record of $1.66 trillion. So far, the heavy supply has yet to cause a sustained widening in spreads. However, stress indicators are mounting. Within the IG universe, tech bonds generally have wider spreads as hyperscalers sort out how to monetize the new technology.

Until now, spread dislocations caused by the heavy issuance have tended to last only a couple of days before spreads narrow again thanks to continuing demand — which also adds to the pressure on Treasuries to offer a more competitive yield. To  quote Maria Giraldo of Guggenheim Partners:

The yield surge following the Treasury buyback raises fresh questions. Is AI corporate issuance “almost yield-agnostic” — meaning borrowers think the returns justify whatever they pay, as Bessent argued after the buyback announcement? Probably. Even as Treasury yields have climbed to multi-year highs, AI issuance powers on.

The supply is premised on the logic that the return on investment in AI should be so high that the cost of debt is essentially irrelevant. That assumption can only hold to an extent, and it is increasingly hitting its limits as investor fatigue sets in and new-issue concessions creep higher. Growing expectations of tighter policy are another headwind. That’s the part the yield-agnostic thesis never really answers: Issuers may not care what they pay, but someone on the other side has to want the paper at that price.
—Richard Abbey

As Bessent fights bond market “fever,” I have more nominations for songs on his soundtrack. Try Full Moon Fever by Tom Petty, The Fever by Southside Johnny and the Asbury Jukes, Burning Up With Fever by Kiss, Fever by Carly Rae Jepsen, Kylie Minogue’s Fever, Hot-Blooded by Foreigner, Cat Scratch Fever by Ted Nugent, Bruce Springsteen’s I’m On Fire, and maybe The Cure’s Hot! Hot! Hot!  Any more?
Shana Tova to Jewish readers as the new year celebration continues; and for everyone, have a great week ahead.

items.title: Robinhood Can't Disrupt Its Way Into the IPO Club
body: Robinhood Markets Inc. made it easier and cheaper for armchair investors to trade all kinds of financial markets and now it wants to open doors to initial public offerings, too. The online broker will get a chance to show what it can do with its first underwriting role, on the $3 billion listing of smart-ring maker Oura Inc.

Don’t expect a revolution, though. Robinhood is trying to bridge a tricky gap between its image as a disruptive outsider and the access to hot new stocks that’s limited to Wall Street insiders. It risks disappointing both the companies selling shares and its herd of clients clamoring to buy them.

There are good reasons to connect retail investors with IPOs — and for Oura to be Robinhood’s first live deal. The Finnish fitness-tracking startup has Silicon Valley backers and a major contract with the US military, making it catnip for the kind of lifestyle optimizers who likely also trade and gamble on smartphone apps. It probably helped that Robinhood’s former chief financial officer, Jason Warnick, recently joined Oura’s board.

Elon Musk might be the highest-profile proponent of getting everyday investors in on the action: He wanted to exploit his hordes of excitable fans by setting aside as much as 30% of the stock in SpaceX’s record-breaking IPO this year for retail buyers, who would typically get 5% to 10%. In the end, however, about 20% went to this crowd, with many customers of Robinhood and other consumer brokers getting just one share each.

Retail investors have become much more important to stock markets since the Covid pandemic. They now account for about 20% of US equity market volume, making them the largest single trading group — ahead of quant funds, which have averaged a less than 16% share over the past six years, and hedge funds with less than 10%, according to data complied by Bloomberg Intelligence.

Robinhood, with its fee-free trading, and a myriad of firms offering other slick apps have made it easier and more fun to buy and sell stocks, daily options and crypto, as well as bet on sports and prediction markets. Meanwhile, long-term rallies for high-growth tech stocks, like Alphabet Inc., Apple Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc., and fads for small names like GameStop Inc., have supported an army of influencers who encourage people to play the markets.

But what’s surprising is that this retail stock-trading boom has gone on so much longer than previous bouts of excitement in the late 1980s or 1990s, says Larry Tabb, head of market structure research at BI. “We've seen this show before. Typically, it doesn't end very well,” he told me. “Is it sustainable? I doubt it. Something will occur that will cause a big moment of doubt and fear among these investors.”

For Robinhood, that’s another good reason to broaden its business beyond trading. It already faces more competition from both traditional banks and brokers and smaller fintechs such as Revolut Plc, all of which are adding consumer-friendly trading to their own apps. Robinhood has diversified into more mature advisory services to help its clients with taxes, capital gains, education funds for their kids and retirement accounts. It also offers credit cards.

The platform has given clients the chance to buy into IPOs for a while, but only by surveying demand and then competing with other big investors for a slug of a deal from underwriters. Reddit’s chat boards have plenty of complaints from Robinhood clients who say they barely got a fraction of the deal shares they ordered.

The aim in becoming an underwriter is to secure a bigger allocation that Robinhood can parcel out among customers. That won’t be easy. On the Oura deal, the trading platform is last on the list of the 18 firms lining up to sell the stock, behind the traditional leaders like Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and the smaller, established wealth managers like Raymond James Financial Inc.

It will never compete with the top-tier underwriters because it can’t match the other services the bulge bracket offers, such as lending, syndicating bonds or stabilizing the share price after the IPO.

Even breaking into the lower ranks will be hard unless Robinhood can prove that its clients are not only a good source of demand on day one, but also reliable owners of the stock. Robinhood Chief Executive Officer Vlad Tenev has long insisted that his customers are long-term stock owners, although in recent earnings calls he has talked about aiming to be No. 1 among active traders, too.

To get a good allocation for an IPO, Tenev will have to show that most of his customers aren’t looking to flip shares for a fast profit. Selling quickly can upset issuers (and the lead underwriters) if it means the stock price falls quickly. Robinhood already has a policy that clients who sell within 30 days can be blocked from access to other IPOs, at least temporarily.

The trouble with armchair traders is they aren’t always reliable. When billionaire investor Bill Ackman sold shares in his Pershing Square fund and management company, he did a YouTube interview with Tenev to promote the deal. But when one of the two stocks was widely dumped straight away, Ackman complained that retail investors didn’t understand how to behave in an IPO.

A lot of trading on Robinhood is very likely short-term. The company doesn’t put out any data on average holding periods for stocks, but the kinds of trading volumes produced by retail investors just don’t make sense unless there’s a lot of turnover in their portfolios.

Still, BI’s Tabb reckons there is a path for Robinhood to make headway in underwriting — eventually. “If Robinhood can show reliable demand and its investors hold onto the stocks for a while, then I expect they will get better allocations over time.”

When Tenev announced on X.com in June that Robinhood had won regulatory approval to start underwriting, he said his company would be “disruptive in this space.” I doubt that. The trading platform may become more of a Wall Street insider, but it will only get there by toeing the traditional line. And there will be plenty of underfilled orders — and disappointed customers — along the way.  More from Bloomberg Opinion:

items.title: Bank of England's Dovish Majority Tested by Oil Price Surge
body: Governor Andrew Bailey gave journalists an unusually frank message after July’s interest-rate decision: “Please do not leave this room thinking that the Bank of England is edging toward a hike.”
He may struggle to be quite so emphatic when the central bank announces its next decision on Thursday.
Upside pressures are coming hard and fast from the unresolved Iran war, with the price of Brent crude oil firmly above $100 a barrel and gas costs proving a particular challenge to the UK.
New risks are approaching too, threatening to keep inflation above the BOE’s 2% target well into next year.

Bailey told lawmakers earlier this week that energy prices “could be higher still” and that risks are also emerging for food costs, following widespread drought in the UK and the looming effects of a supersized El Niño. Other parts of the consumer shopping basket look ominous too, such as air fares, while fast growth suggests stronger than expected demand in the economy.

“Energy passes the baton on to food prices in a way,” said Hetal Mehta, chief economist at St James’s Place. “The broader El Niño effect is likely to keep inflation much stickier next year. Even if the Iran-related energy price disinflation happens, you’ll have a different wave of food price inflation to overlay, which just prevents the overall numbers from coming down materially.”

Markets have shifted accordingly. In the days after Bailey’s July press conference traders were pricing in less than a full quarter-point rate hike by the end of the year. But with Brent crude prices surging above $108 on Monday, investors see a growing risk of a move this week.
Money markets now put the implied probability of a hike at around 34%. Traders are pricing in two increases by the end of the year and at least another two next year.
Read more: Oil Surges on Report Saudi Pipeline Will Take Weeks to Reopen

Most BOE officials have argued that a weak labor market and slower anticipated growth in the second half of this year can help contain the price pressures triggered by the Iran war. While GDP data for July suggested the economy may be resilient, evidence generally supports the view that second round effects are under control.

There is little sign yet inflation is becoming embedded. The BOE’s inflation expectations survey for August published on Friday showed a dip to 3.2% over the coming year, from 4% in May. For the following 12 months, expectations fell to 2.9% from 3.5% in May. The BOE’s agents survey of businesses across the country found that pay settlements for 2027 will be “broadly in line with or lower than 2026,” when they averaged 3.6%.

However, the BOE may have to change tack at some point. Oxford Economics estimates that UK inflation — currently at 2.9% — could hit almost 4% by the turn of the year. That would be double the BOE’s target and above levels at which the central bank believes households start to notice more rapid price increases.

One key driver will be the UK’s energy price cap, which limits how much suppliers can charge consumers per unit. Regulator Ofgem has announced it will hit a three-year high in October and experts say it could rise further still in early 2027.

“We think the impact of the Middle East conflict is still building,” said Andrew Goodwin, chief UK economist at Oxford Economics. “We think the price cap could rise by another 13% in January. Wholesale prices are currently well above the level of the previous observation window.”
The food industry is also warning that a combination of higher energy costs, harvests impacted by the scorching UK weather and El Niño will feed grocery bills well into next year.
The Food and Drink Federation expects food inflation to jump to almost 4% by Christmas and peak at 6.4% in July 2027.

“The biggest risk is really what’s going to happen to to commodities, and then therefore what’s happening with with El Niño,” said Liliana Danila, chief economist at the FDF, who pointed to a possible effect on crops such as cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rice and sugar. “It is possible that we’ll see worse than we anticipate... for now we haven’t seen the true impact on the ground.”

Most economists expect the Monetary Policy Committee to split 6-3 again to hold rates at 3.75% on Thursday. Matt Swannell, chief economic adviser to the ITEM Club, said the panel is likely to “talk tough about its readiness to fight inflation to avoid any unwanted loosening in financial conditions.”

The MPC is widely predicted to reduce the pace at which its gilt portfolio is unwound to acknowledge the fragile state of bond markets. The portfolio has already been shrunk to £489 billion from £875 billion since quantitative tightening began in 2022. The BOE is expected to slow the pace to £50 billion over the 12 months from October from £70 billion in the last period.
Domestically, a key unknown is whether the strong UK growth in the first half of the year will persist and even cause firms to begin hiring again.

While forecasters expected growing inflationary pressures to weigh on consumers and economic activity, surveys suggest both consumer and business sentiment have picked up since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July, potentially adding to demand in the economy.

items.title: Portsmouth Violence: British Balaclava Mob Deserves a Hard Response
body: Although its leader Nigel Farage successfully campaigned for Brexit, Reform UK conforms to standard European practice in one important respect. The hard-right populist party’s continental counterparts frequently brush with the law over campaign-finance irregularities, and now Reform, too, is reeling from funding scandals that have led to a criminal inquiry by the Metropolitan Police. Farage is to be interviewed as a witness by detectives after he was allegedly filmed by undercover journalists being told about a prospective plan to accept illegal foreign funding.

Marine Le Pen, leader of the French National Rally, was temporarily banned from standing for office after she was found guilty of misusing EU funds. Yet she is now favorite to win the election for president next year. Perhaps the British floating voter will be less forgiving of Farage’s financial foibles — there is mounting evidence that centrist and left-wing voters, and even some Tories, intend to vote tactically to keep out Reform candidates.

But Farage has always survived setbacks by giving voice to simmering popular discontents less squeamishly than the main parties. He has rich friends, too. Reform has just been given £72 million ($97 million) by two British cryptocurrency billionaires that, in his words, will fund “the best research and policy department British politics has ever seen” — not to say a wall of advertising. Its obvious points of attack are the cost of living and migration, which continue to top voters’ concerns.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government can only alleviate at the margins the effects of an inflationary spiral made in the Strait of Hormuz — immigration and law and order, however, are his direct responsibility. If he drops that baton, the increasingly wealthy populist party will surely pick it up.
Farage will also be hoping that funding scandals don’t provide the TV and social-media footage that sticks in the voters’ collective memory, because other images are more troubling right now.

Earlier this month television coverage was dominated by 400 or so balaclava-clad men, dressed in black, blockading the port of Dover, protesting against migrants who had evaded border controls. The other abiding image was a news clip of a super-dinghy carrying another 140 undocumented arrivals across the sea from France. In Portsmouth they were greeted by more demonstrators in black who blocked roads to prevent them leaving the city.

Cheering on the vigilantes was one Daniel Thomas, a former bodyguard of the far-right rabble-rouser Tommy Robinson. “Danny Thommo” served time in prison for an attempted kidnapping, but now wears his cultural Christianity as a badge of honor. In Portsmouth the police were taken by surprise by  violent disorder on the streets and temporarily lost control.

Reform’s leader was quick to describe the actions of the masked men as “horrible.” Farage keeps a distance from the likes of Robinson, just as Le Pen emphasizes her respectability by disavowing her father Jean-Marie’s anti-Semitic party comrades. Yet when the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch condemned the protesters, Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesman, responded on X, “How dare you call them ‘thugs.’”

Farage is losing votes to the more extreme Restore Britain party and some of his top team are tempted to harden their line. The insurgent German populist party, the AFD, provides an umbrella for right-wingers and neo-Nazis alike.

The blockade of ports demoralizes law-abiding voters and invites further copycat action by an unruly element. Similarly demoralizing, however, is the sight of migrants or asylum seekers gaining entry to the country illegally, with apparent impunity. The number of small boat arrivals has fallen this year, but any visible loss of control by the authorities still feeds the populist narrative that “Britain is broken.”

Former Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair successfully campaigned on the slogan, “Tough on crime, tough on the causes of crime.” Burnham’s government needs to be tough on the far right and tough on the causes of the far right. That entails being even-handed in applying the law. Failures by the police and local politicians to tackle grooming gangs of men of largely Pakistani origin have led to claims of two-tier policing. Demonstrations over Israel’s conduct in Gaza by middle-class radicals that teeter at the edge of legality have inspired a White working-class, nationalist response.

In the UK the traditional parties have boosted support for both the populist and extremist right by failing to keep promises about immigration. Only belatedly have they got serious as the challenge from Reform became too great to ignore. Today inflows are declining. Net migration dropped to 171,000 for the year ending December 2025, well below the levels seen during the Conservative administration of Boris Johnson.

This year some 14,200 people had arrived by small boat by the end of July, far less than the same period in 2025, but a less dramatic decline compared with 2024. These dinghies are not only evidence of state incompetence, they suggest there is no penalty for law breaking. That is damaging in voters’ eyes.

Even the liberal United Nations refugee commissioners reckon half of asylum claims are mishandled by the Home Office. A departmental whistleblower told the Times of London this week that only one in a hundred asylum applications “at best” are likely genuine. Perhaps they exaggerate, but the stories of bureaucratic incompetence and torpor are shocking. Bangladeshi claimants routinely describe themselves as members of the banned Awami League but can’t name a single party policy. Scores of professed Kurdish dissidents claim the same politician as their father. Many seem to be coached by lawyers and charity workers.

Voters do support migrants who bring needed skills, academic and technical qualifications and business acumen to the UK. It’s not a question of race and religion, or even numbers. But the Home Office needs to demonstrate it conducts migration policy in the country’s economic interests. Its procedures, once famously described as “not fit for purpose,” must be seen as fair.

Although Reform in recent weeks has done a first class job of sabotaging its own prospects, the government cannot be playing the part of amused bystander. With Farage it’s often a case of one step backward and two forward, as this weekend’s colossal party donations illustrate. Political leadership demands a language of reassurance to citizens about migration, and the enforcement of law and order on the streets.

items.title: Switzerland Debates Longstanding Neutrality Ahead of Vote This Month
body: For Swiss billionaire Christoph Blocher, there’s always one more fight.

The 85-year-old built his business reputation at manufacturer EMS-Chemie, then turned his political party into the country’s biggest by pushing a nationalist and anti-immigration message. He’s stepped back somewhat in recent years, but never sits on the sidelines. With the country about to vote on its longstanding neutrality this month, he’s in full campaign mode.

The proposal on the ballot wants to change the constitution, eliminating any flexibility in how neutrality is applied. At the root of the campaign is Switzerland’s shock 2022 decision to adopt European Union sanctions against Russia, which Blocher and the Swiss People’s Party have opposed.

The debate reflects bigger questions about where the country sees itself in a world of increasingly fractured international relations. For many on the right, it’s lost much of what made it special, and can’t afford to let neutrality be weakened.

It’s a head-to-head between two competing visions. One points to sovereignty, neutrality and distance from larger powers — particularly the EU — as the foundations of Switzerland’s success. The second sees international cooperation as essential for a small economy which can steer its own fate only so far.

“Swiss neutrality — not just any neutrality, but Swiss neutrality — is part of the Swiss identity,” Blocher told Bloomberg.  He’s put 2 million francs ($2.5 million) of his own money into a media blitz ahead of the vote on Sep. 27.

Supporters of the constitutional change say a strict interpretation of neutrality is indispensable to make sure Switzerland isn’t pulled into wars. Posters across the country have pushed that message, with the slogan: “No War. Yes to Swiss Neutrality.”

The government supports staying neutral, but wants some flexibility, and rejects the amendment as unnecessary. Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis says  neutrality works and “we don’t need to reinvent it.”
But for many conservative voters, leaders of recent years have stripped away the country’s identity bit by bit.

That feeling covers everything from Swiss banking secrecy, which was dismantled under US pressure, to anger over immigration, to a recent set of treaties with the EU that opponents say constitutes “subordination” to the bloc. Watering down neutrality is perceived as another retreat from traditions.

“Since the end of the Cold War, Switzerland has been gradually giving up the things that make it unique — and thereby ultimately its identity,” said Rene Roca, a high school teacher and historian from Oberrohrdorf-Staretschwil in the canton of Aargau, about half-way between Zurich and Basel.
While polls put support for the neutrality campaign at about 40% — so it may not get over the line — broader frustration is a recurring issue that won’t go away.
The country held a plebiscite earlier this year to cap its population (it fell short at 45%), and is set to vote as soon as next year on the contentious EU deal.

On neutrality, the government argues that it’s best to be pragmatic rather than dogmatic, and can point to the economy’s successes as part of its case. Switzerland benefits from close ties to the EU while maintaining independence. That allows it to strike its own trade deals, as it did with China last month. It earned its exporters near-universal tariff-free access, something the EU lacks.
Other European nations have been prompted by Russia’s aggression to rethink non-alignment. Both Finland and Sweden shed their longstanding positions and joined NATO.

But Switzerland’s attachment runs deep because the country lacks many of the markers that hold other countries together. It has four national languages and strong regional identities, while political power is dispersed among 26 cantons.

“Historically, neutrality served as a safeguard against external threats, but it also played an integrative role internally,” said Lucas Renaud, a researcher at ETH Zurich’s Center for Security Studies. “Switzerland is no nation-state like Germany, France or Italy, it’s a nation by will.”

A key reference point for right-wing supporters of tightening the doctrine is the World Wars, during which Switzerland managed to escape hostilities. Its record during World War II is controversial, however, with Switzerland helping Nazi Germany with financing for weapons while turning away thousands of Jewish refugees.

The Kremlin recently cited this when it got involved in the campaign, saying Switzerland no longer adheres to neutrality. That prompted opponents to call the proposal a “pro-Putin initiative” because it would force the country to scrap its Russia sanctions.
Despite the dispute over interpretation, broad domestic support for neutrality remains strong. A survey by ETH Zurich recently showed 85% of the population back it.
For Blocher and his peers, that’s not enough, because of the perceived threats to peaceful Switzerland.
“It was able to sidestep every war for some 200 years,” Blocher said. “Because it has broken its neutrality, Switzerland has today essentially become a belligerent against the nuclear power Russia.”

items.title: Europe's Fractured Stock Market Finally Gets a Single Data Feed
body: Europe’s protracted efforts to turn its much maligned markets into a more attractive proposition for investors reach a momentous juncture Monday: the arrival of a consolidated tape.

The fragmentation of trading across venues is often blamed for the view that markets in Europe have lower liquidity versus the US, which introduced a country-wide tape five decades ago. Regulators hope the rollout of a unified feed of prices and trading across 29 countries’ markets will start changing perceptions.

Besides issues like diverging legal systems and patchy settlement infrastructure, the European Union has identified piecemeal trading data as one reason investors see the bloc as multiple different markets rather than a single unified one. The tape aims to counter that view by displaying supply and demand data for company shares and exchange-traded funds across the region.

The tape, run by EuroCTP BV, a body backed by Europe’s exchanges, won’t be just for professional investors and traders. Retail investors can also subscribe via a website, helping to level the playing field with larger institutions.

“Am I excited for Monday? Yes, from a symbolic standpoint,” said Alexandre Roubaud, head of ETF markets at BlackRock Inc. in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. “Will we see the benefit of the tape overnight? Certainly not.”

It’s been a slog getting here, almost 20 years since the EU broke up stock exchanges’ grip on trading. In that time, there have been plenty of delays and arguments as countries and industries fought to protect their corners in the change.

While Monday’s unveiling marks a moment, it isn’t like flicking a light switch. EuroCTP needs to get people to sign up to and trust the product, and only time will tell whether it can shift perceptions of Europe’s capital markets and lead to better outcomes for investors and companies.

Unlike the US tape, the EU’s will offer best bid and ask prices for a particular security without disclosing the trading venue that generated the quotes. Instead, market participants will see more granular data after a transaction has taken place.
That’s sparked criticism from banking and asset management associations, who argue that won’t be good enough for members to trade on.

Just over half of respondents to a recent Bloomberg Intelligence survey of 108 senior buyside traders said they planned to access the EU tape either directly from EuroCTP or third-party providers. Only a fifth thought it could reduce their reliance on direct data feeds from stock exchanges.

Eleanor Beasley, chief operating officer for Goldman Sachs’ EMEA equities business, says the fastest moving investors may not use it for trading at first as they assess the data, but there are still benefits.

“It is a really useful tool to improve the understanding of the total traded volume,” she said. “If you’re a company looking to list or are listed in the region and you think the only volume that trades in your name is on the primary market, I think that this will give you a much better idea as to the total traded volume.”

Goldman Sachs will contribute to the tape by supplying data from its Sigma X Europe trading venue, as well as consuming data from the feed through its trading operation. Bloomberg LP, the parent of Bloomberg News, aggregates and distributes trading data throughout Europe.
A consolidated tape is a single feed that aggregates data across multiple execution venues for equity trading.

In Europe, trading is split across different venues, including primary exchanges like Euronext, alternative venues like Cboe Europe, investment bank trading desks known as systematic internalizers and so-called dark pools.
Currently, it’s difficult to see the total volume of trading across all of these venues, a problem the consolidated tape is intended to rectify.

Within the tape there are two types: pre-trade and post-trade. A post-trade tape collects all of the data about trades after they have been executed. A pre-trade tape, however, shows the offers to buy or sell a security before they are made.
A pre-trade tape may have different levels of depth to it. The most simple will show an aggregated feed of buy and sell orders across all venues. This is the type that will go into effect on Monday.

A more complicated version being discussed in Brussels would show on which venue the shares are being bought and sold. This could allow traders to choose the most liquid venue, or the venue where the costs of execution are lowest.
According to Roubaud, that could “have a knock-on effect because liquidity pools will have to compete more for order flow,” he said.

Industry groups are at odds over the speed and extent to which the tape should evolve, with stock exchanges that make a significant portion of their revenue from selling data reticent to move at the pace banks and asset managers are calling for.
But even in its initial form, the tape could help unlock more capital into European equities, according to Eglantine Desautel, CEO of EuroCTP.

For example, how big a position an asset manager can build in a single instrument according to their internal rules is at times a function of the average traded volume in that security. If the tape can provide a more comprehensive view of volumes, investors would be able to commit more capital, she said.

The origins of consolidated tape stem from Europe’s MiFID I regulation in 2007, which broke up the national monopolies over stock exchanges and allowed alternative trading venues. That increased the fragmentation of Europe’s stock markets and led to a situation where there wasn’t a single clear view of equity prices.

Then MiFID II, the follow up legislation in 2018, allowed for consolidated tape providers to service the market. Over the next few years the EU made progress toward establishing a tape backed by Brussels. A tender was launched, which was won by EuroCTP.

“The launch of the consolidated tape is a major achievement,” said Pete Tomlinson, managing director of equities and post-trade at banking association AFME. “Europe should now build on this foundation by enhancing the depth and quality of the data available through the tape, making it an even more valuable tool for investors.”

items.title: South Korea's $1.4 Trillion National Pension Fund Picks New CIO
body: South Korea’s National Pension Service named Kyuhong Lee as chief investment officer to oversee its $1.4 trillion portfolio, handing him the reins of one of the world’s largest pools of retirement savings after a sharp surge in investment returns in the first half.
NPS Chairman Kim Sung-joo appointed Lee to a two-year term beginning Tuesday, the fund said in a statement Monday. His tenure can be extended annually based on performance.

Lee takes over at a pivotal time for the pension giant, whose investment decisions are closely watched because of its enormous presence in South Korea’s financial markets and large allocation to overseas assets. The fund managed 1,866 trillion won ($1.4 trillion) as of the end of June after posting a preliminary 27.2% investment return in the first half, its best performance for the period since at least 2022, according to its website.

NPS described Lee as an asset management expert with extensive experience spanning private-sector money managers and public pension funds. He previously served as the CIO of the Korea Teachers’ Pension and has held positions at firms including NH-Amundi Asset Management, CapitaLand’s South Korean operations, and Samsung Asset Management, the statement said.

NPS, which provides retirement benefits for South Korea’s rapidly aging population, has increasingly sought investments abroad and in alternative assets as it diversifies beyond the domestic market. Its investment strategy is taking on added importance as one of the world’s lowest birth rates puts growing pressure on South Korea’s pension system.
Read More: Korea’s $1.4 Trillion Pension Posts 27% Return in First-Half

items.title: Beijing Bans Drones in Broad Curbs After Citic Tower Crash
body: Beijing has banned the possession and use of recreational drones as part of moves to bolster security in the capital after a light plane crashed into the city’s tallest skyscraper in June.

The restrictions — some of the tightest in the world on drones — come after a two-seat light plane flew into the 109-story Citic Tower in June, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others. The incident took place just several kilometers away from the headquarters of the ruling Communist Party and residence of top leaders.
The measures are Beijing’s toughest yet in response to the accident, which caused one of the most serious civil aviation and public security breaches in highly sensitive airspace.

Residents won’t be allowed to posses or store drones, or drone parts from Nov. 15, the Beijing Daily reported. They will have until Nov. 14 to relocate them outside the city, and the government will offer a buyback program, capping purchases subsidies at 3,000 yuan ($447) per unit.

While several global cities such as Washington and Paris effectively ban recreational drones, Beijing stands out by moving beyond a blanket flight restriction to a prohibition on ordinary residents and visitors possessing or bringing drones into the city at all.
Read More: China Said to Restrict Small Aircraft After Beijing Tower Crash

The rules designate all of Beijing as controlled airspace, the newspaper said, covering and prohibiting any recreational flying. Officials will also tighten controls of airspace in and around the capital within a 300 kilometer radius (186 miles) of the city.

While commercial flights aren’t impacted, aircraft must have back-up tracking. New rules for aircraft using Beijing’s airspace include maintaining two-way contact with air traffic controllers at all times, according to an official aviation safety advisory published Sunday.

The pilot in the Citic incident deliberately crashed after deviating from his flight plan, and likely ignored contact with air traffic controllers. The plane nearly collided with commercial jet in the process.

Shares of companies related to China’s low-altitude aircraft industry fell slightly in Monday trading. Nanjing LES Information Technology, a provider of low-altitude flight management and air traffic control systems, fell as much as 2.1%, aircraft manufacturer Zhejiang Wanfeng Auto Wheel was down 1.5%, while helicopter service provider Citic Offshore Helicopter dropped 1.7%.

items.title: China Spy Chief Warns of AI Risks as US Tech Leaders Urge Brakes
body: China’s top intelligence official delivered one of Beijing’s most detailed warnings yet about AI, saying rapid advances in the technology could threaten political stability and critical infrastructure.

Abusive use of AI by adversaries could “directly threaten China’s political security, institutional security and ideological security,” State Security Minister Chen Yixin wrote in an article posted Sunday on the official China Cyberspace magazine. He also cited AI’s increasing ability at discovering flaws in systems and creating malware or software to exploit those weaknesses.

The article represents one of the clearest accounts to date on how China assesses the dangers posed by AI. It appeared as leaders of top US technology firms urged a more measured pace of development, although there is no sign the timing was coordinated. The piece made no mention of the calls by Anthropic PBC and OpenAI to slow down the pursuit of cutting-edge models.

Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei has argued in a blog post on Saturday that AI capabilities are outpacing safeguards and proposed coordination between companies, the US and other democracies. Chen also emphasized safety in his article, but he views the risks mainly through the lenses of political control, technological sovereignty, foreign threats and strategic rivalry.

At the top of Beijing’s concerns is the potential for what Chen described as “hostile forces” to wage “public-opinion wars” and “cognitive warfare.” Deepfakes, AI-generated text and images, and social media bots could be used to fabricate political rumors, spread harmful information and incite social divisions, he wrote in the magazine managed by the Cyberspace Administration of China.

AI-powered web crawlers, data mining and profiling systems could strengthen foreign intelligence agencies’ ability to collect sensitive information, including state data, trade secrets and personal information, according to the article.

Chen also warned that countries with an advantage in AI may invoke national security to impose technology controls, “monopolize” industry standards and build closed-source ecosystems, echoing Chinese President Xi Jinping’s stated opposition to stretching the concept of national security in a July speech.

items.summary_zh: 中国国安部长陈一新警告，AI快速发展可能威胁政治稳定和关键基础设施，敌对势力或利用其发动认知战、窃取敏感数据。

items.title: Easing the Diesel Crunch Is Harder Than Keeping Planes in the Air
body: In times of crisis, the oil industry delivers a perennial warning: “You can’t print barrels.” While central banks can — and do — run their presses to soothe financial markets, the same option isn’t available in energy markets. And if conjuring crude is implausible, delivering diesel out of thin air is even more impossible.

Right now, the world wishes it had a diesel printer as two wars — US-Iran and Russia-Ukraine — combine to create an enormous shortage, pushing the cost of the fuel to all-time highs. In the US, the retail price topped $6 a gallon last week for the first time; it was about $3.50 at the beginning of the year. In the wholesale market, it’s changing hands above $5, pointing to further pain at the pump.

The energy industry can be forgiven for feeling déjà vu: It battled a similar shortage in the jet-fuel market earlier this year, as holidaymakers fretted their summer vacation plans would be ruined. Sadly, increasing diesel output is a lot harder.

Diesel is the world’s most-consumed refined petroleum product, accounting for nearly 30% of total oil demand. The trucking industry swallows about half of the world’s output, with railway freight, construction, factories, mining and agriculture absorbing the rest. The current shortage and accompanying elevated prices hurt some countries more than others; China and India are more dependent on the fuel, while the US uses twice as much gasoline. Even so, officials are worried: US National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told Fox News on Friday that the cost of diesel was “a major concern for us.”

The crux of the crisis is a shortage of global refining capacity. That’s partly due to the wars themselves, but it’s also an unintended consequence of actions taken to ease the global shortfall in crude.

Let’s start with the direct effect. About a year ago, Russia and the Persian Gulf nations exported 2.2 million barrels a day of diesel; flows have since plunged by around 75% to 520,000 daily barrels in August, according to Kpler, an energy intelligence firm. Russia accounts for nearly half of the decline, as attacks by Ukraine have crippled many of its largest refineries.

Saudi Arabia accounts for another significant percentage. Unlike Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Iraq, Saudi Arabia has so far made only limited use of clandestine tanker runs across the Strait of Hormuz; its exporting refineries inside the Persian Gulf have remained largely idle since the war began.

Then there’s the indirect impact. China has reduced its crude imports since the US-Iran conflict started. Previously, Beijing bought about 11.5 million barrels a day of crude; last month, its daily purchases amounted to little more than 7 million barrels, according to Vortexa, another energy consultancy. As China buys less oil, it’s also cutting back on refining, in turn curtailing its typically large exports of diesel. So by reducing oil imports, China is simultaneously worsening the scarcity of refined products.

Other factors are also in play. The US and Japan have both tapped their large strategic petroleum reserves, but those are mostly in the form of crude, rather than refined productsEurope, on the other hand, keeps most of its strategic petroleum reserves in the form of refined products, and could release diesel to ease the shortage. There's historical precedent: after hurricanes Rita and Katrina knocked out a large chunk of US refining capacity in 2005, Europe tapped its reserves to ease a shortage of gasoline and diesel from America.. The releases have eased the pressure in the oil market but done very little for diesel. American oil producers have also responded to higher prices by boosting drilling, a move that’s echoed in Canada, Brazil, Venezuela, Argentina and Guyana. But, again, that only boosts the flow of crude: While shale drillers can increase output in a matter of weeks or months, adding refining capacity takes years.
The only — partial — solution is a combination of running existing refineries harder and letting elevated prices kill some demand. Both are happening.

There’s nothing like record margins to prompt every plant to go into what the industry calls “max diesel" mode. Of course, “max” is relative; refineries can tweak their operations here and there, but typically can’t boost diesel output by more than a couple of percentage points before engineering limits prevent further increases. And boosting diesel means reducing output of other refined products, mostly jet fuel. Over the summer, US and European refiners have been focused on making as much fuel for airlines as they could.

Refineries are complex machines, capable of processing multiple streams of crude into dozens of different petroleum products. For simplicity’s sake, the industry measures refining margins using a rough calculation called the “3-2-1 crack spread” — for every three barrels of oil a refinery “cracks,” or processes, it generates two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillate fuel such as diesel.

This month, the 3-2-1 spread — the difference between the cost of a barrel of oil and the premium available from selling those refined products — has surged to about $65, a record high. History illustrates the magnitude of the rally. From 1985 to 2021, the crack spread averaged about $10.50. Even between 2004 and 2008 — the so-called golden age of refining, when Chinese oil demand exploded — it never surpassed $30. As refining has become ever more lucrative in recent months, every plant outside Russia, the Middle East and China is running as fast as it can.

Unfortunately, the large size of the diesel market, at about 29.5 million barrels a day, means significant shifts in refinery output would be needed to move the dial on either supply or prices. To put this into perspective, jet fuel has a daily volume of less than 8 million barrels, so relatively small changes in refining output and airline consumption were able shift the supply and demand balance more easily.

With that in mind, short of the two wars ending, the diesel shortage is set to persist for the foreseeable future. The only relief on the horizon comes from the weather: The recurrent El Niño phenomenon typically brings fewer hurricanes to the US Gulf of Mexico and warmer winters to some regions. So far this season, storm activity in the Atlantic, measured by the so-called accumulated cyclone energy indicator, has been the tamest since 1950, according to data compiled by Colorado State University. Thus, American oil refineries in Texas and Louisiana have suffered less disruption than usual, improving their productivity.
And if the winter is warmer than normal, as long-range weather models suggest, demand for heating oil will decline in Europe and North America, easing pressure on the wider diesel market.

Betting on favorable weather, however, is hardly a strategy. Ultimately, higher diesel prices should push demand lower, rebalancing the market — but that carries an economic cost, particularly for those countries that are more reliant on the fuel.

items.title: Australian Gold Miner Northern Star Appoints Cutifani to Board
body: Australia’s largest gold miner, Northern Star Resources Ltd., has appointed mining industry veteran Mark Cutifani to its board, as well as a second non-executive director proposed by activist shareholder Elliott Investment Management LP.
Cutifani, a former chief executive officer of Anglo American Plc, and veteran mining engineer Peter Rozenauers will join Northern Star’s board from Oct. 1, the company said in a statement.
The announcement came on Monday shortly after Woodside Energy Group Ltd. said that Cutifani had resigned as a non-executive director effective Sept. 13, citing personal reasons.

Elliott, a prominent activist investor, said in June that it had built a stake worth more than A$1 billion ($715 million) in Northern Star and was pushing for a strategic review, including a potential sale. The miner has cut its production guidance several times over the past year, with issues at its Kalgoorlie processing plant in Western Australia constraining production and weighing on its performance relative to peers.

Cutifani and Rozenauers were among six candidates recommended by Elliott in August as it stepped up its campaign to lift the miner’s performance. In July, Northern Star appointed Glencore Plc executive Suresh Vadnagra as its next CEO, to replace outgoing boss Stuart Tonkin on Oct. 5.
Northern Star’s shares rose as much as 3.4% on Monday morning in Sydney.

items.title: Funds Bet New Zealand Bonds Will Beat Global Peers on Slow Hikes
body: Some investors are snapping up New Zealand bonds, betting sluggish economic growth will keep the central bank cautious on interest-rate hikes and extend the debt’s outperformance over global peers.

Asset manager Insight Investment favors bonds with shorter maturities, arguing the market has priced in too many rate hikes by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. The nation’s debt also benefits from a steep yield curve and government spending that’s relatively contained compared with its Group-of-10 peers, according to Harbour Asset Management.

The bullish bets come after New Zealand bond yields jumped to multiyear highs on Friday as a surge in oil prices fueled wagers of an October rate hike. Prior to crude’s most-recent rally, RBNZ officials had signaled the pace of rate increases is set to slow, with the economic recovery from a recession remaining uneven and fragile. Traders are pricing in four more rate hikes by August next year, adding to the RBNZ’s two hikes this year.

Bonds maturing in two- to five-years are “close to, or at the top of the pack” in terms of attractiveness versus global peers, said Harvey Bradley, head of global rates at Insight Investment in London. “We don’t see the RBNZ delivering on the hikes priced, and with a steeper curve than developed market peers,” the returns look compelling, he said.

The central bank has tied future rate hikes to incoming data before bringing its policy rate to neutral. While RBNZ Assistant Governor Karen Silk has said the next hike may not occur until December, board member Prasanna Gai has suggested the policy rate is already in neutral territory.

A Bloomberg gauge of New Zealand bonds had lost 0.3% for the year as of Friday’s close. That compares with more than 1% loss for indexes tracking Canadian and US debt, almost 3% for UK gilts and more than 4% for Japanese bonds, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

“The last week has been a bit painful,” said Fergus McDonald, head of bonds and currency at Amova Asset Management’s NZ unit. Still, “10-year New Zealand government bond yields over 5% look good value to us, especially if viewed through the lens of where the Official Cash Rate is likely to peak in the short term and average over the medium term,” he said.

The outperformance may not last long. New Zealand bonds appear expensive, with the benchmark 10-year yield more than 30 basis points below its Australian peer, said Tamsin Wilding, a portfolio manager at Harbour in Wellington. While Harbour has a small position in the short end of the yield curve to take advantage of its steepness, the firm prefers inflation-linked bonds, she said.
“This provides a good hedge for us,” she said. “At the same time, given the inflation track over the next year, there’s a lot of carry that’s embedded in those inflation linkers at the moment too.”

New Zealand’s inflation is running above the central bank’s 1-3% target band, and the central bank doesn’t see it returning to the 2% midpoint until early 2028. In addition, data this week may show the economy expanded 2.2% in the second quarter from a year ago before slowing into year-end, according to a survey of economists.

items.title: Sungrow Hikes Product Prices After Raw Material Cost Increase
body: Sungrow Power Supply Co., one of the world’s largest renewable energy equipment makers, will raise product prices this month after higher raw material costs squeezed margins.

Prices for inverters, energy storage converters and energy storage systems will increase by 5% to 15% effective Sept. 20, according to a letter the company sent to clients. Sungrow shares rose as much as 3.4%.

The increase follows rising costs for materials like lithium, copper and aluminum. The company said in a written statement it needed to adjust prices to cover those costs and continue to seek technological upgrades and maintain product quality.
“The price increase of the upstream materials has exceeded expectations with the upward trend in costs not showing any significant easing,” the company said in the written response to Bloomberg News.
Read More: Sungrow Shares Slump After Profit Tumbles by Almost a Third

The price hike also comes after Sungrow reported a 32% drop in first-half net income as competition in China intensified and overseas markets faced growing challenges, including higher trade barriers from the US and the European Union.
China’s economy is moving into a period that could determine the course of stimulus through the end of the year, as consumers remain gripped by malaise despite signs of stabilizing growth.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first sit-down on Indian soil in seven years signaled a will to further repair ties and manage an unpredictable Donald Trump. But fundamental differences remain despite the good vibes flowing from the 10-nation BRICS summit in New Delhi.
Haidilao International Holding Ltd.’s sudden slump after its co-founder sold about $350 million worth of shares is putting the spotlight on other stocks that may be vulnerable to similar selling.

items.title: Z.AI's Cash Burn Drives Alibaba-Like HK Fundraising Spree
body: Z.AI Co. dashed back to Hong Kong’s equity market as soon as its last lockup expired, underscoring a cash burn rate that leaves the artificial intelligence model maker’s hunger to take advantage of any fundraising opportunity.

The Beijing-based firm’s $5 billion stock-and-convertible offering, unveiled on Friday, is the latest sign that soaring AI spending is pushing Chinese technology firms to keep tapping investors for fresh capital through repeated fundraisings. It’s forming a pattern after Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s surprise $10 billion deal just last month, which became the biggest-ever follow-on offering in Hong Kong.

Including the latest deal, Z.AI has raised about $9.6 billion in Hong Kong this year alone, more than any issuer in the city except Alibaba, an outsize haul for a company that listed only in January. Its total fundraise is also about on par with the initial public offering of chip giant CXMT Corp., which in a short time has grown to become China’s biggest listed company.

Z.AI took advantage from investor appetite for meaningful AI plays, with a delay to the highly anticipated IPO of its US competitor OpenAI and tapping the market before the listing of Claude chatbot maker Anthropic PBC.

The company formerly known as Zhipu is racing ahead to fund its own buildout even as much of the industry is discussing a slowdown in development to assess the safety and impact of advanced AI models. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei said Saturday that the company would introduce additional safeguards, including independent third-party evaluations OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed the proposal, while xAI’s Elon Musk said “Dario is right.”
Read More: Chinese Tech Firms’ Share Sale Spree Sparks Valuation Concerns

Companies have raised more than $42 billion through additional share offerings in Hong Kong this year, already the most since 2021, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Apart from Alibaba and Z.AI’s placements, major deals included MiniMax Group Inc. and Shanghai Biren Technology Co.

Z.AI rushed back to the market a few months after it raised $4 billion in a share sale that priced at the low end of its marketed range. While the latest fundraising was still priced well above the IPO, the shares have come under pressure in recent months, retreating more than 60% from the record high set in June amid broader market caution around the volatility of AI names. The shares fell as much as 10% on Monday.

And they face more overhang, with a lockup on about 178 million shares held by employees and pre-IPO investors, equal to more than 35% of its total issued shares, set to expire in January, according to Bloomberg calculations.

“Capital raise creates a better entry,” according to Mo Aziz, an equity long-short analyst who publishes on Smartkarma. Z.AI’s annual recurring revenue “grew from $250 million to $1.6 billion in five months,” but customer concentration risk remains as two customers represent more than 31% of the ARR base, he added.

The proceeds will fund AI research, computing infrastructure and business expansion initiatives, while supporting strategic investments, potential acquisitions and general corporate needs, the company said.
Investors are also watching MiniMax, another Chinese AI firm that listed in Hong Kong this year, for signs it could follow with its own cash call.

items.title: Copper Drops as Spreads Loosen and Traders Boost Rate Hike Bets
body: Copper fell towards $14,000 a ton as traders ramped up wagers on a US rate hike and price spreads loosened after fresh deliveries of metal into exchange warehouses.

Three-month futures dropped as much as 1.6% to $14,018.50 a ton, the lowest in over three weeks, after data from the London Metal Exchange showed an 8,425-ton rise in copper inventories in its warehouse network.

The LME copper market faced a severe squeeze in August as stockpiles declined, with prices pushing to new record highs amid fears that global supplies would be drained as traders continued to ship large volumes to the US in anticipation of potential tariffs.

But the gap between global benchmark prices in London and those on New York’s Comex has been narrowing over recent weeks, eroding the incentive for traders to ship metal to the US, and easing worries about further outflows from the LME.

Key price spreads also pointed to loosening supply conditions in the LME’s warehouse network on Monday, with cash contracts trading at a $45-a-ton discount to three-month futures after inventories rose. That’s a stark reversal from August, when the spread reached a $545-a-ton premium, in a condition known as backwardation that signals tight supply.

Copper and other metals are also facing broader pressures as traders ramp up wagers that the Federal Reserve will soon start raising interest rates. Five of the LME’s six main metal contracts traded lower on Monday, hit by a strengthening dollar and a downbeat mood for risk assets.

“With speculative length reduced but prompt tightness also easing, copper is likely to remain choppy around current levels until stronger dip-buying returns or a fresh macro or fundamental catalyst provides clearer direction,” analysts at Sucden Financial Ltd. wrote in a note.

Bets on rate hikes are rising ahead of the Fed’s policy meeting this week, with Friday’s stronger-than expected inflation print underscoring growing price pressures. Tighter monetary policy is typically a headwind for industrial metals like copper, raising borrowing costs for manufacturers and consumers.
Copper on the LME declined 1% to $14,077 a ton at 12:32 p.m. local time. Zinc was down 1.5%, while aluminum edged higher.

items.title: Samsung, SK Hynix Reject Kepco's Power Grid Prepayment Plan
body: Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc. have rejected a proposal from Korea Electric Power Corp. that would have seen the two pay in advance for electricity in order to finance the construction of grids to power new technology clusters.

Cash-strapped utilities across Asia are struggling to keep up with the growing demand from the semiconductor and artificial intelligence industries. Kepco’s plan — estimated by local media at a combined 25 trillion won ($18 billion), equivalent to five years of bills — was an effort to work around that mismatch.
“The companies have ultimately rejected Kepco’s proposal,” a Kepco spokesman said in a text message.

The two chipmakers were concerned about committing such large sums upfront given uncertainty over whether the current semiconductor boom would continue for the next five years, according to local media reports.
Samsung and SK Hynix declined to comment.
Read More: Lee’s $880 Billion AI Bet Ties Legacy to Korea’s Chip Boom

Under the proposal, the chipmakers would have paid the 25 trillion won over about a year. Kepco would have paid interest on the remaining prepaid balances. The alternative source would have reduced Kepco’s reliance on bond issuance for funding.

items.title: Korea's Gender Minister Nominee Pulls Out in Fresh Blow to Lee
body: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s 36-year-old gender minister nominee stepped down before gaining confirmation of her position amid a public backlash over her suitability for the job in the latest negative fallout from the president’s cabinet reshuffle.

Yong Hye-in, a lawmaker of the minor Basic Income Party, pulled out of consideration for the position Sunday after controversy erupted over her insistence that she wouldn’t give up her parliamentary seat while serving in the cabinet.
Yong said the ruling Democratic Party had urged her to make a decision, citing the custom that lawmakers elected through proportional representation vacate their seats when taking a cabinet post.
Read more: South Korea’s Lee Shakes Up Cabinet to Restore Momentum

“A Cabinet minister is expected to serve as a bridge between the government and the National Assembly and help foster cooperation. However, I concluded that it would be difficult to effectively fulfill that role when even the ruling party has expressed concerns,” Yong told reporters.
Yong’s withdrawal is the latest setback for Lee following a hasty cabinet reshuffle two weeks ago that was aimed at freshening up his administration and stopping a slide in public support.

Lee’s approval rating fell to a new low of 38%, according to a Gallup Korea survey released Friday. Among those who disapproved of Lee’s performance, 24% cited housing while another 16% pointed to the reshuffle. The poll showed 61% of respondents viewed Yong as not qualified for the job while 13% supported her.

Yong earlier said she would retain her parliamentary seat because she is her party’s sole lawmaker and giving it up would leave the party without representation in parliament. Announcing her withdrawal from the nomination, Yong criticized the opposition for what she described as mockery of the difficulties faced by a minor party, and media outlets for publishing “malicious and distorted” reports.
The presidential office said it respected Yong’s decision.

“We believe the nominee made the decision to minimize the burden on state affairs and people’s livelihoods,” Lee’s spokesperson, Kang Yu-jung, said in a statement. “The Blue House will make every effort in its vetting and selection process to ensure that future appointments meet the public’s expectations.”

The surprise nomination was widely viewed as part of Lee’s efforts to win back approval from younger voters, a demographic that is showing an increasing drift away from the liberal president.  A two-term lawmaker, Yong has been vocal about advancing gender equality, highlighting challenges facing working mothers. She brought her infant to parliament in 2021 and, two years later, held a press conference with her toddler calling for banning the so-called “no-kid zones” in South Korea.

Yet critics questioned whether the lawmaker had sufficient experience to lead the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family, replacing the current minister, Won Min-kyong, who has worked in the field for decades.
Read more: Korea Policy Chief Who Pushed Leveraged ETFs Quits After Shuffle

Lee’s abrupt reshuffle caught many by surprise, including ministers who were axed at short notice. But the revamp didn’t initially include Lee’s outspoken policy chief, Kim Yong-beom, a figure who attracted attention both for his influence on the president and his backing of policies that have drawn criticism, such as the introduction of leveraged single-stock ETFs.
Kim eventually stepped down following criticism that Lee’s initial overhaul didn’t add up to a meaningful shift in direction.
